stem: A community nurse teaches home fire safety. Which instruction about smoke alarms is best?
options:
A) Test smoke alarms every month and replace units that are more than 10 years old
B) Testing once every 10 years is sufficient if the alarm looks clean
C) Smoke alarms are unnecessary if the home has a fire extinguisher
D) Never place alarms near bedrooms because nighttime waking is harmful
rationales:
A: Correct. Health Canada and NFPA: test monthly; replace alarms more than 10 years old.
B: Incorrect. Monthly testing is required; a 10-year interval is for replacement, not testing.
C: Incorrect. Smoke alarms provide early warning and are not replaced by extinguishers alone.
D: Incorrect. Install alarms in/near bedrooms and on every level, including basement.
topic: Smoke alarms — monthly testing; replace units older than 10 years
source_2_section: Safety Tips; How do I take care of my smoke alarms?

stem: Which home smoke-alarm actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options:
A) Install alarms in bedrooms, outside sleeping areas, and on every level including the basement
B) Test alarms monthly using the test button
C) Replace alarms that fail testing or are more than 10 years old
D) Disable alarms permanently after one nuisance alarm from cooking
E) Create and practise a home fire escape plan
rationales:
A: Correct. Health Canada/NFPA placement guidance for bedrooms, hallways/outside sleeping areas, every level including basement.
B: Correct. Monthly testing is required.
C: Correct. Replace failed or >10-year-old units.
D: Incorrect. Do not permanently disable alarms; investigate false alarms and keep working devices (Health Canada).
E: Correct. Both advise having/practising an escape plan alongside working alarms.
topic: Smoke-alarm SATA — placement, monthly test, replace old units, escape plan

stem: Complete the TeamSTEPPS DESC mnemonic used for conflict resolution.
options: {"template": "D = {B1}; E = {B2}; S = {B3}; C = {B4}.", "blanks": {"B1": [{"key": "B1a", "text": "Describe the specific situation"}, {"key": "B1b", "text": "Deny that conflict exists"}, {"key": "B1c", "text": "Delay all feedback forever"}, {"key": "B1d", "text": "Delegate blame to the client"}], "B2": [{"key": "B2a", "text": "Express concerns about the action"}, {"key": "B2b", "text": "Erase the medical record"}, {"key": "B2c", "text": "Encourage public shaming"}, {"key": "B2d", "text": "Exclude safety concerns"}], "B3": [{"key": "B3a", "text": "Suggest other alternatives"}, {"key": "B3b", "text": "Silence the colleague permanently"}, {"key": "B3c", "text": "Substitute insults for solutions"}, {"key": "B3d", "text": "Skip straight to punishment"}], "B4": [{"key": "B4a", "text": "State the consequences"}, {"key": "B4b", "text": "Conceal outcomes from everyone"}, {"key": "B4c", "text": "Celebrate personal victory"}, {"key": "B4d", "text": "Cancel the conversation mid-sentence without closure"}]}}
rationales:
B1a: Correct. D — Describe the specific situation.
B1b: Incorrect. Denial is not Describe.
B1c: Incorrect. DESC includes timely discussion, not endless delay.
B1d: Incorrect. Clients are not blamed as the Describe step.
B2a: Correct. E — Express concerns about the action.
B2b: Incorrect. Not Express.
B2c: Incorrect. Public shaming is contrary to DESC.
B2d: Incorrect. Safety concerns must be addressed.
B3a: Correct. S — Suggest other alternatives.
B3b: Incorrect. Not Suggest.
B3c: Incorrect. Insults are not alternatives.
B3d: Incorrect. Suggest alternatives before punitive framing.
B4a: Correct. C — Consequences should be stated.
B4b: Incorrect. Consequences are stated, not concealed.
B4c: Incorrect. Focus on what is right, not who wins.
B4d: Incorrect. DESC aims for constructive closure.
topic: NGN cloze — TeamSTEPPS DESC mnemonic letters (Describe, Express, Suggest, Consequences)

stem: A client with heart failure starts spironolactone. Which teaching point is most important to prevent a serious electrolyte complication?
options:
A) Avoid potassium-based salt substitutes and unnecessary potassium supplements
B) Take an extra potassium tablet with each dose of spironolactone
C) Increase bananas and salt substitutes freely because this drug wastes potassium
D) Stop checking laboratory potassium once therapy begins
rationales:
A: Correct. Spironolactone is potassium-sparing; OpenStax cautions against potassium salt substitutes and potassium-rich excess. Merck advises stopping potassium supplements and monitoring serum potassium because of hyperkalemia risk.
B: Incorrect. Adding potassium increases hyperkalemia risk with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists.
C: Incorrect. Unlike loop/thiazide diuretics, potassium-sparing agents do not waste potassium; encouraging salt substitutes is unsafe teaching.
D: Incorrect. Merck: check potassium and creatinine regularly after starting or changing MRA dose.
topic: Spironolactone — avoid potassium salt substitutes / supplements; monitor for hyperkalemia

stem: Complete the teaching plan for a client newly prescribed oral levothyroxine.
options: {"template": "Take levothyroxine in the {B1} on an {B2}, at least {B3} before food. Separate doses from calcium or iron supplements by about {B4}.", "blanks": {"B1": [{"key": "B1a", "text": "morning"}, {"key": "B1b", "text": "late evening with a large meal"}, {"key": "B1c", "text": "afternoon with coffee only"}, {"key": "B1d", "text": "middle of the night after a snack"}], "B2": [{"key": "B2a", "text": "empty stomach"}, {"key": "B2b", "text": "full stomach after a high-fiber meal"}, {"key": "B2c", "text": "empty bladder only"}, {"key": "B2d", "text": "empty schedule with no timing guidance"}], "B3": [{"key": "B3a", "text": "30 to 60 minutes"}, {"key": "B3b", "text": "5 seconds"}, {"key": "B3c", "text": "12 hours"}, {"key": "B3d", "text": "3 days"}], "B4": [{"key": "B4a", "text": "4 hours"}, {"key": "B4b", "text": "30 seconds"}, {"key": "B4c", "text": "1 week"}, {"key": "B4d", "text": "no separation needed"}]}}
rationales:
B1a: Correct. OpenStax and DailyMed: take in the morning.
B1b: Incorrect. Evening with a large meal decreases absorption.
B1c: Incorrect. Caffeinated fluids can interfere with absorption.
B1d: Incorrect. Not standard dosing guidance.
B2a: Correct. Empty stomach improves absorption (OpenStax; DailyMed).
B2b: Incorrect. Food decreases absorption.
B2c: Incorrect. Bladder status is irrelevant to absorption teaching.
B2d: Incorrect. Timing relative to food matters.
B3a: Correct. At least one-half to one hour before food (OpenStax; DailyMed).
B3b: Incorrect. Far too short.
B3c: Incorrect. Excessively long and not the labeled interval.
B3d: Incorrect. Not a dosing interval for this teaching point.
B4a: Correct. Separate from calcium/iron by about 4 hours (OpenStax; DailyMed).
B4b: Incorrect. Inadequate separation.
B4c: Incorrect. Unnecessarily long.
B4d: Incorrect. Calcium/iron decrease absorption.
topic: Levothyroxine — morning empty stomach; separate from calcium/iron
source_2_publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine — DailyMed

stem: A client takes combination cold remedies that contain acetaminophen plus as-needed acetaminophen tablets for pain. Which instruction is the priority safety teaching?
options:
A) Count acetaminophen from all products and do not exceed 4000 mg in 24 hours to reduce liver injury risk
B) Acetaminophen from cold products does not count toward the daily total
C) Unlimited acetaminophen is safe because it has no hepatic risk
D) Only aspirin-containing products require daily dose limits
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: tally all sources; limit 4000 mg/24 h because of liver injury risk. Merck: acetaminophen poisoning causes hepatotoxicity; many OTC products contain APAP.
B: Incorrect. Combination products are a common hidden source of acetaminophen.
C: Incorrect. Overuse can cause serious hepatotoxicity.
D: Incorrect. Acetaminophen has a specific daily ceiling related to hepatotoxicity.
topic: Acetaminophen — count all sources; max 4000 mg/24 hours
source_1_section: Check for All Sources of Acetaminophen

stem: An adult presents several hours after a large intentional acetaminophen overdose. Complete the bowtie.
options: {"conditions": [{"key": "K1", "text": "Acetaminophen poisoning with risk of hepatotoxicity"}, {"key": "K2", "text": "Opioid overdose with pinpoint pupils alone"}, {"key": "K3", "text": "Simple foodborne gastroenteritis without toxin risk"}, {"key": "K4", "text": "Hypoglycemia as the sole diagnosis"}], "actions": [{"key": "A1", "text": "Obtain timed serum acetaminophen level and initiate N-acetylcysteine per protocol when indicated"}, {"key": "A2", "text": "Advise the client that no antidote exists and discharge immediately without evaluation"}, {"key": "A3", "text": "Support airway/circulation and escalate for hepatotoxicity monitoring as ordered"}, {"key": "A4", "text": "Give additional acetaminophen to “compete” with the overdose"}, {"key": "A5", "text": "Delay all care until liver failure is irreversible"}], "parameters": [{"key": "P1", "text": "Serial liver enzymes / clinical hepatotoxicity course"}, {"key": "P2", "text": "Response to N-acetylcysteine and ongoing mental status/vitals"}, {"key": "P3", "text": "Whether the client likes the hospital cafeteria menu"}, {"key": "P4", "text": "Single blood pressure only at triage with no reassessment"}, {"key": "P5", "text": "Room paint colour preference"}]}
rationales:
K1: Correct. Merck: acetaminophen poisoning risks hepatotoxicity; treat with N-acetylcysteine.
K2: Incorrect. Opioid overdose is a different toxidrome.
K3: Incorrect. Early GI symptoms may occur, but this is a toxic ingestion scenario.
K4: Incorrect. Hypoglycemia alone does not explain this ingestion history.
A1: Correct. Severity predicted by serum levels; NAC prevents/minimizes hepatotoxicity (Merck).
A2: Incorrect. An antidote (N-acetylcysteine) exists and early care matters.
A3: Correct. Supportive care and monitoring are required alongside antidote therapy.
A4: Incorrect. More acetaminophen worsens toxicity.
A5: Incorrect. Prompt treatment is required.
P1: Correct. Hepatotoxicity evolves over 1–3 days; monitor liver injury course.
P2: Correct. Evaluate antidote response and clinical status.
P3: Incorrect. Not a clinical parameter for toxicity care.
P4: Incorrect. Ongoing reassessment is required.
P5: Incorrect. Irrelevant.
topic: Acetaminophen overdose — N-acetylcysteine and hepatotoxicity monitoring
source_2_section: Check for All Sources of Acetaminophen

stem: A hospitalized client has sudden vomiting and watery diarrhea consistent with norovirus gastroenteritis. Which infection-control action is most appropriate?
options:
A) Place the client on Contact Precautions and wear gown and gloves on room entry
B) Use Standard Precautions only with no gown or gloves for diarrhea care
C) Use Airborne Precautions with an N95 for all staff regardless of symptoms
D) Stop all hand hygiene because norovirus is not transmitted on hands
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC norovirus guidance: Contact Precautions; gowns and gloves on entry. OpenStax supports PPE/gown-gloves for contact transmission risks.
B: Incorrect. CDC updated norovirus care to Contact + Standard, not Standard alone.
C: Incorrect. Routine Airborne isolation is not the norovirus recommendation.
D: Incorrect. Hand hygiene is essential; CDC promotes adherence during outbreaks.
topic: Norovirus — Contact Precautions with gown and gloves

source_1_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_1_section: Patient Cohorting and Isolation Precautions; Personal Protective Equipment

stem: A nurse finishes care for a client on transmission-based precautions while wearing gown, gloves, eye protection, and a respirator. Which action is correct when leaving the room?
options:
A) Remove all PPE except the respirator before exiting, then perform hand hygiene; remove the respirator after leaving
B) Walk into the hallway still wearing contaminated gloves and gown to chart at the desk
C) Remove the respirator inside the room first, then leave wearing the contaminated gown
D) Skip hand hygiene after PPE removal if gloves looked clean
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: doff all PPE except a respirator before exiting, then hand hygiene. CDC PPE sequence: remove PPE before exiting except a respirator if worn.
B: Incorrect. Contaminated PPE should not be worn into clean areas.
C: Incorrect. Respirator is removed after leaving; gown/gloves are removed before exit.
D: Incorrect. Hand hygiene is required immediately after PPE removal.
topic: PPE doffing — remove PPE except respirator before exiting; hand hygiene
client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
source_2_title: Sequence for Putting On and Removing PPE
source_2_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

stem: Parents of a 2-month-old ask how to place the infant for sleep to reduce SIDS risk. Which instruction is correct?
options:
A) Place the baby on the back for every sleep, including naps and nighttime
B) Place the baby prone for all sleeps because back sleeping increases choking
C) Alternate side-lying and prone nightly without using the back position
D) Sit the baby upright in a car seat overnight as the primary sleep space
rationales:
A: Correct. CPS Caring for Kids and CDC: always place baby on the back for every sleep.
B: Incorrect. Prone sleep increases SIDS risk; CPS notes even babies who spit up are safer on their backs.
C: Incorrect. Back sleeping for every sleep is the key recommendation.
D: Incorrect. Sitting devices are not recommended as primary sleep spaces.
topic: Infant safe sleep — back to sleep for every sleep
jurisdiction_note: Stem teaching aligns with CPS Caring for Kids and CDC/AAP-concordant back-to-sleep guidance; Canadian primary citation used.

stem: A nurse teaches parents of a newborn about safe sleep. Which actions are indicated?
options: {"columns": ["Indicated", "Not indicated"], "rows": [{"key": "R1", "text": "Place the infant supine (on the back) for every sleep"}, {"key": "R2", "text": "Use a firm, flat crib/bassinet mattress with a fitted sheet only"}, {"key": "R3", "text": "Keep soft bedding, pillows, bumper pads, and soft toys out of the sleep space"}, {"key": "R4", "text": "Encourage routine bed sharing on an adult mattress with pillows and blankets"}]}

R1: Indicated. CPS and CDC: back for every sleep.
R2: Indicated. Firm, flat surface with fitted sheet only (CPS; CDC).
R3: Indicated. No loose soft items in the sleep area (CPS; CDC).
R4: Not indicated. Bed sharing increases SIDS/suffocation risk; room sharing without bed sharing is preferred.

stem: An unsensitized Rh-negative postpartum client delivered an Rh-positive newborn 6 hours ago. Which action is the priority related to Rh sensitization prevention?
options:
A) Administer Rho(D) immune globulin as ordered within 72 hours of delivery
B) Withhold Rh immune globulin because it is never given after birth
C) Give Rh immune globulin only if the newborn is also Rh-negative
D) Delay Rh immune globulin until the next pregnancy begins
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck postpartum care and OpenStax maternal-newborn: give Rho(D) immune globulin within 72 hours when an Rh-negative mother delivers an Rh-positive infant and is not sensitized.
B: Incorrect. Postpartum dosing is a key prevention step.
C: Incorrect. Postpartum dose is indicated when the newborn is Rh-positive (or type unknown per teaching), not when both are Rh-negative.
D: Incorrect. Waiting until the next pregnancy misses the postpartum prevention window.
topic: Rho(D) immune globulin within 72 hours after Rh-negative mother delivers Rh-positive newborn
source_2_title: 20.3 Nursing Care During the Postpartum Period

stem: Which statement about the Apgar score is accurate?
options:
A) It is typically assigned at 1 and 5 minutes to describe the newborn’s condition at birth and does not determine an individual newborn’s long-term neurologic prognosis
B) It replaces the need for any neonatal resuscitation assessment before 1 minute of life
C) A single Apgar of 10 at birth guarantees lifelong normal neurodevelopment for every infant
D) Apgar scoring is performed only at hospital discharge, not immediately after birth
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: describes condition at birth; does not determine individual prognosis; usually at 1 and 5 minutes. OpenStax: assessed at 1 and 5 minutes; does not predict neurologic outcome/mortality/morbidity for the neonate.
B: Incorrect. Merck: Apgar is not the tool that guides resuscitation; initial resuscitation steps occur before 1 minute.
C: Incorrect. Neither source treats Apgar as a lifelong prognosis guarantee.
D: Incorrect. Scoring is done right after birth at standard intervals.
topic: Apgar score — 1 and 5 minutes; describes condition; not individual neurologic prognosis

stem: An adolescent with anorexia nervosa has rapid severe weight loss, symptomatic hypotension, and extreme bradycardia. Which action is the priority?
options:
A) Support prompt medical stabilization/hospitalization for weight restoration and correction of dangerous physiologic instability
B) Discharge home immediately with advice to exercise more to “build appetite”
C) Ignore vital-sign abnormalities because anorexia never has medical complications
D) Start unsupervised rapid overfeeding at home without monitoring
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: life-saving short-term intervention may be required for symptomatic hypotension, extreme bradycardia/arrhythmia, severe/rapid weight loss; consider hospitalization. OpenStax: hospitalization when medical monitoring is required; refeeding needs careful monitoring.
B: Incorrect. Extreme exercise and discharge with instability are unsafe.
C: Incorrect. Bradycardia, hypotension, and electrolyte complications are recognized.
D: Incorrect. Rapid unsupervised refeeding risks refeeding syndrome; medical monitoring is needed.
topic: Anorexia nervosa — hospitalize/stabilize for extreme bradycardia, hypotension, severe weight loss

stem: A client with anorexia nervosa is beginning supervised nutritional rehabilitation. Which nursing actions are indicated?
options: {"columns": ["Indicated", "Not indicated"], "rows": [{"key": "R1", "text": "Support slow, measured oral intake with monitoring for refeeding complications"}, {"key": "R2", "text": "Monitor vital signs and collaborate on medical complications (e.g., bradycardia, electrolyte shifts)"}, {"key": "R3", "text": "Provide emotional support and avoid shaming about eating"}, {"key": "R4", "text": "Encourage secretive binge–purge behaviours as “coping”"}]}
rationales:
R1: Indicated. OpenStax: slow measured meals with careful monitoring; refeeding syndrome risk. Merck: nutritional supplementation with clear goals.
R2: Indicated. Merck highlights bradycardia/electrolyte/arrhythmia risks; OpenStax notes medical monitoring needs.
R3: Indicated. OpenStax emphasizes supportive therapeutic approaches during rehabilitation.
R4: Not indicated. Encouraging disordered behaviours contradicts treatment goals.
topic: Anorexia refeeding — supervised nutrition, monitor complications; no shame or purge encouragement
source_2_section: Treatment of Anorexia Nervosa; Complications of Anorexia Nervosa

stem: The nurse prepares to ambulate an unsteady adult client with a gait belt. Which action is correct?
options:
A) Apply the gait belt snugly over clothing around the waist so fingers can fit underneath, and ensure nonskid footwear
B) Apply the gait belt directly on bare skin as tightly as possible with no finger space
C) Skip footwear because the belt alone prevents falls
D) Place the belt loosely around the chest over the breasts
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: place gait belt snugly over a layer of clothing with two fingers fitting between belt and client; ensure nonslip footwear. Open RN (NCBI): apply gait belt on top of clothing/gown and snugly over clothing with proper footwear such as nonslip socks or shoes.
B: Incorrect. Belt goes over clothing to protect skin; it should allow finger space for safe hold, not maximum tightness on bare skin.
C: Incorrect. Both sources emphasize nonskid/nonslip footwear before ambulation or transfer.
D: Incorrect. Gait belts are placed around the waist, not loosely around the chest.
topic: Gait belt — snug over clothing; fingers fit underneath; nonskid footwear

stem: A client with left leg weakness is learning to walk with a single-point cane. Which teaching point is correct?
options:
A) Hold the cane in the right (stronger) hand so it moves with the weaker left leg
B) Always hold the cane in the left hand next to the weak leg
C) Carry the cane in both hands in front of the body
D) Use the cane only when sitting, never when walking
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: hold the cane in the opposite hand of the weak or painful limb; cane moves with the affected leg. Open RN Nursing Assistant: place the cane on the stronger side.
B: Incorrect. Holding the cane on the weak side reduces the widened base of support that opposite-hand use provides.
C: Incorrect. A single cane is held in one hand for balance and support during gait.
D: Incorrect. Canes are assistive devices for ambulation/balance when walking.
topic: Cane — hold on stronger (opposite) side of weak limb

stem: An older adult in a monitored unit becomes agitated amid continuous alarms, bright lights, and frequent interruptions. For each intervention, indicate whether it is Indicated or Not indicated to reduce sensory overload.
options: {"columns": ["Indicated", "Not indicated"], "rows": [{"key": "R1", "text": "Dim lights and reduce unnecessary noise when safe"}, {"key": "R2", "text": "Offer earplugs or headphones to limit auditory overload"}, {"key": "R3", "text": "Keep the environment continuously loud to maintain alertness"}, {"key": "R4", "text": "Provide a calmer, quieter setting with orientation cues as able"}]}
rationales:
R1: Indicated. OpenStax: dim lights and reduce noise levels to minimize sensory input.
R2: Indicated. OpenStax: provide earplugs or headphones; ICU exemplar used earplugs/noise-canceling headphones.
R3: Not indicated. Increasing noise worsens overload; Merck delirium care uses a quiet, stable environment.
R4: Indicated. OpenStax supports calming supportive environment; Merck: stable, quiet, well-lit setting with orientation cues.
topic: NGN matrix — sensory overload: reduce noise/lights; earplugs; quiet supportive environment

stem: An infant is admitted with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) bronchiolitis. Which isolation plan is appropriate?
options:
A) Contact Precautions for the duration of illness, with gown and gloves for patient-care contact
B) Airborne Precautions only in a negative-pressure room with N95 for all staff
C) No transmission-based precautions beyond Standard Precautions
D) Droplet Precautions only until the first afebrile hour
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC Appendix A: RSV in infants, young children, and immunocompromised adults — Contact + Standard for duration of illness. OpenStax: Contact Precautions use gown and gloves for direct/indirect contact pathogens.
B: Incorrect. CDC lists Contact (not Airborne) for RSV in this population.
C: Incorrect. Transmission-based Contact Precautions are indicated for RSV in infants/young children.
D: Incorrect. CDC duration is duration of illness for Contact Precautions, not a one-hour fever rule.
topic: RSV — Contact Precautions for duration of illness (infants/young children)
client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
source_1_title: Appendix A: Type and Duration of Precautions
source_1_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

stem: A school-age child is admitted with widespread impetigo and started on effective antimicrobial therapy. Which precaution guidance is correct?
options:
A) Use Contact Precautions until 24 hours after initiation of effective therapy
B) Use Airborne Precautions for 7 days after the rash appears
C) Discontinue all precautions immediately when therapy is ordered, before the first dose
D) Use only Droplet Precautions without gown or gloves
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC Appendix A: Impetigo — Contact + Standard until 24 hours after initiation of effective therapy. OpenStax: Contact Precautions include gown and gloves for contact-transmitted infections.
B: Incorrect. Impetigo is not managed with Airborne Precautions per CDC Appendix A.
C: Incorrect. CDC continues Contact Precautions until 24 hours after effective therapy starts.
D: Incorrect. CDC specifies Contact Precautions for impetigo.
topic: Impetigo — Contact Precautions until 24 hours after effective therapy
client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
source_1_title: Appendix A: Type and Duration of Precautions
source_1_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

stem: A client will self-inject enoxaparin from a prefilled syringe at home. Which instruction is essential?
options:
A) Do not expel the air bubble before injection; inject subcutaneously in the abdomen and do not rub the site
B) Expel all air from the syringe, then inject intramuscularly into the deltoid
C) Inject through clothing into any bruised area to hide the site
D) Massage the site vigorously for 5 minutes after each dose
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax and DailyMed Lovenox: avoid ejecting/expelling the air bubble; inject into abdominal wall sites; do not rub after injection.
B: Incorrect. Expelling the air bubble can lose drug; route is subcutaneous, not IM deltoid.
C: Incorrect. Both sources: do not inject through clothing or into bruised/scarred skin.
D: Incorrect. Rubbing increases bruising risk; teaching is not to rub.
topic: Enoxaparin — do not expel air bubble; subcutaneous abdomen; do not rub
source_2_publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine — DailyMed

stem: A client starts lisinopril for hypertension. Complete the teaching using the drop-down choices.
options: {"template": "Teach the client that a serious adverse effect of ACE inhibitors is {B1}. If swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat occurs, the client should {B2} and {B3}. ACE inhibitors are also {B4} in pregnancy.", "blanks": {"B1": [{"key": "B1a", "text": "angioedema"}, {"key": "B1b", "text": "photosensitivity only"}, {"key": "B1c", "text": "orange urine"}, {"key": "B1d", "text": "excessive hair growth"}], "B2": [{"key": "B2a", "text": "stop the ACE inhibitor and seek emergency care"}, {"key": "B2b", "text": "double the next dose"}, {"key": "B2c", "text": "switch to a potassium supplement"}, {"key": "B2d", "text": "wait one week before calling anyone"}], "B3": [{"key": "B3a", "text": "treat airway swelling as an emergency because oropharyngeal angioedema can be fatal"}, {"key": "B3b", "text": "ignore mild tongue swelling"}, {"key": "B3c", "text": "restart the drug once swelling decreases slightly"}, {"key": "B3d", "text": "take an extra dose with food"}], "B4": [{"key": "B4a", "text": "contraindicated"}, {"key": "B4b", "text": "preferred first-line"}, {"key": "B4c", "text": "required"}, {"key": "B4d", "text": "harmless"}]}}
rationales:
B1a: Correct. OpenStax and Merck list angioedema as a serious ACE inhibitor adverse effect.
B1b: Incorrect. Photosensitivity is not the key ACEI safety teaching here.
B1c: Incorrect. Not an ACEI hallmark adverse effect.
B1d: Incorrect. Not associated with ACE inhibitors.
B2a: Correct. Prior angioedema is a contraindication; stop the drug and seek urgent care for swelling.
B2b: Incorrect. Increasing the dose worsens risk.
B2c: Incorrect. Potassium supplements increase hyperkalemia risk with ACEIs.
B2d: Incorrect. Airway-threatening angioedema requires immediate care.
B3a: Correct. Merck: angioedema affecting the oropharynx can be fatal.
B3b: Incorrect. Tongue/airway swelling is an emergency.
B3c: Incorrect. History of ACEI angioedema contraindicates rechallenge.
B3d: Incorrect. Not a treatment for angioedema.
B4a: Correct. OpenStax and Merck: ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy.
B4b: Incorrect. ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy, not preferred first-line then.
B4c: Incorrect. Pregnancy is a contraindication; ACE inhibitors are not required therapy in pregnancy.
B4d: Incorrect. Fetal harm risk means they are not harmless in pregnancy.
topic: NGN cloze — ACE inhibitor angioedema: stop drug; seek emergency care for face/tongue swelling

stem: A parent of a 6-month-old with gastroenteritis asks which finding means the infant needs prompt medical evaluation for dehydration. Which finding should the nurse emphasize?
options:
A) Sunken soft spot (fontanelle) and sunken eyes
B) One loose stool with normal wet diapers and tears
C) Brief spit-up after feeding with a moist mouth
D) Occasional hiccups after burping
rationales:
A: Correct. CPS Caring for Kids lists sunken fontanelle and sunken eyes among dehydration warning signs needing medical advice. Merck: moderate dehydration includes sunken eyes and fontanelles.
B: Incorrect. CPS notes healthy children may have an occasional loose stool without dehydration danger when other signs are absent.
C: Incorrect. Isolated spit-up with moist mucosa is not a dehydration red flag.
D: Incorrect. Hiccups are not a dehydration indicator.
topic: Infant dehydration — sunken fontanelle/eyes are warning signs needing prompt care
source_1_title: Dehydration and diarrhea in children: Prevention and treatment
source_1_publisher: Canadian Paediatric Society — Caring for Kids
source_1_section: What are the signs of dehydration?
source_2_section: Symptoms and Signs of Dehydration in Children

stem: A community nurse teaches caregivers of toddlers living in aging housing about lead exposure. Which statement is the priority teaching point?
options:
A) A blood lead test is the best way to know if a child has been exposed; peeling paint dust in older homes is an important risk
B) Lead exposure always causes an obvious bright red rash, so testing is unnecessary if the skin looks normal
C) Only outdoor soil matters; indoor paint dust cannot affect children
D) Home sanding of old paint is the safest way to remove lead without professional advice
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC: blood lead test is the best way to detect exposure; children often have no obvious symptoms; older housing paint dust is a key source. Health Canada: babies/small children ingest household dust including from lead-based paints; older homes more likely painted with lead-based paint.
B: Incorrect. CDC: most children with lead in blood have no obvious immediate symptoms.
C: Incorrect. Health Canada and CDC describe indoor paint dust as an important pathway for young children.
D: Incorrect. Health Canada warns mechanical removal/sanding can release hazardous lead dust.
topic: Childhood lead — blood test is how exposure is detected; older housing paint dust risk
jurisdiction_note: Blood lead testing as detection method is concordant; housing paint eras differ by country (US often cites pre-1978; Health Canada emphasizes older pre-1960 homes)—item tests testing + paint-dust risk without a contested year cutoff.
source_1_title: Testing for Lead Poisoning in Children
source_1_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_1_section: Why get tested / Who should be screened

stem: A client begins crying while describing fear about a new cancer diagnosis. Which nurse response is nontherapeutic?
options:
A) "Let's not talk about that—tell me what you want for lunch instead."
B) "This sounds frightening. What worries you most right now?"
C) Sitting quietly for a moment, then saying, "I'm here with you; go on when you are ready."
D) "Help me understand what the diagnosis means for you."
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax PMH: changing the subject is a barrier that can feel insensitive. Open RN Nursing Assistant: changing the subject blocks communication and conveys lack of empathy.
B: Incorrect. Open-ended exploration of feelings is therapeutic.
C: Incorrect. Silence/presence supporting the client is therapeutic.
D: Incorrect. Clarifying/exploring meaning is therapeutic.
topic: Therapeutic communication — abruptly changing the subject is nontherapeutic

stem: Before a planned invasive procedure in Ontario, the nurse reviews whether consent is informed. Which set of information must have been provided for consent to be considered informed under CNO guidance?
options:
A) Nature of the treatment, expected benefits, material risks and side effects, alternative courses of action, and likely consequences of not having the treatment
B) Only the scheduled time of the procedure, without discussion of risks or alternatives
C) A guarantee that no adverse effects are possible
D) The nurse’s personal preference about whether the client should proceed
rationales:
A: Correct. CNO Consent guideline: informed consent requires information a reasonable person would need, including nature, expected benefits, material risks/side effects, alternatives, and likely consequences of not having the treatment.
B: Incorrect. Scheduling alone does not meet informed-consent content requirements.
C: Incorrect. Material risks must be disclosed; guarantees of no adverse effects are not the standard.
D: Incorrect. Consent must be voluntary and free of misrepresentation; the nurse’s personal preference is not the required content.
topic: CNO Consent — informed consent includes nature, benefits, risks, alternatives, consequences of refusal
jurisdiction_note: CNO Consent practice guideline (July 2025) interpreting Ontario HCCA requirements for informed consent.

stem: A hospitalized adult develops fever, confusion, tachycardia, and hypotension concerning for septic shock. Complete the bowtie: most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
options: {"conditions": [{"key": "K1", "text": "Allergic rhinitis"}, {"key": "K2", "text": "Septic shock from dysregulated response to infection with hypoperfusion"}, {"key": "K3", "text": "Simple tension headache"}, {"key": "K4", "text": "Uncomplicated localized bruise"}], "actions": [{"key": "A1", "text": "Obtain cultures and start prompt broad-spectrum antibiotics"}, {"key": "A2", "text": "Begin aggressive IV fluid resuscitation per sepsis protocol"}, {"key": "A3", "text": "Delay all fluids until cultures return in 72 hours"}, {"key": "A4", "text": "Discharge home without treatment"}, {"key": "A5", "text": "Give only oral acetaminophen and reassess next week"}], "parameters": [{"key": "P1", "text": "Blood pressure / MAP and perfusion response after fluids (and pressors if needed)"}, {"key": "P2", "text": "Serum lactate and ongoing organ perfusion indicators (e.g., urine output)"}, {"key": "P3", "text": "Fashion preference for hospital gown color"}, {"key": "P4", "text": "Favorite television channel"}, {"key": "P5", "text": "Number of visitors on the unit whiteboard only"}]}
rationales:
K1: Incorrect. Allergic rhinitis does not explain hypotension and organ hypoperfusion.
K2: Correct. Merck/OpenStax: septic shock is sepsis with persistent hypotension/hypoperfusion related to infection.
K3: Incorrect. Headache alone does not match this shock picture.
K4: Incorrect. Localized bruise is not systemic septic shock.
A1: Correct. Merck: collect cultures then give prompt empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics; OpenStax one-hour bundle includes cultures and antibiotics.
A2: Correct. Merck and OpenStax: aggressive IV fluid resuscitation is foundational; vasopressors if hypotension persists.
A3: Incorrect. Delaying fluids for culture results increases mortality risk.
A4: Incorrect. Septic shock requires urgent inpatient/ICU-level care.
A5: Incorrect. Antipyretic alone is not sepsis resuscitation.
P1: Correct. OpenStax targets MAP ~65 mm Hg with fluids/vasopressors; monitor perfusion response.
P2: Correct. OpenStax bundle includes lactate; Merck monitors lactate and urine output as perfusion markers.
P3: Incorrect. Irrelevant to septic shock monitoring.
P4: Incorrect. Irrelevant.
P5: Incorrect. Irrelevant.
topic: NGN bowtie — septic shock: early fluids, cultures, antibiotics; monitor lactate/perfusion

stem: Which teaching points about childhood lead exposure are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options:
A) A blood lead test is the best way to determine whether a child has been exposed
B) Children may have lead in their blood without obvious immediate symptoms
C) Peeling lead-based paint dust in older homes is an important exposure pathway for young children
D) Dry sanding old lead paint at home is the preferred first action for families
E) Young children are at higher risk because of hand-to-mouth behavior and floor-level exposure
F) Lead exposure is impossible if the child has never left the city limits
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC: blood lead test is the best way to know exposure.
B: Correct. CDC: most children with lead in blood have no obvious immediate symptoms.
C: Correct. CDC and Health Canada identify paint dust in older homes as a key pathway.
D: Incorrect. Health Canada: mechanical removal/sanding can release hazardous lead dust.
E: Correct. Health Canada: hand-to-mouth activity and low breathing zone increase risk.
F: Incorrect. Lead sources exist indoors (paint, dust, products) regardless of city limits.
topic: Lead exposure teaching SATA — blood test; older paint dust; avoid sanding; children often asymptomatic
jurisdiction_note: Concordant prevention teaching; year cutoffs for lead paint differ by country and are not keyed.
source_1_title: Testing for Lead Poisoning in Children
source_1_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_2_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

stem: On the first postoperative day after major abdominal surgery, which nursing action best helps prevent deep vein thrombosis?
options:
A) Promote early and frequent ambulation as soon as the client is cleared to mobilize
B) Keep the client on strict bed rest for one week without leg movement
C) Limit all fluids to concentrate the blood
D) Elevate only the head of the bed and avoid moving the legs
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: early and frequent ambulation stimulates blood flow and avoids stasis. Merck DVT prevention: ambulation and prevention of immobility are core preventive measures.
B: Incorrect. Immobility increases DVT risk.
C: Incorrect. Fluid restriction to concentrate blood is not a DVT prevention strategy.
D: Incorrect. Leg movement/ambulation is needed to reduce venous stasis.
topic: Postoperative DVT prevention — early and frequent ambulation

stem: The nurse fits axillary crutches for a client with a non-weight-bearing lower extremity injury. Which teaching point is correct?
options:
A) Keep about two finger widths between the axilla and the crutch pad, and bear weight through the hands on the handgrips
B) Rest the axilla firmly on the crutch pads so the armpits carry most of the body weight
C) Adjust the crutches so the pads sit tightly against the armpits with no space
D) Hold both crutches in one hand and hop without using the handgrips
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: axillary crutch should be two fingers distant between axilla and pad; weight focused on hand grips, not armpits, to prevent axillary nerve damage. StatPearls: shoulder pad about 2 inches (2 finger widths) below axilla; do not rest axilla on shoulder pad (crutch palsy risk).
B: Incorrect. Resting weight on the axilla risks brachial plexus/crutch palsy; weight belongs on the hands.
C: Incorrect. Both sources require space under the axilla, not a tight fit against the armpit.
D: Incorrect. Proper crutch gait uses handgrips with crutches positioned for support.
topic: Axillary crutches — two-finger space under axilla; weight on handgrips not armpits

stem: During colostomy pouch care, which stoma finding should the nurse report to the provider immediately?
options:
A) A moist, dark pink to red stoma
B) A purple or black stoma
C) Mild postoperative stoma edema that is expected to shrink over weeks
D) A small amount of mucus on the stoma surface
rationales:
A: Incorrect. OpenStax and MedlinePlus describe a healthy stoma as moist and pink or red.
B: Correct. OpenStax: bluish, purple, black, or pale stomas should be reported. MedlinePlus: contact the provider if the stoma turns purple, black, or white.
C: Incorrect. OpenStax/MedlinePlus note expected postoperative swelling that shrinks over weeks.
D: Incorrect. MedlinePlus notes mucus may be seen on a healthy stoma.
topic: Ostomy stoma — moist pink/red healthy; purple/black report promptly
source_2_publisher: MedlinePlus / U.S. National Library of Medicine
source_2_section: About Your Stoma / When to Call the Doctor

stem: A client has a new ileostomy. For each nursing action, specify whether it is Indicated or Not indicated.
options: {"columns": ["Indicated", "Not indicated"], "rows": [{"key": "R1", "text": "Document that a moist pink-to-red stoma is an expected healthy finding"}, {"key": "R2", "text": "Notify the provider promptly if the stoma becomes purple or black"}, {"key": "R3", "text": "Reassure the client that a dry, pale stoma is preferred over a moist one"}, {"key": "R4", "text": "Ignore peristomal skin redness because leakage never irritates skin"}]}
rationales:
R1: Indicated. OpenStax/MedlinePlus: healthy stoma is moist pink/red.
R2: Indicated. Both sources: purple/black color change warrants provider contact.
R3: Not indicated. Dry/pale is abnormal and should be reported, not preferred.
R4: Not indicated. OpenStax: leakage/adhesive can irritate peristomal skin; breakdown should be addressed/reported.
topic: NGN matrix — ostomy stoma assessment actions indicated vs not

stem: An adolescent is admitted with mumps parotitis. Which isolation plan is appropriate?
options:
A) Droplet plus Standard Precautions until 5 days after onset of parotid swelling
B) Airborne Precautions alone for 24 hours after antibiotics begin
C) Contact Precautions only, discontinued when fever resolves
D) No transmission-based precautions because mumps is not contagious after symptoms begin
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC Appendix A: mumps Droplet + Standard until 5 days after onset of swelling. Merck: isolate 5 days from parotitis onset; CDC recommends standard and droplet precautions for 5 days after parotitis onset.
B: Incorrect. Mumps is managed with droplet, not airborne-only, precautions; antibiotics are not the keyed duration trigger.
C: Incorrect. Contact-only and fever resolution are not the CDC/Merck isolation standard for mumps.
D: Incorrect. Contagiousness continues around symptom onset; isolation for 5 days after swelling is required.
topic: Mumps — Droplet + Standard precautions until 5 days after parotitis onset
client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
source_1_title: Appendix A: Type and Duration of Precautions
source_1_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

stem: Complete the following for inpatient mumps care.
options: {"template": "Place the client on {B1} Precautions and continue isolation until {B2} after the onset of parotid swelling.", "blanks": {"B1": [{"key": "B1a", "text": "Airborne"}, {"key": "B1b", "text": "Droplet"}, {"key": "B1c", "text": "Contact only"}], "B2": [{"key": "B2a", "text": "24 hours"}, {"key": "B2b", "text": "5 days"}, {"key": "B2c", "text": "21 days"}]}}

B1b: Correct. CDC/Merck: droplet (with Standard) precautions for mumps.

B2a: Incorrect. Duration is 5 days after swelling onset, not 24 hours.
B2b: Correct. CDC Appendix A and Merck: isolate until 5 days after onset of swelling/parotitis.
B2c: Incorrect. 21 days is not the keyed post-parotitis isolation duration.

stem: A nurse has just inserted a nasogastric feeding tube. What is the priority action before initiating the first feeding?
options:
A) Verify tube placement with x-ray imaging before use
B) Begin the feeding immediately after feeling resistance during insertion
C) Rely only on air insufflation (whoosh test) without imaging
D) Clamp the tube for 24 hours before any verification
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: placement must be verified via x-ray imaging prior to use. Open RN Nursing Advanced Skills: placement must be verified immediately after insertion by an X-ray before use.
B: Incorrect. Resistance alone does not confirm gastric placement; feeding into a misplaced tube risks aspiration.
C: Incorrect. Open RN: air auscultation (whoosh) is unreliable and should no longer be used to verify placement.
D: Incorrect. Verification is needed before use; an arbitrary 24-hour delay without confirmation is unsafe.
topic: Nasogastric tube — verify placement by x-ray before initial use/feeding
source_2_title: Chapter 5 Insert Nasogastric and Feeding Tubes

stem: When interpreting the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) after head trauma, which statement is correct?
options:
A) A combined score less than 8 is typically regarded as coma
B) The highest possible combined GCS score is 8
C) GCS scores are based only on pupil size, not eye/verbal/motor responses
D) A score of 15 always means the client requires immediate intubation
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: combined scores < 8 are typically regarded as coma. OpenStax: GCS score lower than 8 indicates problems with consciousness / monitor for increased ICP.
B: Incorrect. OpenStax: highest possible GCS score is 15.
C: Incorrect. Both sources describe eye opening, verbal, and motor response components.
D: Incorrect. 15 is the maximum (least impaired) score; it does not itself mandate intubation.
topic: Glasgow Coma Scale — combined score < 8 typically indicates coma
source_1_title: Overview of Coma and Impaired Consciousness
source_1_section: Neurologic examination / Glasgow Coma Scale table

stem: Which findings are characteristic of Cushing syndrome? Select all that apply.
options:
A) Facial rounding (moon face)
B) Dorsal cervical fat pad (buffalo hump) with truncal obesity
C) Purplish abdominal striae
D) Diffuse bronze hyperpigmentation as the only expected skin change from primary adrenal failure
E) Central obesity with relatively slender extremities
F) Acute hypothermia with areflexia as the defining presentation
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck and OpenStax describe moon face / facial rounding.
B: Correct. Merck: truncal obesity with dorsal cervical fat pads (buffalo hump). OpenStax: fatty deposits between the shoulders (buffalo hump).
C: Correct. Merck lists striae; OpenStax notes purplish striae.
D: Incorrect. Bronze hyperpigmentation is classic for primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison), not Cushing.
E: Correct. Merck: truncal obesity with slender distal extremities; OpenStax: central obesity with thin extremities.
F: Incorrect. Extreme hypothermia with areflexia describes myxedema coma, not Cushing.
topic: Cushing syndrome cues SATA — moon face, buffalo hump, truncal obesity, striae
source_1_section: Symptoms and Signs of Cushing Syndrome

stem: A client with long-standing hypothyroidism presents unresponsive with severe hypothermia and hypoventilation. Complete the bowtie: most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
options: {"conditions": [{"key": "K1", "text": "Thyroid storm"}, {"key": "K2", "text": "Myxedema coma"}, {"key": "K3", "text": "Adrenal crisis from abrupt steroid withdrawal only"}, {"key": "K4", "text": "Serotonin syndrome"}], "actions": [{"key": "A1", "text": "Administer intravenous thyroid hormone (T4/T3) as ordered"}, {"key": "A2", "text": "Give glucocorticoids as ordered while adrenal insufficiency is not yet excluded"}, {"key": "A3", "text": "Rapidly rewarm with aggressive external heating to reverse hypotension"}, {"key": "A4", "text": "Start high-dose oral methimazole immediately as first-line therapy"}, {"key": "A5", "text": "Encourage ambulation without airway or temperature support"}], "parameters": [{"key": "P1", "text": "Core temperature (avoid missing severe hypothermia)"}, {"key": "P2", "text": "Airway/ventilation and PaO2 / respiratory status"}, {"key": "P3", "text": "Serial peak flow only as the sole monitoring plan"}, {"key": "P4", "text": "Orthostatic blood pressure after sprint exercise"}, {"key": "P5", "text": "Urine specific gravity every minute without respiratory assessment"}]}
rationales:
K1: Incorrect. Thyroid storm is a hyperthyroid emergency (hyperthermia/tachycardia), not hypothyroid coma.
K2: Correct. Merck/OpenStax: myxedema coma — life-threatening hypothyroidism with hypothermia, altered mentation, respiratory depression.
K3: Incorrect. While glucocorticoids are given because adrenal insufficiency cannot be excluded, the presentation described is myxedema coma.
K4: Incorrect. Serotonin syndrome is a toxidrome unrelated to this hypothyroid picture.
A1: Correct. Merck: treat with IV T4 (or T3); OpenStax: intravenous thyroid hormone replacement.
A2: Correct. Merck: glucocorticoids given because central hypothyroidism/adrenal insufficiency often cannot be initially excluded.
A3: Incorrect. Merck: do not rewarm rapidly — may precipitate hypotension or arrhythmias.
A4: Incorrect. Methimazole treats hyperthyroidism/thyroid storm, not myxedema coma.
A5: Incorrect. Supportive airway/temperature care is required; ambulation is not priority.
P1: Correct. Extreme hypothermia is characteristic; low-reading thermometers may be needed (Merck).
P2: Correct. Respiratory depression/CO2 retention and hypoxemia require ventilation/PaO2 monitoring (Merck/OpenStax).
P3: Incorrect. Peak flow alone does not address hypothermia/coma monitoring needs.
P4: Incorrect. Not a priority parameter in unresponsive hypothermic myxedema coma.
P5: Incorrect. Omits essential respiratory assessment.
topic: NGN bowtie — myxedema coma: IV thyroid hormone + glucocorticoids; hypothermia/respiratory depression
units_note: Doses cited from Merck for clinician review context; item keys actions/parameters, not a calculation.

stem: A client has a chest tube connected to a specialized drainage device after pneumothorax. What is the primary purpose of this drainage system design?
options:
A) Allow air and fluid to leave the pleural space while preventing room air from flowing back in (one-way drainage)
B) Force room air into the pleural space to reinflate the lung
C) Replace the need for any occlusive dressing if the tube becomes dislodged
D) Eliminate the need to monitor respiratory status after insertion
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: drainage devices are designed for one-way drainage so air/fluids flow out but nothing flows back in. Merck: ambulatory devices connect to a one-way valve (e.g., Heimlich valve).
B: Incorrect. Re-entry of air into the pleural space would worsen pneumothorax.
C: Incorrect. OpenStax separately notes three-sided occlusive dressing readiness if a chest tube becomes dislodged; the canister design does not replace that emergency action.
D: Incorrect. Respiratory monitoring remains essential while a chest tube is in place.
topic: Chest tube drainage — one-way system so air/fluid leave but cannot re-enter pleural space
source_1_title: 11.6 Disorders of the Lower Respiratory System: Pneumothorax

stem: An Ontario RN is assisting a nurse practitioner who is providing medical assistance in dying (MAID). Which action is within the RN’s legal role?
options:
A) Insert an intravenous line with an order for later use by the NP/physician administering MAID medications
B) Personally administer the medications that will cause the client’s death
C) Independently determine MAID eligibility and write the MAID medication order
D) Pressure the client to choose MAID to free a hospital bed
rationales:
A: Correct. CNO: RNs/RPNs may assist by activities such as inserting an IV line (with an order) that will be used to administer MAID medications; only NPs and physicians may administer those medications.
B: Incorrect. CNO: only NPs and physicians may administer medications to cause death for practitioner-assisted MAID; RNs/RPNs are not permitted to administer them.
C: Incorrect. Eligibility assessment/administration authority is limited to NPs and physicians.
D: Incorrect. CNO: nurses giving information must not encourage or pressure the client to choose MAID.
topic: Ontario MAID — RN/RPN may support care but cannot administer MAID medications
jurisdiction_note: CNO guidance and Canadian federal MAID framework; RNs/RPNs support but only NP/physician may administer MAID medications.
source_1_title: Guidance on Nurses’ Roles in Medical Assistance in Dying

stem: An Ontario nurse conscientiously objects to participating in MAID for an assigned client. What is the correct next action?
options:
A) Transfer care to another appropriate provider and continue other nursing care unrelated to MAID until replacement is arranged, without expressing moral judgment to the client
B) Tell the client that choosing MAID is morally wrong and refuse all care immediately
C) Abandon the client without arranging alternate care
D) Administer the MAID medications personally despite the objection
rationales:
A: Correct. CNO: conscientious objection must not be directly conveyed to the patient; transfer care to another nurse/provider; continue other nursing care unrelated to MAID until a replacement is found.
B: Incorrect. Objection must not be conveyed; moral judgments about the client must not be expressed; unrelated care continues until transfer.
C: Incorrect. Care must be transferred appropriately; abandonment is not permitted.
D: Incorrect. Objection means the nurse does not provide/assist MAID activities; administration is also outside RN authority.
topic: Ontario MAID conscientious objection — transfer care; continue unrelated care; do not convey objection to client
jurisdiction_note: CNO conscientious objection rules for MAID participation.
source_1_title: Guidance on Nurses’ Roles in Medical Assistance in Dying

stem: The nurse prepares a term newborn for overhead phototherapy for hyperbilirubinemia. Which action is correct?
options:
A) Place the infant under the lights wearing only a diaper with eye patches/mask in place, and monitor temperature frequently
B) Dress the infant in a heavy sleeper and leave the eyes uncovered for bonding under the lights
C) Cover the infant completely with blankets so no skin is exposed to the light
D) Skip temperature checks because phototherapy cannot affect body temperature
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: infant wears only a diaper and eye patches; monitor temperature every 2 hours because phototherapy can elevate temperature. Open RN: usually only a diaper; patches/mask protect eyes; monitor temperature frequently for overheating.
B: Incorrect. Clothing blocks light exposure; eyes require protection under phototherapy lights.
C: Incorrect. Maximal safe skin exposure (with genital/eye protection) is needed for effective phototherapy.
D: Incorrect. Both sources require temperature monitoring because of overheating risk.
topic: Neonatal phototherapy — diaper only + eye protection; monitor temperature
source_1_title: 24.2 Care of Common Problems in the Newborn
source_1_section: Nursing Care Plan for the Jaundiced Newborn
source_2_title: HEALTHY NEWBORN CARE — Nursing Health Promotion

stem: A newborn is receiving overhead phototherapy. For each action, specify Indicated or Not indicated.
options: {"columns": ["Indicated", "Not indicated"], "rows": [{"key": "R1", "text": "Keep eye patches or an opaque eye mask in place while under the lights"}, {"key": "R2", "text": "Expose maximal skin by using only a diaper (genital coverage)"}, {"key": "R3", "text": "Monitor temperature frequently for overheating"}, {"key": "R4", "text": "Leave the eyes uncovered continuously under the lights to promote bonding"}]}

R3: Indicated. Both sources: monitor temperature; phototherapy can overheat the infant.
R4: Not indicated. Eyes must be protected while under the lights; uncovering for feeding/assessment is timed, not continuous under lights.

stem: The nurse teaches a client starting home oxygen therapy. Which instruction is correct?
options:
A) Do not smoke or allow smoking near oxygen; keep oxygen away from open flames/heat sources; avoid petroleum-based lotions on the face or upper body
B) Smoking is safe if the oxygen flow is turned down to 1 L/min
C) Petroleum jelly is preferred on the nose and face while oxygen is in use
D) Place oxygen equipment next to a wood stove to warm the gas before use
rationales:
A: Correct. MedlinePlus: no smoking where oxygen is used; keep oxygen about 6 feet from heat; avoid Vaseline/petroleum creams unless advised. COPD Foundation: do not smoke; keep equipment 5–10 feet from open flames; avoid oil/petroleum-based products on face/upper chest.
B: Incorrect. Smoking near oxygen is prohibited regardless of flow rate.
C: Incorrect. Petroleum-based products are discouraged; water-based preferred.
D: Incorrect. Keep oxygen away from open flames/heat.
topic: Home oxygen safety — no smoking; keep away from open flame/heat; avoid petroleum-based lotions

stem: Which nursing action best supports prevention of postoperative deep vein thrombosis related to mobility?
options:
A) Promote early ambulation and limit prolonged immobility as the client’s condition allows
B) Keep the client on strict bed rest for several days even when medically cleared to walk
C) Discourage all leg movement so the surgical incision can rest completely
D) Massage the calves vigorously every hour to break up clots
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: early mobilization/ambulation supports thromboprophylaxis. Merck: preventive measures include ambulation and prevention of immobility.
B: Incorrect. Prolonged immobility increases DVT risk.
C: Incorrect. Mobility supports venous return.
D: Incorrect. Vigorous calf massage is not evidence-based prevention.
topic: Postoperative DVT prevention — early ambulation / prevent immobility

stem: A school-age client is admitted with confirmed rubella (German measles). Which isolation plan is appropriate?
options:
A) Droplet Precautions until 7 days after the onset of the rash
B) Airborne Precautions only until the fever resolves
C) Standard Precautions alone with no transmission-based isolation
D) Contact Precautions for 24 hours after starting antibiotics
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC Appendix A: Droplet + Standard until 7 days after rash onset. Merck: isolate 7 days after rash; droplet precautions in hospital.
B: Incorrect. Rubella uses Droplet, not Airborne.
C: Incorrect. Droplet Precautions are required.
D: Incorrect. Not keyed to antibiotics.

stem: An older adult is admitted with disseminated herpes zoster (shingles with lesions outside the primary dermatomes). Which precautions are required?
options:
A) Airborne and Contact Precautions (with Standard Precautions) for the duration of illness / until lesions are dry and crusted
B) Droplet Precautions only for 24 hours after starting antivirals
C) Standard Precautions alone with lesions left uncovered in a shared room
D) Contact Precautions without airborne isolation for disseminated disease
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC Appendix A: disseminated zoster — Airborne + Contact + Standard for duration of illness. CDC shingles IC: disseminated — Airborne and Contact until lesions dry and scabbed.
B: Incorrect. Requires Airborne + Contact, not Droplet-only.
C: Incorrect. Transmission-based precautions required.
D: Incorrect. Airborne also required when disseminated.

stem: The nurse teaches a client who self-injects insulin subcutaneously. Which teaching point is correct?
options:
A) Rotate injection sites and avoid repeatedly using the same spot, especially areas that are lumpy, firm, or numb
B) Always inject into the exact same abdominal spot for consistent absorption
C) Inject only into bruised areas so healing tissue absorbs insulin faster
D) Shake NPH insulin vigorously until foamy before every dose
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: rotate sites to prevent fatty deposits and site irritation. MedlinePlus: keep a chart so you do not inject the same place all the time; avoid lumpy, firm, or numb spots.
B: Incorrect. Repeated same-site use risks lipohypertrophy/poor absorption.
C: Incorrect. Avoid bruised/swollen/tender spots.
D: Incorrect. Cloudy insulin is rolled, not shaken vigorously (OpenStax/MedlinePlus teaching).
topic: Insulin injection — rotate sites; avoid repeated use of lumpy sites

stem: A peripheral IV site is swollen and cool to the touch, and the client reports pain at the site. What is the priority nursing action?
options:
A) Stop the infusion and remove the IV catheter per protocol, then restart access at another site if still needed
B) Increase the infusion rate to clear the swelling
C) Ignore the findings if the pump is not alarming
D) Flush forcefully with 20 mL of undiluted potassium chloride
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: infiltration causes pain, swelling, cool skin; stop IV fluids immediately and remove the IV. NCBI Open RN: discontinue the site and relocate the IV per policy.
B: Incorrect. Increasing rate worsens tissue fluid extravasation.
C: Incorrect. Clinical signs require action even without pump alarms.
D: Incorrect. Dangerous and unrelated; do not force flush into an infiltrated site.
topic: IV infiltration — cool swollen site; stop infusion and remove catheter

stem: Which finding best suggests phlebitis at a peripheral IV site, requiring the nurse to stop the infusion and remove the catheter?
options:
A) Redness and tenderness along the path of the vein
B) A cool, pale swollen area without vein inflammation signs
C) A dry intact dressing with no client discomfort
D) Blood return present with a soft, nontender site
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: phlebitis causes redness and tenderness along the vein; stop fluids and remove IV. NCBI Open RN: phlebitis can cause redness and tenderness along the vein.
B: Incorrect. Cool swollen site is more consistent with infiltration.
C: Incorrect. No complication cues.
D: Incorrect. Expected patent nontender site.
topic: IV phlebitis — redness and tenderness along the vein; stop and remove catheter

stem: A client in acute mania is agitated, speaking rapidly, and making grandiose plans to leave against advice. Which nursing approach is most appropriate?
options:
A) Use a calm demeanor, give concise clear directions, avoid arguing about grandiose ideas, and prioritize a safe environment
B) Loudly debate each grandiose claim until the client admits they are false
C) Encourage a large stimulating group activity to burn off energy
D) Leave the client unsupervised in a crowded waiting area
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: during manic phases maintain a calm demeanor, provide concise clear directions, avoid challenging grandiosity, and ensure a safe environment. Merck: manic episodes involve severe impairment/risky behavior that may require hospitalization — safety is priority.
B: Incorrect. Challenging grandiosity can escalate agitation.
C: Incorrect. High stimulation is counterproductive in acute mania.
D: Incorrect. Safety requires supervision/structured environment.
topic: Acute mania — calm clear communication; do not challenge grandiosity; prioritize safety

stem: A client who recently started a first-generation antipsychotic develops sudden torticollis and tongue spasms. Complete the bowtie: most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
options: {"conditions": [{"key": "K1", "text": "Tardive dyskinesia only (late irreversible choreiform movements)"}, {"key": "K2", "text": "Acute dystonic reaction (extrapyramidal)"}, {"key": "K3", "text": "Serotonin syndrome"}, {"key": "K4", "text": "Hypoglycemic seizure"}], "actions": [{"key": "A1", "text": "Notify the provider and administer benztropine or diphenhydramine as ordered (IV/IM)"}, {"key": "A2", "text": "Hold further doses of the causative antipsychotic pending provider guidance"}, {"key": "A3", "text": "Encourage the client to ignore the spasms and continue the same antipsychotic dose without assessment"}, {"key": "A4", "text": "Start a high-dose SSRI immediately as first-line therapy for the spasms"}, {"key": "A5", "text": "Force oral intake of a large high-carbohydrate meal as the only intervention"}], "parameters": [{"key": "P1", "text": "Airway patency and ability to swallow/speak (watch for laryngeal involvement)"}, {"key": "P2", "text": "Resolution of muscle spasms / dystonic movements after treatment"}, {"key": "P3", "text": "Peak expiratory flow only as the sole monitoring plan"}, {"key": "P4", "text": "Urine specific gravity every minute without neuromuscular assessment"}, {"key": "P5", "text": "Orthostatic blood pressure after sprint exercise only"}]}
rationales:
K1: Incorrect. Tardive dyskinesia is a late effect, not the acute spasmodic torticollis/tongue spasm picture.
K2: Correct. OpenStax: dystonia includes spasms of tongue, back, legs, neck — an EPS of antipsychotics. Merck: acute dystonic reactions (e.g., torticollis, oculogyric crisis).
K3: Incorrect. Serotonin syndrome is a different toxidrome.
K4: Incorrect. Not a hypoglycemic presentation.
A1: Correct. Merck: treat acute dystonia with benztropine IV/IM or diphenhydramine IV/IM.
A2: Correct. OpenStax/Merck: monitor EPS so treatment can be given and antipsychotic regimen adjusted/changed.
A3: Incorrect. Acute dystonia requires prompt treatment.
A4: Incorrect. SSRIs are not treatment for dystonia.
A5: Incorrect. Not the antidote pathway.
P1: Correct. Merck notes laryngeal dystonia may threaten airway.
P2: Correct. Reassess spasm resolution after anticholinergic/antihistamine therapy.
P3: Incorrect. Peak flow alone misses airway/neuromuscular priorities.
P4: Incorrect. Omits essential neuromuscular/airway assessment.
P5: Incorrect. Not priority monitoring for acute dystonia.
topic: NGN bowtie — acute dystonia from antipsychotic: recognize and treat with benztropine/diphenhydramine

stem: An Ontario nurse reviews consent for two different procedures proposed for the same client. Which statement reflects CNO/HCCA capacity principles?
options:
A) Capacity is treatment-specific — a client may be capable for one treatment and incapable for another; if capable, the client decides
B) Once found incapable for any decision, the client is permanently incapable for all future treatments
C) Nurses may independently override a capable client’s refusal whenever the nurse disagrees
D) A family member may consent for a clearly capable adult who refuses treatment
rationales:
A: Correct. CNO Consent: capacity relates to a specific treatment; a person could be capable for one treatment and incapable for another; if the client is capable, the client makes the decision.
B: Incorrect. Capacity is decision/treatment-specific and can change.
C: Incorrect. Practitioners lack authority to decide for capable clients except limited emergencies.
D: Incorrect. Capable clients decide for themselves; SDM is used when the client is incapable.
topic: Ontario consent — capacity is treatment-specific; capable client decides
jurisdiction_note: CNO Consent practice guideline under Ontario HCCA: capacity assessed relative to a specific treatment.

stem: The nurse teaches a client to use an ice pack for a soft-tissue injury. Which instruction is correct?
options:
A) Wrap the ice in a cloth and apply it; do not place ice directly on the skin
B) Place bare ice cubes directly against the skin for continuous 2-hour contact
C) Apply uncovered dry ice directly over open abrasions
D) Heat the ice pack in a microwave before applying it to the skin
rationales:
A: Correct. MedlinePlus: wrap ice in cloth; do not place ice directly on the skin. Merck: apply ice wrapped in a towel or cloth.
B: Incorrect. Direct ice and prolonged unprotected cold risk skin injury.
C: Incorrect. Ice should not be placed directly on skin; open skin needs separate wound care.
D: Incorrect. Ice packs are used cold; heating defeats cold therapy and risks burn.
topic: Cold therapy — wrap ice in cloth; do not place ice directly on skin

stem: The nurse prepares to assist a partially weight-bearing client from bed to a wheelchair. Which action is essential before the transfer?
options:
A) Lock the wheelchair brakes and stabilize the chair; clear footrests/leg rests as needed
B) Leave the wheelchair unlocked so it can roll toward the client
C) Ask the client to hold the moving wheelchair while standing unsupported
D) Place the wheelchair at the far end of the room without locking it
rationales:
A: Correct. MyHealth Alberta: prepare the wheelchair by locking the brakes and removing/swinging away leg rests. OpenStax: before transfer, lock and stabilize equipment.
B: Incorrect. An unlocked wheelchair can roll and cause a fall.
C: Incorrect. The chair must be locked/stabilized; the client should not stabilize a moving chair.
D: Incorrect. Chair should be positioned close and locked.
topic: Bed-to-wheelchair transfer — lock wheelchair brakes before transfer

stem: A preoperative nurse prepares the surgical site. Which hair-removal practice best aligns with SSI prevention guidance?
options:
A) Do not remove hair unless it will interfere with the operation; if removal is needed, use clippers (not a razor)
B) Shave the entire surgical field with a razor the night before surgery
C) Always remove all hair at every incision site with a disposable razor in the OR
D) Use a razor immediately before incision because microscopic cuts reduce infection
rationales:
A: Correct. SHEA: do not remove hair unless it interferes; if needed, clip outside the OR; do not use razors. ACS/SIS: avoid hair removal unless hair interferes; if needed use clippers instead of a razor.
B: Incorrect. Routine razor shaving increases SSI risk.
C: Incorrect. Routine removal is discouraged; razors are not preferred.
D: Incorrect. Razor microtrauma is linked to higher SSI risk.
topic: SSI prevention — avoid hair removal unless necessary; clippers not razors

stem: Environmental services asks which product to use for daily cleaning of a room occupied by a client with Clostridioides difficile infection. Which response is best?
options:
A) Use a C. difficile sporicidal disinfectant (for example, an EPA List K agent) for daily and terminal cleaning
B) Wipe surfaces with plain water only; spores are removed by rinsing
C) Use alcohol wipes alone as the primary room disinfectant for C. difficile spores
D) Skip terminal cleaning after discharge because spores die within minutes on dry surfaces
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC CDI guidance: daily and terminal cleaning with a C. difficile sporicidal agent (EPA List K). Public Health Ontario: use a sporicidal agent for CDI bathroom cleaning and for discharge/transfer cleaning of the room/bathroom.
B: Incorrect. Cleaning alone without a sporicidal disinfectant is inadequate for CDI rooms.
C: Incorrect. Alcohol is not relied on as a sporicidal agent for C. difficile environmental disinfection.
D: Incorrect. Terminal cleaning with a sporicidal agent after transfer/discharge is recommended.
topic: C. difficile — environmental cleaning with sporicidal agent

stem: A nurse discovers a small wastebasket fire in an unoccupied patient room. Which response sequence best reflects standard healthcare fire response (RACE)?
options:
A) Rescue anyone in immediate danger, activate the alarm, confine/contain the fire (close doors), then extinguish if safe
B) Ignore the alarm pull stations and first search for an elevator to evacuate the whole building
C) Open all doors on the unit to improve airflow before calling for help
D) Leave clients in the fire room while gathering personal belongings from the nursing station
rationales:
A: Correct. NCBI/StatPearls (OSHA fire safety): RACE = rescue, alarm, confine, extinguish. Ohio healthcare fire tip sheet: Rescue, Alarm, Contain, Extinguish — rescue persons in immediate danger.
B: Incorrect. Elevators are not used for fire evacuation; alarm activation is required.
C: Incorrect. Confinement requires closing doors, not opening them to feed the fire.
D: Incorrect. Rescue of those in danger and alarm/confine take priority over retrieving belongings.
topic: Facility fire response — RACE: Rescue, Alarm, Confine/Contain, Extinguish
client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
source_2_publisher: Ohio Department of Commerce — Division of State Fire Marshal

stem: A client on long-term antipsychotic therapy develops involuntary lip smacking and tongue protrusion. Which nursing interpretation and action are most appropriate?
options:
A) Suspect tardive dyskinesia; assess with an involuntary-movement tool (e.g., AIMS) and notify the provider
B) Reassure that these movements always resolve within minutes and require no follow-up
C) Immediately double the antipsychotic dose without notifying the provider
D) Interpret the movements as voluntary attention-seeking and ignore them
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: tardive dyskinesia presents with involuntary facial movements (lip smacking, tongue protruding); use AIMS to assess EPS/TD. Merck: TD involves involuntary lip/tongue movements; patients on long-term therapy should be evaluated periodically with AIMS.
B: Incorrect. TD may persist and needs assessment/provider notification.
C: Incorrect. Dose increases are not an independent nursing action and may worsen EPS/TD risk.
D: Incorrect. TD movements are involuntary adverse effects, not voluntary behaviour.
topic: Tardive dyskinesia — involuntary orofacial movements; assess/report (AIMS)
source_2_section: Treatment of Adverse Effects of Antipsychotic Medications

A2: Correct. Maintaining safety/observation and team notification are priority actions.

A4: Incorrect. Command hallucinations are not harmless.
A5: Incorrect. Never encourage acting on harmful commands.
P1: Correct. Monitor hallucination content and intent to act.
P2: Correct. Observation level and means restriction are key safety parameters.
P3: Incorrect. Not a safety parameter for command hallucinations.
P4: Incorrect. Irrelevant.

stem: Two days after starting a first-generation antipsychotic, a client paces constantly and says, “I feel like I can’t sit still.” Which nursing conclusion is best?
options:
A) This may be akathisia (motor restlessness); assess and notify the provider because it is distressing and can lead to nonadherence
B) This is always intentional hyperactivity and should be ignored
C) This proves the client needs a higher antipsychotic dose immediately without assessment
D) This is pathognomonic of tardive dyskinesia lip-smacking that requires no reporting
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: akathisia includes restlessness and inability to sit still, often early after starting/increasing dose. Merck: akathisia (motor restlessness) is particularly unpleasant and may lead to nonadherence.
B: Incorrect. Akathisia is an adverse effect, not willful behaviour.
C: Incorrect. Dose increases without assessment may worsen EPS; notify provider.
D: Incorrect. Classic TD is late orofacial involuntary movements, not acute restlessness.
topic: Akathisia — motor restlessness from antipsychotics; report; do not ignore

stem: An Ontario RN is charting after a busy morning. Which action meets CNO Documentation accountabilities?
options:
A) Document care in a timely manner at the time of care or as soon as possible afterward — and do not document care before it is provided
B) Pre-chart anticipated care for the entire shift before assessing any clients
C) Delete another nurse’s entry that the RN disagrees with
D) Falsify a late vital-sign entry to match expected values
rationales:
A: Correct. CNO Documentation: document in a timely manner at the time of care or as soon as possible after; nurses do not document before the care is provided.
B: Incorrect. Documenting before care is provided is prohibited.
C: Incorrect. CNO: do not delete, alter, or modify documentation produced by others.
D: Incorrect. CNO: do not falsify a record relating to practice.

stem: The nurse teaches a client recovering from right hip surgery to use a pickup walker. Which instruction is correct?
options:
A) Move the walker forward, ensure all four tips or wheels are on the ground, then step with the weaker (surgical) leg first, followed by the stronger leg
B) Step with the stronger leg first while lifting two walker tips off the floor
C) Pull up from the chair by tipping the walker toward you
D) Look continuously at your feet while leaning far over the front bar
rationales:
A: Correct. MedlinePlus: all 4 tips/wheels on ground before stepping; step with weak/surgical leg first, then the other. AAOS: position walker with all four legs on even ground; move injured leg into walker first.
B: Incorrect. Weight should not be placed until all tips/wheels are down; weak/injured leg steps first for typical weight-bearing walker gait.
C: Incorrect. MedlinePlus: do not pull on or tilt the walker to stand; use chair armrests.
D: Incorrect. MedlinePlus/AAOS: look forward, not down at feet; keep toes inside the walker frame.

stem: The nurse teaches a postoperative client about graduated compression stockings. Which instruction is correct?
options:
A) Put the stockings on first thing in the morning before getting out of bed, and smooth out wrinkles so they do not bunch
B) Wait until evening when legs are most swollen before applying the stockings
C) Roll or fold the tops of the stockings down to create a tighter cuff
D) Apply only one stocking on the unaffected leg
rationales:
A: Correct. MedlinePlus: put on first thing in the morning before out of bed; smooth wrinkles; do not let stockings bunch. Cleveland Clinic: smooth out rolls; avoid bunching.
B: Incorrect. Morning application is preferred because legs have least swelling then.
C: Incorrect. Cleveland Clinic: never turn tops over — tourniquet-like effect. MedlinePlus: avoid bunching/wrinkles.
D: Incorrect. Stockings are applied as prescribed, typically to both legs when ordered for DVT risk/venous support.

stem: The nurse teaches an older adult about removable denture care. Which instruction is correct?

A) Take dentures out overnight and place them in water or a mild denture-soaking solution
B) Leave dentures in continuously day and night without removal
C) Scrub dentures vigorously with whitening toothpaste and a stiff brush
D) Soak metal-attachment dentures in undiluted household bleach overnight
rationales:
A: Correct. MedlinePlus Dentures/Denture problems: take out at night; store in water or denture-cleansing liquid. Mayo Clinic: soak overnight in water or mild soaking solution.

stem: The nurse reinforces hearing-aid care teaching for a client. Which instruction is correct?
options:
A) Keep hearing aids away from heat and moisture, turn them off when not in use, and avoid hairspray while wearing them
B) Rinse hearing aids under running water each night and dry with a hair dryer on high heat
C) Leave hearing aids powered on continuously, including overnight storage
D) Apply hairspray freely while the aids are in place to protect electronics
rationales:
A: Correct. FDA and NIDCD: keep away from heat/moisture; turn off when not in use; avoid hairspray/hair products while wearing. FDA also advises against water on aids.
