stem: A client has an indwelling urinary catheter. Which nursing action best supports infection prevention during maintenance?
options:
A) Keep the collecting bag below the level of the bladder at all times and do not rest the bag on the floor
B) Hang the drainage bag above bladder level to improve gravity flow into the bladder
C) Place the drainage bag on the floor beside the bed for stability
D) Raise the bag above the bladder when transferring so tubing stays taut
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC CAUTI guideline: keep collecting bag below bladder at all times; do not rest bag on floor. MedlinePlus: bag always lower than bladder; do not place bag on floor.
B: Incorrect. Bag above bladder risks backflow of urine into the bladder.
C: Incorrect. CDC/MedlinePlus: do not place/rest bag on the floor.
D: Incorrect. Raising bag above bladder promotes reflux and contamination risk.

stem: Which practice meets CDC safe injection recommendations?
options:
A) Use a new sterile needle and syringe for each patient — do not reuse a syringe on another patient even if the needle is changed
B) Change only the needle and reuse the same syringe for the next patient
C) Draw medication for several patients from one syringe by changing needles between patients
D) Access a multidose vial with a syringe that was already used on a patient, then use that vial for others
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC: One Needle, One Syringe, Only One Time; do not administer from the same syringe to multiple patients even if the needle is changed.
B: Incorrect. Changing the needle does not make a used syringe safe for another patient.
C: Incorrect. Syringes are single-use; reuse between patients transmits infection.
D: Incorrect. CDC: do not enter a medication vial with a syringe/needle used on a patient for subsequent patients.
topic: Safe injection — one needle, one syringe, only one time (even if needle changed)

stem: A client with PTSD suddenly appears terrified, stares past the nurse, and seems to be re-experiencing a past assault. Which nursing action is the priority?
options:
A) Calmly orient the client to the present using grounding (e.g., what they can see/hear/touch now) and reassure that they are safe
B) Insist the client immediately recount every detail of the trauma aloud
C) Leave the client alone in a dark room until the episode ends
D) Argue that the trauma never happened and demand they 'snap out of it'
rationales:
A: Correct. NHSGGC: grounding pulls attention back to here-and-now during flashbacks (senses). VA Stress First Aid: orient to present; describe surroundings/non-distressing sensory details; slow breathing as needed.
B: Incorrect. Forcing detailed trauma recounting during an acute flashback is not first-line acute grounding care.
C: Incorrect. Leaving an acutely distressed/disoriented client alone is unsafe.
D: Incorrect. Arguing/denying experience is nontherapeutic and escalating.
topic: PTSD flashback — ground in present (senses/here-and-now); reassure safety
source_1_section: Managing nightmares and flashbacks / Grounding / Coping with flashbacks

stem: An Ontario RN working in a long-term care home has reasonable grounds to suspect that a resident was abused by a staff member and that the resident was harmed. Which action meets legal and professional accountabilities?
options:
A) Immediately report the suspicion through the required LTC reporting pathway (to the Director / designated reporting line) — confidentiality does not excuse failing to report
B) Wait several weeks to see whether the resident complains formally before taking any action
C) Keep the information confidential and tell no one because of PHIPA
D) Confront the alleged abuser privately and close the matter without any report
rationales:
A: Correct. CNO: FLTCA requires nurses to report improper/incompetent care or abuse resulting in harm or risk of harm. Steps to Justice: LTC workers/regulated health professionals must report suspected abuse/neglect; duty applies even if information would otherwise be confidential.
B: Incorrect. Reporting is required when there are reasonable grounds to suspect; delaying undermines resident protection.
C: Incorrect. Mandatory reporting duties override ordinary confidentiality in this setting.
D: Incorrect. Informal confrontation without required reporting does not meet FLTCA/CNO accountabilities.
topic: Ontario LTC — nurse must report suspected resident abuse/neglect (FLTCA / CNO)

stem: The nurse fits a single-point cane for a client with left-leg weakness. Which fitting instruction is correct?

B) Set the handle at shoulder height so the elbow is locked straight
C) Set the handle below the knee so the client must lean far forward

stem: The nurse teaches stair safety with a cane after right ankle surgery. Which instruction is correct?
options:
A) Going up, step up with the stronger (uninjured) leg first; going down, lead with the cane and the weaker/injured leg, then the stronger leg
B) Always lead with the injured leg when going up and down
C) Carry the cane and hop on the injured leg without using a handrail when available

A: Correct. MedlinePlus: up — stronger leg first, then cane and weaker leg; down — cane then weaker then stronger. AAOS: up on good leg first; down cane then injured then good leg.
B: Incorrect. Leading with the injured leg when ascending is unsafe.
C: Incorrect. AAOS: use free hand on handrail when available; do not hop on injured leg.
D: Incorrect. Sequence depends on stronger vs weaker leg for ascent and descent.

stem: The nurse teaches a client home use of an electric heating pad for muscle spasm pain. Which instruction is the priority safety teaching?
options:
A) Do not fall asleep with the heating pad in place
B) Sleep all night with the pad on the highest setting
C) Place the bare heating element directly on open broken skin
D) Ignore redness or blistering because warmth always means healing

A: Correct. MedlinePlus: to prevent skin injury, do not fall asleep with a heating pad in place. Mayo Clinic: never sleep with a heating pad.

C: Incorrect. Heat on open/broken skin is contraindicated in heat-safety teaching.

stem: A small amount of blood spills on a hard floor in a client care area. Which nursing action is correct?
options:
A) Don gloves (add gown/face protection if splash risk), wipe up the blood, apply facility-approved disinfectant, then remove PPE and perform hand hygiene
B) Wipe the spill with bare hands and leave the area wet without disinfectant
C) Spray disinfectant into the air over the spill without wearing gloves
D) Ignore small blood spills because housekeeping surfaces never transmit bloodborne pathogens
rationales:

stem: Before entering an Airborne Precautions room, the nurse dons a fit-tested N95 respirator. Which action is required?
options:
A) Perform a user seal check each time the respirator is put on; a seal check does not replace fit testing
B) Skip the seal check because last year's fit test permanently guarantees today's seal

B: Incorrect. Fit testing selects model/size; seal must still be checked with each donning.
C: Incorrect. NIOSH explicitly states seal check is not a substitute for fit testing.
D: Incorrect. Tight face seal is required for FFR protection.

stem: A client says, "I feel like everything is falling apart." Which nurse response best uses therapeutic communication?
options:
A) "Tell me more about what has been going on for you."
B) "Why did you let things get this bad?"
C) "At least you are not as sick as some other people here."
D) "You should just stop worrying and think positive."
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax Fundamentals: open-ended questions support therapeutic communication. OpenStax PMH: explore with open-ended questions rather than accusatory why or minimizing remarks.
B: Incorrect. OpenStax PMH: asking why can imply accusation/judgment and provoke defensiveness.
C: Incorrect. Minimizing remarks belittle the client's feelings.
D: Incorrect. Advice-giving/false positivity is nontherapeutic compared with open exploration.

stem: An Ontario RN considers posting a selfie from the unit that clearly shows a client's face and unique wound dressing in the background, with the caption "Tough day in wound care." Which action meets privacy accountabilities?
options:
A) Do not post the photo or any identifiable client health information on social media
B) Post it because the client's name is not written in the caption
C) Post it on a private account because private platforms never create privacy risk
D) Post it first and ask the client for consent afterwards
rationales:
A: Correct. CNO: do not share client information/images on social media; health-record content including unique findings is inappropriate to post. PHIPA guidance: never disclose PHI on social media without unpressured consent; be prudent not to post workplace pictures that may include clients.
B: Incorrect. Omitting a name does not prevent identification from a face/unique clinical image.
C: Incorrect. CNO cautions against sharing even on private platforms because content may still be identifiable/shared.
D: Incorrect. Consent must be obtained before disclosure; posting first violates privacy.

stem: The nurse teaches a client starting oral ferrous sulfate for iron-deficiency anemia. Which instruction is correct?
options:
A) Take on an empty stomach if tolerated; avoid taking with milk, calcium, or antacids; vitamin C (e.g., orange juice) can enhance absorption
B) Always crush the tablet into a glass of milk at bedtime for best absorption
C) Take with a calcium antacid every dose to protect the stomach and improve absorption
D) Stop the supplement if stools turn black because black stools always mean gastrointestinal bleeding
rationales:
A: Correct. MedlinePlus: iron best absorbed on empty stomach; separate milk/calcium/antacids (≥2 hours); vitamin C/orange juice can help absorption. Merck: absorbed best empty stomach; antacids/calcium reduce absorption; vitamin C enhances; black stools are a harmless side effect.
B: Incorrect. Milk/calcium impair absorption; bedtime-with-milk is not preferred teaching.
C: Incorrect. Antacids and calcium reduce iron absorption.
D: Incorrect. Black stools are expected with oral iron; tarry stools with red streaks or severe pain warrant provider contact.
topic: Oral iron — best absorbed empty stomach; separate from milk/calcium/antacids; vitamin C enhances

stem: A nurse is assigned to direct care in an intensive care unit. Which fingernail practice is appropriate?
options:
A) Keep natural nails short (not extending past the fingertip) and do not wear artificial nails or extensions for this high-risk direct care
B) Wear long acrylic nails because alcohol hand rub always sterilizes under artificial nails
C) Grow natural nails well past the fingertip to protect the nail bed during glove use

A: Correct. CDC: natural nails should not extend past the fingertip; do not wear artificial nails/extensions when having direct contact with high-risk patients (e.g., ICU/OR). B: Incorrect. Germs can persist under artificial nails even after hand hygiene; CDC/PHO advise against artificial nails in high-risk/direct care.
C: Incorrect. Long nails harbour more organisms and are harder to clean.
D: Incorrect. Nail enhancements are not recommended for direct care hand hygiene effectiveness.

stem: A community health nurse teaches safe home cooking. Which statement shows correct understanding?
options:
A) Use a food thermometer to check that meat and poultry reach a safe internal temperature; colour alone is not a reliable doneness guide
B) If ground beef looks brown in the middle, it is always safe without checking temperature
C) A food thermometer is unnecessary if the outside of poultry looks crispy
D) Guessing doneness by smell is as accurate as a thermometer for leftovers
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC: only way to tell if food is safely cooked is a food thermometer; colour/texture (except seafood) are unreliable. Health Canada: use a food thermometer in the thickest part to verify safe cooking temperatures.
B: Incorrect. Colour alone does not confirm a safe internal temperature.
C: Incorrect. External appearance does not replace thermometer verification.
D: Incorrect. Smell is not a substitute for measured internal temperature.

stem: A nurse teaches a family about protecting children from secondhand tobacco smoke. Which teaching is correct?
options:

B) Smoking in a bedroom with the door closed fully protects children elsewhere in the home

stem: The nurse teaches parents about care of the newborn umbilical cord stump. Which instruction is correct?
options:
A) Keep the stump clean and dry, fold the diaper below the stump, sponge bathe until it falls off naturally, and do not pull it off
B) Pull the stump off as soon as it looks loose to speed healing
C) Cover the stump tightly with an occlusive plastic dressing at all times
D) Give full tub baths daily until the stump falls off
rationales:
A: Correct. MedlinePlus/OpenStax: keep stump clean (gauze and water) and dry; fold diaper down; sponge bathe / no tub bath until stump falls off; let it fall off naturally—do not pull.
B: Incorrect. Pulling can cause bleeding; allow natural separation.
C: Incorrect. Stump should be kept dry and exposed to air; not sealed in plastic.
D: Incorrect. Avoid tub baths until the stump has fallen off.

stem: A nurse nearly administers the wrong medication but catches the error before giving it. Which response best reflects a just culture of safety?
options:
A) Report the near miss so system factors can be reviewed; human error is addressed without blame, while reckless violations remain unacceptable
B) Hide the near miss because no patient was harmed and reporting would only create punishment
C) Punish every near miss the same as intentional reckless harm, regardless of system design
D) Tell the nurse never to speak of it so the unit's quality scores stay high
rationales:
A: Correct. AHRQ: just culture addresses systems issues that lead to unsafe acts while maintaining accountability; human error vs at-risk vs reckless. OpenStax: just culture is nonpunitive for errors/near misses with clear lines for reckless behaviour; reporting improves safety.
B: Incorrect. Near misses should be reported for learning; silence blocks safety improvement.
C: Incorrect. Just culture is not blanket punishment; response depends on behaviour type, not only outcome severity.
D: Incorrect. Suppressing reports undermines a culture of safety.

B) Competence is fixed at graduation; no further learning or QA participation is expected
C) Only nurse managers must participate in Quality Assurance; staff nurses are exempt

rationales:

B: Incorrect. Continuing competence and continuous learning are required.

stem: A client believes a nurse shared their personal health information without authorization. Under Ontario privacy expectations, which teaching is correct?

stem: Which set correctly lists Ontario/Canada's 4 Moments for Hand Hygiene in health care?

stem: A nurse sustains a needlestick after giving an injection. Which immediate actions are correct?
options:
A) Do not recap used needles; dispose sharps in a marked container; after a stick, wash/flood the area, report immediately to the employer, and seek prompt medical attention
B) Recap the used needle with two hands, then throw it in the regular trash
C) Ignore the stick if bleeding is light and never report it
D) Force the needle deep into an overfilled sharps box using bare fingers
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: never recap used needles; dispose in marked sharps container; if needlestick occurs, report immediately and follow facility protocols. OSHA: flood/clean exposed area, report immediately, seek immediate medical attention.
B: Incorrect. Never recap used needles; never discard sharps in regular trash.
C: Incorrect. Reporting and medical follow-up are required after exposure.
D: Incorrect. Never force sharps or reach into the container.
topic: Sharps safety — never recap used needles; immediate sharps container disposal; needlestick: wash, report, seek care

stem: The nurse teaches a client newly prescribed insulin lispro. Which instruction is correct?
options:
A) Take rapid-acting insulin about 15 minutes before a meal or immediately after; it works quickly and hypoglycemia risk rises around peak action
B) Take lispro once weekly only, with no relation to meals
C) Rapid-acting insulin has no onset for 12 hours, so meals are irrelevant
D) Mix insulin glargine into every lispro dose in the same syringe at home without checking instructions
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: rapid-acting (lispro/aspart/glulisine) onset ~15–30 min; take 15 min before or immediately after a meal; peak 1–2 h with hypoglycemia risk. Merck: rapid-acting best used at mealtime for postprandial glucose. ADA: rapid-acting onset ~15 min; bolus covers meals.
B: Incorrect. Rapid-acting is meal-related (bolus), not a weekly dose.
C: Incorrect. Onset is minutes, not hours.
D: Incorrect. Merck: insulin glargine should never be mixed with any other insulin.
topic: Rapid-acting insulin (lispro/aspart/glulisine) — give with meals; onset ~15 min; monitor hypoglycemia at peak
source_1_title: 28.2 Insulin and Non-Insulin Injectable Diabetes Drugs

stem: For a client on basal-bolus insulin (glargine + lispro), indicate whether each teaching point is Indicated or Not indicated.
options: {"columns": ["Indicated", "Not indicated"], "rows": [{"key": "R1", "text": "Inject rapid-acting (lispro) about 15 minutes before a meal or immediately after eating"}, {"key": "R2", "text": "Watch for hypoglycemia especially around rapid-acting insulin peak"}, {"key": "R3", "text": "Never mix insulin glargine with any other insulin in the same syringe"}, {"key": "R4", "text": "Skip all mealtime insulin forever because basal insulin alone covers every carb"}, {"key": "R5", "text": "Premix glargine and lispro in one home bottle for convenience without manufacturer guidance"}]}

R1: Indicated. Rapid-acting is timed to meals.
R2: Indicated. Peak action increases hypoglycemia risk.
R3: Indicated. Glargine must not be mixed with other insulins.
R4: Not indicated. Bolus/prandial coverage is needed for meals in basal-bolus regimens.
R5: Not indicated. Do not premix glargine with other insulins.

The nurse monitors closely for hypoglycemia especially {B3}.", "blanks": {"B1": [{"key": "B1a", "text": "about 15 minutes before a meal or immediately after a meal"}, {"key": "B1b", "text": "once a month only, unrelated to food"}, {"key": "B1c", "text": "only when the client has no food available for 24 hours"}, {"key": "B1d", "text": "exclusively by crushing tablets into juice"}], "B2": [{"key": "B2a", "text": "never be mixed with any other insulin"}, {"key": "B2b", "text": "always be shaken vigorously with NPH in one bottle at home"}, {"key": "B2c", "text": "be mixed with lispro in every home syringe without checking"}, {"key": "B2d", "text": "be discontinued if meals contain any carbohydrate"}], "B3": [{"key": "B3a", "text": "around the peak action of the insulin"}, {"key": "B3b", "text": "only during dental cleanings years later"}, {"key": "B3c", "text": "never, because insulin cannot lower glucose"}, {"key": "B3d", "text": "only when reading shoe sizes"}]}}

stem: Before an older adult enters the MRI scanner room, which nursing action is the priority safety teaching/screening step?
options:
A) Screen for implants/devices (e.g., pacemaker, aneurysm clips) and remove ferromagnetic objects; do not proceed with unknown devices until MRI safety status is confirmed
B) Bring steel oxygen tanks and loose keys into the magnet room to save time
C) Assume all pacemakers are automatically safe without identifying the model
D) Skip screening because MRI never interacts with metal
rationales:
A: Correct. RadiologyInfo: screen for implants; remove metallic belongings; magnet can move ferromagnetic objects/implants; some devices may malfunction. FDA: careful screening; patients with implants should not receive MRI unless device is identified as MR Safe or MR Conditional; unknown status assumed MR Unsafe.
B: Incorrect. Ferromagnetic objects can become projectiles.
C: Incorrect. Exact device type must be known; many require special conditions or are unsafe.
D: Incorrect. MRI magnetic fields interact strongly with ferromagnetic materials and some implants.
topic: MRI safety screening — report implants/devices; remove ferromagnetic objects; unknown devices assumed unsafe until cleared

stem: The nurse teaches an older adult after cataract surgery. Which instruction is correct?
options:
A) Protect the eye as directed (shield/sunglasses), use prescribed drops, prefer light activity, and avoid heavy lifting and excessive forward bending until cleared
B) Start heavy weightlifting and vigorous forward bending the evening of surgery to speed healing
C) Rub the operative eye firmly several times each hour
D) Stop all prescribed antibiotic/anti-inflammatory eye drops immediately after leaving the OR without orders
rationales:
A: Correct. MedlinePlus: patch/shield as directed; sunglasses; light activities; check before strenuous activity. Merck: activity may be restricted (bending/heavy lifting prohibited); protective shield; avoid rubbing, heavy lifting, excessive forward bending; use prescribed drops.
B: Incorrect. Heavy lifting/bending are restricted early after surgery.
C: Incorrect. Rubbing the eye is contraindicated.
D: Incorrect. Prescribed drops reduce inflammation/infection risk during healing.
topic: Cataract surgery recovery — protect eye; light activity; avoid heavy lifting/excessive bending; use prescribed drops

stem: A 19-year-old client starts a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) for major depression. Which teaching point is the highest priority in the first weeks of therapy?
options:
A) Immediately notify the provider of worsening depression or new or increased suicidal thoughts
B) Stop the SSRI after 3 days if mood has not fully returned to normal
C) Combine the SSRI with a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) to speed recovery
D) Skip doses on weekends to reduce the risk of sexual side effects
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: clients must immediately notify the provider about increased depression or suicidal ideation; FDA boxed warning notes increased suicidal thoughts/behaviour risk in children, adolescents, and young adults under 24. Merck: suicide risk may rise early in antidepressant treatment; carefully monitor for suicidal behaviours and ideation.
B: Incorrect. Therapeutic effects often take about 2 weeks to begin and 4–6 weeks for full effect; abrupt early stopping is not appropriate teaching.
C: Incorrect. SSRIs must not be combined with MAOIs because of serotonin syndrome risk.
D: Incorrect. Skipping doses is unsafe and unrelated to priority suicide-risk monitoring.
topic: Antidepressants/SSRIs — monitor and report increased suicidal ideation especially early in treatment and in younger clients
source_1_section: Nursing Implications / Client Teaching Guidelines / FDA Black Box Warning

rationales:
R1: Indicated. Immediate reporting of suicidal ideation is required teaching.

R3: Indicated. Ongoing monitoring of mood/anxiety during treatment is recommended.
R4: Not indicated. Concurrent MAOI + SSRI risks serotonin syndrome.

stem: A school-age client with autism spectrum disorder becomes distressed when the unit lighting, noise, and schedule change abruptly. Which nursing action best supports the client?
options:
A) Reduce unnecessary noise and bright stimuli when possible, keep routines predictable, and allow preferred communication supports
B) Force prolonged eye contact and hugs so the client learns typical social behaviour
C) Suddenly rearrange meals, clothing, and procedures to increase flexibility
D) Ignore sensory distress because it is attention-seeking and should be extinguished
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: families/nurses adapt with sensory considerations, routines, and communication supports (including pictures/devices). Merck: extreme over- or under-reaction to sensory input and inflexible adherence to routines are core features; supportive environments reduce distress.
B: Incorrect. Forced eye contact or unwanted touch can be aversive for sensory-sensitive clients.
C: Incorrect. Abrupt routine changes often increase extreme distress.
D: Incorrect. Sensory distress is a recognized ASD feature, not mere attention-seeking.
topic: Autism spectrum disorder — support predictable routines and reduce overwhelming sensory input

stem: For a hospitalized child with autism spectrum disorder, indicate whether each action is Indicated or Not indicated.
options: {"columns": ["Indicated", "Not indicated"], "rows": [{"key": "R1", "text": "Keep daily care as predictable as possible and warn before changes"}, {"key": "R2", "text": "Lower noise and harsh lighting when they worsen sensory distress"}, {"key": "R3", "text": "Force eye contact during every interaction to build social skill"}, {"key": "R4", "text": "Allow picture boards or other preferred communication supports"}, {"key": "R5", "text": "Make sudden, unexplained schedule changes to promote flexibility"}]}
rationales:
R1: Indicated. Predictable routines reduce distress from inflexible need for sameness.
R2: Indicated. Reducing overwhelming sensory input is supportive.
R3: Not indicated. Forced eye contact is not required and may increase distress.
R4: Indicated. Picture/gesture/device supports are accepted communication approaches.
R5: Not indicated. Abrupt unexplained changes commonly provoke extreme distress.

stem: A client is 6 hours after a vaginal birth with perineal swelling and discomfort. Which comfort measure is most appropriate now?
options:
A) Apply an ice or cold pack to the perineum during the first 24 hours to reduce swelling and pain
B) Begin prolonged hot tub soaks immediately after delivery before any cold therapy
C) Avoid all perineal cleansing until the 6-week postpartum visit
D) Encourage the client to sit continuously on a hard chair to promote drainage
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: ice/cold packs for the first 24 hours (table also notes early postpartum cold application). MedlinePlus: ice packs in the first 24 hours decrease swelling and help pain. Merck: immediately after delivery, ice packs may help reduce pain and edema; warm sitz baths are used later.
B: Incorrect. Warm baths/sitz are typically deferred until after the early cold period (about 24 hours).
C: Incorrect. Perineal hygiene (e.g., peri-bottle rinsing) is taught during the postpartum stay.
D: Incorrect. Hard prolonged sitting increases discomfort; cushioning/limited sitting is preferred.
topic: Postpartum perineal comfort — ice packs in the first 24 hours to reduce swelling and pain

stem: Parents ask how to care for their newborn after circumcision. Which instruction is most appropriate?
options:
A) Apply petroleum jelly to the penis or diaper area with diaper changes so the healing site does not stick
B) Scrub the incision vigorously with antiseptic soap at every diaper change
C) Leave the site dry with no ointment so a hard scab forms faster
D) Ignore small amounts of yellow crust because infection is inevitable after circumcision
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: gauze with petroleum jelly on the tip/diaper prevents sticking; continue dab of petroleum jelly during healing. MedlinePlus: apply petroleum jelly after diaper changes to protect the healing incision; yellow crust can be normal.
B: Incorrect. Vigorous scrubbing can disrupt healing; gentle cleansing is taught.
C: Incorrect. Petroleum jelly is used specifically to protect the site and prevent diaper adherence.
D: Incorrect. Mild yellow crust may be normal healing, but infection is not inevitable and concerning signs need evaluation.
topic: Circumcision aftercare — petroleum jelly to prevent diaper sticking; monitor bleeding and voiding
source_2_publisher: MedlinePlus / U.S. National Library of Medicine

stem: Parents ask why their healthy term newborn is offered a vitamin K injection soon after birth. Which explanation is best?
options:
A) A single intramuscular vitamin K dose helps prevent vitamin K deficiency bleeding, which can cause serious hemorrhage
B) Vitamin K is given only to treat already-diagnosed jaundice and has no preventive role
C) Oral vitamin K once at birth is proven more effective than intramuscular vitamin K for late bleeding prevention
D) Vitamin K injections are unnecessary for breastfed newborns because breast milk is high in vitamin K
rationales:
A: Correct. CPS: routine IM vitamin K effectively prevents VKDB; recommended for all newborns. Merck: phytonadione IM within 6 hours prevents hemorrhagic disease of the newborn.
B: Incorrect. Vitamin K prophylaxis is preventive, not a jaundice treatment.
C: Incorrect. CPS states oral regimens are less effective than IM, especially for late VKDB.
D: Incorrect. Breast milk is relatively low in vitamin K; exclusively breastfed infants are at risk for late VKDB without prophylaxis.
topic: Newborn vitamin K IM prophylaxis to prevent vitamin K deficiency bleeding
jurisdiction_note: CPS/CFPC recommend routine IM vitamin K for all newborns in Canada; oral regimens only if parents decline IM and are counselled that oral is less protective.

stem: A newborn has scalp swelling after a long vaginal birth. Which finding best supports caput succedaneum rather than cephalohematoma?
options:
A) Soft boggy edema that crosses cranial suture lines
B) A firm swelling sharply limited to one cranial bone that does not cross sutures
C) A fluctuant mass extending into the neck with signs of shock
D) Absence of any scalp changes because molding never involves fluid
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: caput is soft/boggy edema that crosses suture lines. Merck: caput typically crosses suture lines.
B: Incorrect. That pattern describes cephalohematoma (subperiosteal, limited by sutures).
C: Incorrect. Extension with possible shock suggests subgaleal hemorrhage, a different emergency.
D: Incorrect. Caput and molding-related extracranial collections are common after birth.
topic: Caput succedaneum crosses suture lines; cephalohematoma is limited by sutures (subperiosteal)

stem: A parent of a toddler asks how to prevent drowning at home. Which teaching is most accurate?
options:
A) Never leave a child alone in a bathtub or near water, even briefly; keep toddlers within arm’s reach of an adult
B) Bath seats make constant adult supervision unnecessary during tub time
C) Children can be left alone if older siblings are watching from another room
D) Water wings alone are approved safety devices that replace lifejackets and adult supervision
rationales:
A: Correct. CPS: toddlers within arm’s reach; never leave alone in pool/bathtub even for a moment. CDC: designate close constant supervision including bathtubs; drowning is often silent and fast.
B: Incorrect. Bath seats give false security; supervision remains mandatory (CPS household safety teaching).
C: Incorrect. Other children do not replace adult supervision.
D: Incorrect. Water wings/foam toys are not safety devices; supervision and proper flotation as indicated still apply.
topic: Drowning prevention — constant adult supervision; never leave child alone in bathtub or near water
jurisdiction_note: CPS Caring for Kids water safety aligns with CDC drowning prevention on constant supervision; Canada-focused parent teaching.

stem: A small wastebasket fire starts in an unoccupied utility room. After activating the alarm and confirming a clear exit path, the nurse uses a portable extinguisher. Which technique is correct?
options:
A) Pull the pin, aim at the base of the fire, squeeze the handle, and sweep side to side
B) Aim at the top of the flames, then pull the pin and squeeze once briefly
C) Spray water from a pitcher first, then store the extinguisher unused
D) Squeeze the handle continuously while aiming only at smoke near the ceiling
rationales:
A: Correct. OSHA and nursing references teach the PASS technique: Pull the pin, Aim at the base of the fire, Squeeze the handle, and Sweep side to side at the base until the fire appears out.
B: Incorrect. Aiming at the top of the flames misses the fuel source at the base; pin is pulled first.
C: Incorrect. Improvised water is not the extinguisher PASS technique and may be unsafe for some fire types.
D: Incorrect. Aiming at ceiling smoke does not extinguish the fire at its base.

stem: During the first minutes of an IV vancomycin infusion, a client develops flushing and pruritus of the face and neck without wheezing or hypotension. Which action is the priority?
options:
A) Slow or temporarily stop the infusion and resume at a slower rate over at least 60 minutes as ordered/protocol
B) Double the remaining dose into a rapid IV push to finish sooner
C) Immediately give a monoamine oxidase inhibitor to reverse flushing
D) Ignore the flushing because vancomycin never causes infusion reactions
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: vancomycin flushing syndrome from too-rapid IV administration is managed by slowing the infusion and giving each dose over at least 60 minutes. Merck: infuse slowly over ≥60 minutes to avoid histamine-mediated infusion reaction with facial/neck flushing.
B: Incorrect. Faster administration worsens the reaction; IV push is inappropriate.
C: Incorrect. MAOIs are unrelated and unsafe here.
D: Incorrect. Rapid infusion is a recognized cause of vancomycin infusion/flushing reaction.
topic: Vancomycin IV — flushing syndrome from rapid infusion; infuse over ≥60 minutes
source_1_section: Adverse Effects and Contraindications — Vancomycin flushing syndrome

stem: Complete the safe-administration teaching for IV vancomycin.
options: {"template": "Each IV vancomycin dose should be infused over at least {B1}. If vancomycin flushing syndrome occurs from a rapid infusion, the usual first management step is to {B2}.", "blanks": {"B1": [{"key": "B1a", "text": "60 minutes"}, {"key": "B1b", "text": "30 seconds as an undiluted IV push"}, {"key": "B1c", "text": "5 minutes regardless of dose"}, {"key": "B1d", "text": "24 hours without interruption"}], "B2": [{"key": "B2a", "text": "slow the infusion (and follow protocol/provider orders)"}, {"key": "B2b", "text": "give the next dose twice as fast"}, {"key": "B2c", "text": "add an MAOI to the same IV line"}, {"key": "B2d", "text": "stop all future antibiotics permanently without assessment"}]}}
rationales:
B1a: Correct. OpenStax/Merck: infuse each dose over at least 60 minutes.
B1b: Incorrect. IV push of vancomycin is unsafe and promotes flushing reaction.
B1c: Incorrect. Five minutes is too rapid for typical vancomycin doses.
B1d: Incorrect. Continuous 24-hour infusion is not the standard teaching for each intermittent dose duration.
B2a: Correct. OpenStax: management is to slow the infusion; flushing syndrome can be mistaken for allergy.
B2b: Incorrect. Faster infusion worsens histamine release.
B2c: Incorrect. MAOI coadministration is unrelated and dangerous.
B2d: Incorrect. Assessment and protocol-guided management are required; automatic permanent stop without evaluation is incorrect teaching.
topic: NGN cloze — vancomycin infusion duration and flushing-reaction management

stem: While a vesicant chemotherapy infusion is running, the client reports burning at the peripheral IV site and the nurse notes swelling. What is the immediate priority action?
options:
A) Stop the infusion immediately and follow the facility extravasation protocol (including provider notification)
B) Increase the infusion rate to finish the dose before tissue contact continues
C) Flush the line vigorously with a large fluid bolus and ignore the burning
D) Leave the room for 30 minutes to see if the burning resolves on its own
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax Pharmacology: if the IV site may be compromised during vesicant administration, stop the infusion immediately, notify the provider, and follow applicable extravasation protocols. OpenStax Clinical Nursing Skills: for extravasation, stop the infusion and follow agency-specific management (including aspiration steps per policy).
B: Incorrect. Faster infusion increases tissue exposure to the vesicant.
C: Incorrect. Flushing into compromised tissue can worsen extravasation injury; do not ignore burning.
D: Incorrect. Delay allows ongoing tissue injury; extravasation is an emergency.
topic: Vesicant chemotherapy extravasation — stop infusion immediately; follow protocol

stem: A school-age child develops the bright "slapped cheek" rash of fifth disease (parvovirus B19) after a few days of mild cold symptoms and is now afebrile. Which teaching is most accurate about contagiousness and school attendance?
options:
A) The child is usually unlikely to be contagious after the rash appears and can typically return to school if otherwise well and facility policy allows
B) The child must remain home for exactly 30 days after the rash fades
C) The rash means the child is most contagious and must be isolated in a negative-pressure room at school
D) Fifth disease spreads only from dogs and cats, so school contacts are irrelevant
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC: people are most contagious early; unlikely contagious after later symptoms such as rash; usually safe to return to school after the rash appears. VDH school chart: once the characteristic rash appears, the child is not likely contagious and can return; exclusion not otherwise indicated beyond facility fever/rash policies.
B: Incorrect. A fixed 30-day post-rash exclusion is not the standard guidance.
C: Incorrect. Contagiousness is highest before the rash, not after; negative-pressure school isolation is not indicated for typical fifth disease.
D: Incorrect. Human parvovirus B19 spreads person to person (respiratory/blood); pet parvoviruses are different.
topic: Fifth disease (parvovirus B19) — usually return to school after slapped-cheek rash appears
source_1_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_2_title: Communicable Disease Reference Chart for School and Childcare Facility Personnel

options: {"columns": ["Indicated", "Not indicated"], "rows": [{"key": "R1", "text": "Explain that contagiousness is usually low after the rash appears and school return is often appropriate if the child is well"}, {"key": "R2", "text": "Advise pregnant household contacts to notify their obstetric/health care provider about the exposure"}, {"key": "R3", "text": "Teach that the bright red cheek rash is the classic \"slapped cheek\" finding of fifth disease"}, {"key": "R4", "text": "Tell the family fifth disease is spread only by household pets, so human contacts need no guidance"}, {"key": "R5", "text": "Recommend starting an MAOI immediately to shorten the rash"}]}

R4: Not indicated. Human parvovirus B19 is a human infection; pet parvoviruses differ.
R5: Not indicated. No MAOI therapy for fifth disease rash; illness is typically self-limited.

stem: A responsive 4-year-old is choking, cannot speak or cough effectively, and is becoming cyanotic. Which intervention sequence is recommended while emergency help is activated?
options:
A) Repeated cycles of 5 back blows alternating with 5 abdominal thrusts until the object is expelled or the child becomes unresponsive
B) Blind finger sweeps of the throat before any other action
C) Abdominal thrusts only, never back blows, and only after the child becomes unresponsive
D) Infant-style chest thrusts alone without back blows, because abdominal thrusts are preferred in infants
rationales:
A: Correct. 2025 AHA/AAP pediatric BLS: for children with severe FBAO, use repeated cycles of 5 back blows alternating with 5 abdominal thrusts until the object is expelled or the child becomes unresponsive. Merck supports abdominal thrusts for older/conscious children and distinguishes infant technique.
B: Incorrect. Blind finger sweeps are not recommended and may push the object deeper.
C: Incorrect. Current child guidance includes back blows alternating with abdominal thrusts while the child is still responsive with severe obstruction.
D: Incorrect. Infant technique uses back blows and chest thrusts; abdominal thrusts are not used in infants. This client is a child, not an infant.
topic: Child severe FBAO — cycles of 5 back blows alternating with 5 abdominal thrusts

stem: A school-age child had streptococcal pharyngitis about 10 days ago and now has periorbital edema, elevated blood pressure, and cola-colored urine. Which condition should the nurse suspect?
options:
A) Poststreptococcal (postinfectious) glomerulonephritis
B) Immediate anaphylaxis to residual throat lozenges
C) Uncomplicated seasonal allergic rhinitis only
D) Simple dehydration with normal urine colour and no edema
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck/CDC: PSGN/PIGN follows group A strep pharyngitis or skin infection after a latent period and presents with hematuria (often dark/cola-colored), edema, hypertension, and proteinuria.
B: Incorrect. Timing and renal findings do not indicate acute anaphylaxis.
C: Incorrect. Allergic rhinitis does not cause cola urine, edema, and hypertension after strep.
D: Incorrect. The described findings are not simple dehydration.
topic: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis — cola-colored urine, edema, hypertension after strep
source_2_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

stem: For a child with suspected poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis after recent strep infection, indicate whether each action is Indicated or Not indicated.
options: {"columns": ["Indicated", "Not indicated"], "rows": [{"key": "R1", "text": "Monitor blood pressure closely for hypertension"}, {"key": "R2", "text": "Assess edema (including facial/periorbital) and urine colour/output"}, {"key": "R3", "text": "Support fluid/sodium management per provider orders for edema/hypertension"}, {"key": "R4", "text": "Encourage unlimited high-sodium fast food to \"flush the kidneys\""}, {"key": "R5", "text": "Ignore cola-colored urine because color changes are always harmless after strep"}]}
rationales:
R1: Indicated. Hypertension is a core PSGN feature requiring monitoring/management.
R2: Indicated. Edema and dark hematuria/oliguria are key findings to assess.
R3: Indicated. Treatment is supportive, including managing edema and hypertension.
R4: Not indicated. High sodium worsens fluid overload/hypertension risk.
R5: Not indicated. Dark/cola urine is a classic warning sign of glomerulonephritis, not something to ignore.

stem: A client is scheduled for a clean-contaminated abdominal procedure. Which timing best reflects evidence-based surgical antimicrobial prophylaxis for a typical rapidly infused antibiotic (for example, a cephalosporin)?
options:
A) Begin administration within 60 minutes before incision so tissue levels are present when the incision is made
B) Give the first prophylactic dose only after the incision is already closed
C) Start prophylaxis 24 hours before surgery and continue for 2 weeks automatically
D) Omit all antibiotics for every procedure regardless of guideline indications
rationales:
A: Correct. SHEA 2022: begin antimicrobial prophylaxis within 1 hour before incision (2 hours allowed for vancomycin/fluoroquinolones due to longer infusion). CDC 2017: time agents so bactericidal concentrations are established when the incision is made.
B: Incorrect. Prophylaxis should be present at incision; postoperative-only first dose misses the goal of tissue levels at incision.
C: Incorrect. Prolonged automatic courses are not the standard prophylaxis approach and increase harm/resistance risk.
D: Incorrect. Prophylaxis is indicated for many procedures per guidelines.
topic: Surgical antimicrobial prophylaxis — begin within 60 minutes before incision

stem: An older adult with dysphagia is ordered nectar-thick liquids after a swallow evaluation. Which teaching best explains the purpose of thickened liquids?
options:
A) Thickened liquids move more slowly, which can improve swallowing control and help reduce aspiration risk as directed by the speech-language pathologist
B) Thickened liquids permanently cure stroke-related dysphagia within 24 hours
C) Thickened liquids replace the need for upright positioning during meals
D) Any thin liquid is safer than thickened liquid for clients who cough when drinking
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax Fundamentals: thickening increases viscosity so liquids move more slowly and improve swallowing; nurses collaborate with speech pathologists. OpenStax Med-Surg: thickened liquids and texture modification are primary methods to prevent aspiration in at-risk older adults.

stem: On day 7 of unfractionated heparin, a client's platelets fall by more than 50% and a new lower-extremity clot is suspected. Which action is the priority pending HIT evaluation?
options:
A) Stop all heparin products immediately and anticipate a nonheparin anticoagulant per protocol/orders
B) Switch only to low-molecular-weight heparin because HIT never cross-reacts with LMWH
C) Double the heparin infusion rate to overcome platelet clumping
D) Ignore the platelet drop because HIT causes bleeding, not thrombosis
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: stop heparin immediately and use a non-heparin anticoagulant. Merck: stop heparin if platelets drop >50% or new thrombosis occurs; substitute a nonheparin agent.
B: Incorrect. Merck: most HIT antibodies cross-react with LMWH, so LMWH is not an acceptable substitute.
C: Incorrect. Continuing/increasing heparin worsens the immune process and thrombosis risk.
D: Incorrect. HIT is typically a prothrombotic state; bleeding is uncommon.
topic: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) — stop all heparin; start nonheparin anticoagulant

stem: For suspected heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (platelet drop >50% with possible new thrombosis while on heparin), indicate whether each action is Indicated or Not indicated.
options: {"columns": ["Indicated", "Not indicated"], "rows": [{"key": "R1", "text": "Stop unfractionated heparin immediately (including heparin flushes if ordered/protocol)"}, {"key": "R2", "text": "Anticipate a nonheparin anticoagulant (e.g., argatroban) per protocol/provider orders"}, {"key": "R3", "text": "Notify the provider/anticoagulation team and obtain ordered HIT laboratory evaluation"}, {"key": "R4", "text": "Switch the client to enoxaparin (LMWH) as the preferred HIT treatment"}, {"key": "R5", "text": "Increase the heparin infusion rate to 'overcome' thrombocytopenia"}]}
rationales:
R1: Indicated. All heparin exposure should be stopped when HIT is suspected.
R2: Indicated. A nonheparin anticoagulant is substituted until platelets recover.
R3: Indicated. Evaluation and coordinated management are required.
R4: Not indicated. LMWH usually cross-reacts with HIT antibodies and is not used to treat HIT.
R5: Not indicated. Continuing/increasing heparin is harmful in HIT.
topic: NGN matrix — suspected HIT actions indicated vs not

stem: During general anesthesia with a volatile agent and succinylcholine, a client develops rising end-tidal CO₂, jaw rigidity, and tachycardia. Which intervention set is the priority for suspected malignant hyperthermia?
options:
A) Stop triggering volatile anesthetics/succinylcholine and administer IV dantrolene with rapid cooling/support per protocol
B) Continue the volatile anesthetic and give only an antipyretic tablet
C) Give a non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker as first-line therapy instead of dantrolene
D) Ignore rising ETCO₂ because malignant hyperthermia never occurs after the first anesthetic exposure
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: stop volatile agents, give dantrolene, and cool rapidly. GeneReviews: discontinue potent inhalation agents and succinylcholine and give IV dantrolene promptly.
B: Incorrect. Triggering agents must be stopped; antipyretics are not the treatment for MH.
C: Incorrect. Calcium-channel blockers are avoided with dantrolene (hyperkalemia risk); dantrolene is the specific therapy.
D: Incorrect. MH can occur after prior uneventful anesthetics; rising ETCO₂ with rigidity/tachycardia is a classic early pattern.
topic: Malignant hyperthermia — stop triggering anesthetics/succinylcholine and give IV dantrolene

stem: A client with heavy alcohol use arrives hypoglycemic and is about to receive IV dextrose. Which action best prevents precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy?
options:
A) Administer IV thiamine before (or concurrently with) the IV glucose/dextrose as ordered/protocol
B) Withhold all thiamine because vitamins worsen hypoglycemia
C) Give a large oral carbohydrate meal instead of any parenteral vitamins
D) Start a monoamine oxidase inhibitor before the dextrose infusion
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: give IV thiamine before IV glucose in alcohol use disorder because glucose can worsen thiamine deficiency. OpenStax: IV thiamine with dextrose helps prevent Wernicke encephalopathy.
B: Incorrect. Thiamine is protective; withholding it increases Wernicke risk.
C: Incorrect. Carbohydrate loading without thiamine can worsen deficiency; parenteral thiamine is indicated in at-risk clients.
D: Incorrect. MAOIs are unrelated and unsafe here.

stem: A nurse believes a planned action is unsafe and prior statements were not heard. Using TeamSTEPPS CUS, which sequence best escalates the concern?

stem: Before administering a scheduled oral medication, which identification method is correct?
options:
A) Ask the client to state full name and date of birth, then compare with the armband and MAR (at least two identifiers)
B) Use room number alone because it uniquely identifies every client
C) Skip identification if the nurse recognizes the client's face from yesterday
D) Ask only for the client's favourite colour as the sole identifier
rationales:

B: Incorrect. Room number is not a unique identifier and must not be used to confirm identity.
C: Incorrect. Identity must be confirmed every time medications are administered.
D: Incorrect. Favourite colour is not an approved patient identifier.

stem: An older adult with dementia becomes more agitated and confused each late afternoon (sundowning). Which teaching best guides family caregiving?
options:
A) Reduce evening stimulation (limit loud TV/chores), keep a calm routine, and use adequate lighting to lessen shadows and confusion
B) Schedule all medical appointments and baths late at night when agitation peaks
C) Argue firmly until the client accepts that the day is over
D) Keep the home dark after lunch so the client sleeps until morning
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax Fundamentals: reduce evening TV/stimulation, use calming activities, and address triggers; adequate evening lighting helps. OpenStax Psych: confusion often worse in evening (sundowning); calm communication and supportive environment.
B: Incorrect. OpenStax Fundamentals suggests scheduling demanding activities earlier when the person is more alert.
C: Incorrect. Arguing increases agitation; calm, simple communication is preferred.
D: Incorrect. Daylight exposure and adequate evening lighting help; prolonged darkness/shadows can worsen confusion.

stem: A client taking metformin is scheduled for a radiologic procedure with IV iodinated contrast. Which teaching is most accurate?
options:
A) Metformin is often held around IV contrast because contrast plus reduced kidney function can raise the risk of lactic acidosis; follow the provider/protocol hold and restart plan
B) Double the metformin dose the morning of contrast to protect the kidneys
C) Metformin never interacts with contrast dye, so no hold is ever needed
D) Replace metformin with a sulfonylurea only on the day of contrast and stop checking renal function
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: contrast dye can increase lactic acidosis risk with metformin and reduced renal function; withhold per protocol around contrast. Merck: stop metformin temporarily before radiologic procedures requiring contrast agents; lactic acidosis risk.
B: Incorrect. Increasing the dose does not mitigate contrast-related risk and is unsafe.
C: Incorrect. Sources advise temporary hold around IV contrast in at-risk clients.
D: Incorrect. Arbitrary sulfonylurea swap without renal monitoring is not the recommended approach.
topic: Metformin — hold around IV iodinated contrast; lactic acidosis risk

stem: A client's chest tube accidentally pulls out of the insertion site. Which immediate action is best while calling for help/notifying the provider?
options:
A) Cover the site with a sterile occlusive dressing taped on three sides (leave one side open) so air can escape and reduce tension pneumothorax risk
B) Tape an airtight dressing on all four sides with no vent and leave the client unobserved
C) Routinely clamp the remaining tubing for the rest of the shift without assessment
D) Push the contaminated tube back into the chest without sterile technique
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax Med-Surg: if chest tube dislodged, apply three-sided occlusive dressing to allow air escape. Open RN/NCBI: tape dressing on three sides to prevent tension pneumothorax; notify provider.
B: Incorrect. Fully sealed dressing can trap air and promote tension pneumothorax.
C: Incorrect. Routine clamping is not recommended due to tension pneumothorax risk.
D: Incorrect. Do not reinsert a contaminated tube; cover site and notify provider.

stem: A nonviolent client repeatedly reaches for a peripheral IV. Alternatives have failed and a restraint order is obtained. Which choice best reflects least-restrictive practice?
options:
A) Apply padded mitts first because they restrict grasping while preserving more extremity range of motion than wrist ties
B) Apply a vest restraint immediately for an IV-protection problem
C) Use the most restrictive device available so monitoring can be skipped
D) Restrain without trying alternatives because restraints are first-line for all IV sites
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax CNS: select least restrictive restraint; padded mitts are less restrictive than wrist ties for preventing tube dislodgement while preserving ROM. Open RN: hand mitts/soft wrists used for tube protection; alternatives first.
B: Incorrect. Vest restraints are more restrictive and not the least restrictive choice for IV protection.
C: Incorrect. More restrictive devices increase harm; monitoring remains required.
D: Incorrect. Restraints are used only when alternatives cannot meet safety needs.

stem: A client with severe treatment-resistant depression is scheduled for ECT. Which teaching is most accurate?
options:
A) ECT induces a controlled seizure under anesthesia/supportive care and may cause temporary confusion or memory impairment that often improves over time
B) ECT is delivered fully awake without any anesthesia because seizures are painless
C) ECT permanently erases all remote and recent memory in every client and is never used for depression
D) ECT replaces the need for any consent discussion because it is only a psychotherapy technique
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: ECT uses electricity to create a controlled seizure, commonly for major depression. Merck: modern ECT under general anesthesia; confusion and memory impairment may occur acutely and often improve, though some retrograde amnesia can persist.
B: Incorrect. Merck: brief general anesthesia is used because the electrical current can cause muscle contractions and pain.
C: Incorrect. ECT is used for severe depression; memory effects are often temporary, not universal permanent total erasure.
D: Incorrect. ECT is a biological/brain-stimulation treatment requiring informed consent, not talk therapy alone.
topic: ECT — controlled seizure under anesthesia; temporary memory impairment possible

stem: An Ontario nurse hears a patient's credible account that another nurse touched them in a sexual manner during care. What is the reporting obligation?
options:
A) Report the suspected sexual abuse to the College of Nurses of Ontario (CNO) as required; a patient's account can constitute reasonable grounds
B) Wait indefinitely until a criminal conviction is obtained before any report is considered
C) Ignore the disclosure because consensual-appearing relationships with current patients are allowed
D) Post the patient's name and details on social media to warn the public
rationales:
A: Correct. CNO: nurses are legally required to report suspected sexual abuse of a patient by a nurse to CNO. CNO Boundaries: under RHPA/HPPC, nurses must report reasonable grounds to suspect sexual abuse to the appropriate college; a client's account constitutes reasonable grounds. RHPA HPPC s.85.1: member shall report reasonable grounds that another member sexually abused a patient.
B: Incorrect. Reporting obligation does not wait for criminal conviction; report suspected sexual abuse promptly (within RHPA timelines).
C: Incorrect. Any sexual/romantic relationship with a patient is sexual abuse for regulated health professionals.
D: Incorrect. PHI must not be posted publicly; patient name in a CNO report requires written consent.
topic: Ontario — nurse must report suspected sexual abuse of a patient by a nurse to CNO
jurisdiction_note: CNO / RHPA mandatory reporting of suspected sexual abuse of a patient by a nurse

stem: Before giving subcutaneous insulin, which leadership/safety practice best reduces high-alert medication error risk?
options:
A) Have a second nurse independently verify the insulin type and dose (do not draw up until a witness is available per policy)
B) Skip verification because insulin is never classified as high-alert
C) Draw heparin into an insulin syringe to 'save time'
D) Ask an unlicensed visitor to confirm the dose from memory
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax Pharm: insulin/heparin are high-alert; a second nurse verifies the dose; do not draw up until a witness is available. OpenStax 3.2: double-check high-alert medication doses with another provider; ISMP high-alert drugs should have two-provider verification.
B: Incorrect. Insulin is a classic high-alert medication.
C: Incorrect. Never draw heparin into an insulin syringe.
D: Incorrect. Verification must be by a qualified provider/nurse per policy, not a visitor.

stem: An immobilized client is at risk for joint contractures. Which nursing intervention best helps prevent contractures?
options:
A) Perform or assist with regular active or passive range-of-motion exercises and encourage early mobility as tolerated
B) Keep all joints locked in full flexion continuously to "rest" the muscles
C) Avoid all joint movement until the client is fully ambulatory without assistance
D) Place the client in one position for the entire shift to reduce turning-related fatigue
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax CNS: immobility contributes to joint contractures; mitigate with range-of-motion exercises, weight-bearing, and proper positioning. OpenStax Med-Surg: prolonged immobilization causes contractures; promote early mobility and assess ROM. Merck PT: passive ROM when clients cannot move joints themselves; active ROM when able.
B: Incorrect. Prolonged fixed positioning promotes contractures rather than preventing them.
C: Incorrect. Waiting until full independent ambulation delays needed ROM and mobility interventions.
D: Incorrect. Prolonged single positioning increases musculoskeletal and skin complications.
topic: Immobility — active/passive ROM to prevent contractures

stem: A postoperative client has IV patient-controlled analgesia (PCA). Which teaching is most important for safe use?
options:
A) Only the client should press the PCA button; family/staff must not press it for the client, and the lockout interval limits extra doses
B) Family members should press the button whenever the client looks uncomfortable, even if sedated
C) The nurse should press the button every 5 minutes around the clock regardless of sedation
D) Anyone may press the button freely because PCA pumps have no dose or time limits
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax Fundamentals: no one but the patient should press the button; lockout and alertness are safety measures against overmedication/respiratory depression. Merck: only the patient may push the administration button; lockout dosage/interval prevent extra boluses.
B: Incorrect. PCA-by-proxy (others pressing) can cause oversedation and respiratory depression.
C: Incorrect. Staff should not press the demand button for the client as routine "proxy" dosing.
D: Incorrect. PCA pumps are programmed with lockout and maximum limits.
topic: PCA — only the patient presses the demand button; lockout prevents overdose

stem: A client receiving opioid PCA becomes increasingly difficult to arouse with a decreasing respiratory rate. What is the nurse's priority action?
options:
A) Stop/hold further opioid dosing per protocol, support airway/breathing with oxygen as needed, stimulate the client, and notify the provider/rapid response as indicated
B) Increase the PCA basal rate so pain will not wake the client
C) Ask family to keep pressing the PCA button until the client is fully asleep
D) Ignore sedation because PCA lockout makes respiratory depression impossible
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: PCA overmedication can cause sedation and respiratory depression; monitor and intervene. Merck: opioids cause respiratory depression/sedation risk; PCA lockout helps but does not eliminate need for monitoring and response to oversedation.
B: Incorrect. Increasing opioid infusion worsens respiratory depression.
C: Incorrect. Proxy dosing during sedation is dangerous.
D: Incorrect. Lockout reduces but does not eliminate opioid adverse-effect risk; monitoring is required.

stem: A community client finds an attached tick after hiking. Which teaching is correct for immediate removal?
options:
A) Use clean fine-tipped tweezers to grasp close to the skin and pull upward with steady, even pressure; then clean the area—do not use petroleum jelly or heat to force detachment
B) Cover the tick with petroleum jelly or nail polish and wait for it to back out on its own
C) Burn the tick with a hot match while it is still attached
D) Twist and jerk the tick body forcefully to remove it quickly
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC: fine-tipped tweezers close to skin; steady even pressure; clean site; avoid petroleum jelly/heat/nail polish. Canada.ca/PHAC: fine-point tweezers, slow straight pull; do not burn or smother with petroleum jelly/nail polish.
B: Incorrect. Smothering methods can agitate the tick and increase infection risk.
C: Incorrect. Burning is unsafe and not recommended.
D: Incorrect. Twisting/jerking can leave mouthparts in the skin.
topic: Tick removal — fine tweezers, steady pull; no petroleum jelly

stem: A client begins an acute panic attack with intense fear and hyperventilation. Which nursing action is best initially?
options:
A) Stay with the client, reduce environmental stimuli, speak in short calm statements, and coach slow deep breathing
B) Leave the client alone in a crowded hallway so they can "tough it out"
C) Argue that nothing is wrong and demand they immediately stop all symptoms
D) Start a long detailed lecture on cognitive theory while the client cannot process information
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax Psych (Peplau): for panic, stay with the client, keep within eyesight, move to a safe quieter space. OpenStax 17.2: remain calm; coach slow deep breathing; quiet environment; reassure the attack will pass. Cleveland Clinic: stay with them, remain calm, short sentences, deep breathing, reassure temporary safety.
B: Incorrect. Leaving a panicking client alone increases safety risk and distress.
C: Incorrect. Arguing increases stimulation and does not help panic-level anxiety.
D: Incorrect. Complex teaching is ineffective at panic level when processing is impaired.
topic: Panic attack — stay with client; calm presence; reduce stimuli; coach slow breathing

stem: A client with uncomplicated diverticulitis is being managed with bowel rest at home. Which dietary teaching is most appropriate during the acute inflammatory phase?
options:
A) Use a clear liquid diet for a short period as directed, then advance as pain improves; high-fiber foods are avoided while the bowel is inflamed
B) Immediately start a very high-fiber diet with raw vegetables, nuts, and seeds during peak inflammation
C) Eat only fried fatty meats and stop all fluids
D) Force large high-fiber meals every hour to "scrub" the diverticula
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: clear liquid diet for 2–3 days in uncomplicated diverticulitis with advancement when pain abates. OpenStax Med-Surg: liquid diet to rest intestines. OpenStax Nutrition: high fiber contraindicated during diverticulitis inflammation.
B: Incorrect. High fiber is contraindicated during acute GI inflammation/diverticulitis.
C: Incorrect. Fluids/clear liquids support bowel rest; fried meats are not the acute plan.
D: Incorrect. Aggressive high-fiber feeding during acute inflammation is contraindicated.

stem: An Ontario nurse observes a colleague's unsafe practice that places clients at risk. Aside from mandatory sexual-abuse reporting rules, what is the nurse's professional accountability?
options:
A) Report the unsafe practice or unethical conduct to the appropriate authority (typically the employer/supervisor, and CNO when indicated) because client safety comes first
B) Stay silent forever because only sexual abuse can ever be reported
C) Post the colleague's name and client details on social media for public shaming
D) Ignore client risk to avoid uncomfortable workplace conversations
rationales:
A: Correct. CNO Professional Misconduct: failing to report unsafe practice/unethical conduct to the employer/other authority or CNO is misconduct; generally report to employer. OpenStax Med-Surg: nurses must act on incompetent/unethical practice—address colleague/manager and escalate to licensing boards if uncorrected. Client safety is primary.
B: Incorrect. Sexual-abuse reporting is mandatory to CNO, but nurses also must address/report other unsafe/unethical conduct.
C: Incorrect. Public posting of PHI and unprofessional shaming violates privacy and professional standards.
D: Incorrect. Client safety is the primary responsibility.

stem: A school-age child is diagnosed with group A streptococcal pharyngitis and starts appropriate antibiotics. When teaching the family about return to school or daycare, which instruction is most accurate?
options:
A) Return only after completing the full 10-day antibiotic course, even if fever-free earlier
B) Return when afebrile and at least 12–24 hours after starting appropriate antibiotics (Ontario public health commonly uses 24 hours)
C) Return immediately after the first dose because strep is never contagious once diagnosed
D) Stay home for 2 weeks regardless of antibiotics to prevent rheumatic fever
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Full course must be completed, but school return is typically allowed earlier once noninfectious criteria are met.
B: Correct. CDC: stay home until afebrile and at least 12–24 hours after starting appropriate antibiotics. Ontario public-health guidance commonly excludes until 24 hours after starting antibiotics.
C: Incorrect. Contagiousness declines after antibiotic therapy begins; immediate return after one dose is not the standard teaching.
D: Incorrect. Prolonged blanket exclusion is not required when antibiotics are started and the child is improving/afebrile.

stem: A parent asks how to best protect a child from serious head injury while bicycling. Which teaching is most accurate?
options:
A) Wear a properly fitted bicycle helmet, fastened, every time the child rides
B) Helmets are unnecessary if the child rides only on sidewalks
C) Buy a helmet several sizes too large so the child can "grow into" it
D) A cracked helmet is fine to reuse if the outer shell still looks mostly intact
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC: properly fitted bicycle helmets every ride reduce head/brain injury risk. Health Canada: well-fitted, activity-matched helmets protect against serious head injury.
B: Incorrect. Serious crashes can occur off roadways; helmets are recommended whenever riding.
C: Incorrect. Health Canada: helmets should not be large enough to grow into; fit must be snug now.
D: Incorrect. Bike helmets are single-impact devices and should be replaced after impact or if damaged.

stem: The nurse prepares an intramuscular injection for a 6-month-old infant. Which site is preferred?
options:
A) Vastus lateralis muscle of the anterolateral thigh
B) Dorsogluteal muscle of the buttock as first choice
C) Deltoid muscle for all infants under 12 months as first choice
D) Any subcutaneous fat pad because IM sites are unused in infancy
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax CNS: for children <18 months, vastus lateralis is preferred as the most developed muscle. CDC: for most infants, vastus lateralis (anterolateral thigh) is the recommended IM vaccine site.
B: Incorrect. Buttock injections are avoided in infants/children due to sciatic nerve injury risk.
C: Incorrect. Deltoid is not the preferred first-choice IM site for young infants with limited deltoid mass.
D: Incorrect. Many infant vaccines/medications require true IM administration into muscle.

stem: A client is receiving intermittent nasogastric tube feedings. Which nursing action best reduces the risk of aspiration pneumonia?
options:
A) Keep the head of the bed elevated about 30° to 45° during feeding and for a period afterward as tolerated
B) Place the client flat supine for the entire feeding to promote gastric emptying
C) Omit tube-placement checks because aspiration cannot occur with a correctly ordered formula
D) Encourage the client to lie on the left side with the head down during bolus feeds
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax Med-Surg: maintain HOB 30°–45° to reduce aspiration risk. Merck: sit upright 30°–45° during tube feeding and 1–2 hours afterward to minimize aspiration pneumonia.
B: Incorrect. Flat positioning increases aspiration risk.
C: Incorrect. Placement and intolerance assessments remain essential; aspiration is a major complication.
D: Incorrect. Head-down positioning worsens aspiration risk.

stem: A hospitalized client asks to speak with a spiritual advisor from their faith tradition. What is the nurse's best action?

A) Facilitate contact with the hospital chaplain or the client's preferred clergy and protect quiet time for spiritual practices as able

stem: A family asks how hospice care differs from aggressive curative treatment for a terminally ill relative. Which statement by the nurse is most accurate?
options:
A) Hospice focuses on comfort, dignity, and quality of life rather than treatments aimed at curing the disease
B) Hospice requires stopping all medications, including those used for pain or dyspnea
C) Hospice is identical to intensive curative chemotherapy protocols
D) Hospice can be used only in intensive care units and never at home
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: hospice is comfort care at end of life and does not involve treatments aimed at curing the disease. Merck: hospice focuses on comfort and meaningfulness, not cure or extending life.
B: Incorrect. Symptom-relief medications are central to hospice comfort care.
C: Incorrect. Hospice is not curative intensive treatment.

stem: A nurse must mix regular (clear) insulin and NPH (cloudy) insulin in one syringe as ordered. Which technique is correct?
options:
A) Draw the clear short-acting insulin into the syringe first, then the cloudy NPH
B) Draw the cloudy NPH first, then push any extra mixture back into the clear vial
C) Shake both vials vigorously until foamy before drawing either dose
D) Mix insulin glargine with NPH in the same syringe for convenience
rationales:
A: Correct. MedlinePlus: when mixing two insulins, draw the short-acting (clear) dose first, then the longer-acting (cloudy) dose. OpenStax: NPH is cloudy; most other insulins are clear.
B: Incorrect. Drawing cloudy first risks contaminating the clear vial; mixed insulin should not be pushed back into vials.
C: Incorrect. NPH should be gently rolled, not shaken hard into foam/clumps.
D: Incorrect. Long-acting analogs such as glargine are not mixed with other insulins.

stem: According to the WHO “My 5 Moments for Hand Hygiene,” when must the nurse clean hands to protect the client from germs carried on the nurse’s hands from the health-care area?
options:
A) Before touching the patient when approaching them (e.g., before taking a pulse or assisting with personal care)
B) Only at the start of the shift, then gloves replace further hand hygiene
C) Only after leaving the facility at the end of the day
D) Only if the nurse notices visible dirt, never before clean contact
rationales:
A: Correct. WHO Moment 1: clean hands before touching a patient when approaching them to protect against colonization/exogenous infection. OpenStax Fundamentals links timely hand hygiene before direct patient contact to WHO’s Five Moments.
B: Incorrect. Gloves are not a substitute for hand hygiene; moments apply throughout care.
C: Incorrect. End-of-day hygiene does not replace point-of-care moments.
D: Incorrect. Moment 1 applies before patient contact even when hands are not visibly soiled (ABHR is typically appropriate then).
topic: WHO My 5 Moments — hand hygiene before touching a patient

stem: A nurse plans to wear gloves for anticipated contact with body fluids. Which statement best reflects infection-prevention guidance about gloves and hand hygiene?

B) Once gloves are on, hand hygiene is unnecessary for the rest of the shift

stem: A nurse teaches an older adult after total hip replacement about positioning to reduce dislocation risk. Which instruction is most appropriate when postoperative hip precautions are ordered?
options:
A) Avoid bending the hip more than about 90°, do not cross the legs (avoid adduction), and use an abduction pillow in bed as directed
B) Cross the operative leg over the other leg frequently to stretch the joint
C) Sit in low soft chairs so the knees are higher than the hips
D) Bend forward to tie shoes immediately after surgery without adaptive equipment
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax Clinical Nursing Skills: after THR avoid adduction/crossing legs, use abduction pillow, do not bend more than 90° forward, use raised seats so knees stay lower than hips. AAOS: special precautions when sitting/bending/sleeping to prevent dislocation; home planning includes raised seating and aids to avoid excessive bending.
B: Incorrect. Crossing legs adducts the hip and increases dislocation risk.
C: Incorrect. Low soft chairs promote excessive flexion; raised seating keeps knees lower than hips.
D: Incorrect. Excessive bending is avoided; adaptive equipment is recommended.
topic: Total hip replacement — avoid hip flexion >90°, crossing legs, and use abduction pillow as directed

stem: During a therapeutic interaction, a nurse begins sharing detailed personal life problems with a client to “feel closer.” What is the best analysis of this action under Ontario professional standards?
options:
A) It risks a boundary crossing; nurses should avoid inappropriately sharing personal information and keep the focus on the client’s needs
B) It is required by CNO as mandatory personal disclosure with every client
C) It is always appropriate because any personal sharing strengthens professional boundaries
D) It is acceptable if the nurse posts the same details on social media about the client
rationales:
A: Correct. CNO: boundary crossings may include inappropriately sharing personal information; nurses must clarify/reinforce therapeutic boundaries. OpenStax: maintain professional boundaries—general talk may be OK, but avoid specific personal details; keep rapport without crossing boundaries.
B: Incorrect. Personal disclosure is not a mandatory CNO requirement.
C: Incorrect. Inappropriate personal sharing can create role confusion and harm.
D: Incorrect. Discussing/posting client-related content on social media violates privacy/boundaries.

stem: During the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist “sign out,” before the patient leaves the operating room, which confirmation is the circulating/scrub nurse expected to make to help prevent retained surgical items?
options:
A) Verbally confirm that instrument, sponge, and needle counts are complete (and alert the team if counts do not reconcile)
B) Skip counts if the case finished quickly, because retained items are impossible in short procedures
C) Assume counts are correct without verbal confirmation once the surgeon starts closing
D) Discard sponges outside the room before the final count to save time
rationales:
A: Correct. WHO SSC implementation: nurse verbally confirms completion of instrument, sponge and needle counts before the patient leaves the OR; if counts do not reconcile, alert the team. AHRQ: unintended retention of a foreign object after surgery is a serious reportable “never event.”
B: Incorrect. Retained items are uncommon but persistent; counts are required for eligible cases.
C: Incorrect. Verbal confirmation is an explicit checklist step.

stem: A client with a history of severe allergy asks where to use an epinephrine autoinjector in an emergency. Which teaching is correct?
options:
A) Inject into the middle of the outer thigh (anterolateral thigh); do not inject into the buttocks, fingers/hands/feet, or a vein
B) Inject into a fingertip for fastest absorption
C) Inject into the buttock as the preferred adult site
D) Give only as an intravenous push at home without emergency follow-up

A: Correct. Health Canada AUVI-Q: inject into middle outer/anterolateral thigh; do not inject IV, buttocks, or digits/hands/feet. MedlinePlus: inject only in the middle of the outer side of the thigh; do not inject buttocks, fingers, hands, feet, or into a vein.
B: Incorrect. Digit injection risks severe vasoconstriction/ischemia.
C: Incorrect. Buttock injection is specifically contraindicated for autoinjectors.
D: Incorrect. Autoinjectors are IM/SC into the thigh and emergency care must still be sought.

stem: A client says, “Nobody on this unit listens to me.” Which nurse response best uses reflection (restating) as a therapeutic communication technique?
options:
A) “You’re feeling as though staff are not listening to you.”
B) “You shouldn’t feel that way—everyone here cares about you.”
C) “Let’s talk about your discharge plans instead.”
D) “Why are you being so negative about the nurses?”
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax Fundamentals: reflection restates what the patient said so they hear their own words, encourages continued communication, and shows active listening. OpenStax PMH emphasizes active listening to capture meaning without judgment.
B: Incorrect. Minimizing/false reassurance is a nontherapeutic barrier.
C: Incorrect. Changing the subject is a barrier to therapeutic communication.
D: Incorrect. Asking “why” can feel accusatory and is generally nontherapeutic.
topic: Therapeutic communication — reflection restates the client’s words to show active listening
source_2_section: Active listening; Barriers (changing the subject; false reassurance)
