stem: A postpartum client with perineal discomfort after vaginal birth asks how to use a sitz bath at home. Which teaching is correct?
options:
A) Prepare a warm shallow bath; sit in water without soap for about 10–15 minutes up to three times daily, then gently pat the perineum dry
B) Add bubble bath and scrub vigorously with a washcloth after each soak
C) Use only ice water for 45 minutes continuously once a day
D) Fill the basin with hot undiluted antiseptic and leave the area wet without drying
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: warm shallow bath without soap, soak up to three times/day for 10–15 minutes, gently pat dry; do not add additives unless instructed. NYGH: warm water, do not add soap/bubble bath; sit ~10 minutes ≥3 times/day; pat dry, do not rub.
B: Incorrect. Soap/bubble bath is not advised; rubbing can irritate healing tissue.
C: Incorrect. Guidance is warm (not ice-only prolonged) soaks for comfort/healing; ice packs are a separate early measure.
D: Incorrect. Do not add chemicals unless instructed; pat dry after soaking.
topic: Postpartum sitz bath — warm shallow soak without soap; pat dry

stem: A community health nurse teaches adult vehicle-occupant safety. Which statement is correct?
options:
A) Wear a seat belt in front and rear seats on every trip, no matter how short; air bags add protection but do not replace seat belts
B) Seat belts are unnecessary for trips under 5 minutes in residential areas
C) Rear-seat passengers do not need seat belts if the driver is belted
D) Air bags alone provide complete crash protection, so seat belts are optional
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC: use a seat belt every trip, no matter how short, including back seats; air bags are not a substitute. Transport Canada: buckle up every time, every trip; passengers must always wear seat belts.
B: Incorrect. Short trips still require buckling up.
C: Incorrect. Rear-seat occupants should buckle up as well.
D: Incorrect. Air bags complement—not replace—seat belts.
topic: Seat belts — buckle up every trip, every seat; air bags are not a substitute

stem: A provider gives a telephone medication order. Which nursing action best reduces miscommunication risk?
options:
A) Record the complete order and read it back to the provider for confirmation (closed-loop read-back)
B) Memorize the order and administer immediately without documenting until the end of the shift
C) Repeat only the drug name aloud and assume the dose is the usual one for that drug
D) Enter a different dose than stated if it seems safer, without clarifying with the provider
rationales:
A: Correct. AHRQ PSNet: recipients should record and read back verbal orders; read-back verifies hearing and transcription. AHRQ TeamSTEPPS check-back example: nurse records telephone order and reads it back; provider confirms “Correct.”
B: Incorrect. Delayed documentation increases transcription/memory error risk.
C: Incorrect. Full order elements must be verified, not assumed.
D: Incorrect. Do not silently change orders; clarify/confirm with the provider.
topic: Verbal/telephone orders — record and read back for confirmation (closed loop)
source_1_title: Verbal Orders and Medication Overrides: A Dangerous Combination
source_1_publisher: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) — PSNet

stem: An Ontario nurse considers sharing personal details to support an anxious client. According to CNO guidance on self-disclosure, which approach is appropriate?
options:
A) If used, keep disclosure brief and relevant to the client’s needs, then immediately return the focus to the client’s care
B) Share extensive details about the nurse’s own illness and family problems so the client can comfort the nurse
C) Use self-disclosure mainly to meet the nurse’s need for emotional support during the shift
D) Discuss whatever personal topics the client asks about without limit
rationales:
A: Correct. CNO Dear CNO / case scenarios: limited self-disclosure may be appropriate if brief, relevant, and immediately returns focus to the client. Excessive disclosure can shift focus, create dependence, and cross boundaries. OpenStax PMH: limit self-disclosure within professional boundaries.
B: Incorrect. Detailed personal sharing that shifts the client into comforting the nurse is a boundary concern.
C: Incorrect. Disclosure must address the client’s therapeutic needs, not the nurse’s personal needs.
D: Incorrect. Nurses must remain mindful of how much they disclose.
topic: CNO — limited brief self-disclosure only when therapeutic; keep focus on client
jurisdiction_note: CNO Professional Boundaries / Dear CNO self-disclosure guidance for Ontario practice

stem: A family caregiver asks how to reduce harm if a person with advanced dementia wanders. Which teaching is the priority safety recommendation?
options:
A) Have the person wear an ID/medical bracelet (or necklace) with name, address/phone, and caregiver contact information
B) Leave car keys in plain sight by the door so the person can drive home independently
C) Remove all door/window alarms because they are too noisy
D) Avoid telling neighbors about wandering risk to protect privacy completely
rationales:
A: Correct. MedlinePlus: wear ID bracelet/necklace with name, address, phone, and caretaker contact. NIA: medical bracelet with name/address and caregiver phone number; label clothes if bracelet may be removed.
B: Incorrect. Keep car keys out of sight to reduce unsafe departure.
C: Incorrect. Door/window alarms are recommended prevention supports.
D: Incorrect. Informing neighbors is recommended so they can help if wandering occurs.

stem: An older adult is taught to use ordered thromboembolic deterrent (TED) hose after surgery. Which teaching is correct?
options:
A) Apply as instructed, smooth out wrinkles, and avoid walking without assistance or nonslip socks/shoes to prevent falls
B) Leave large wrinkles at the ankles because wrinkles improve compression
C) Walk freely in stocking feet on polished floors without nonslip footwear
D) Roll the top tightly as a tourniquet band to keep the stocking from slipping
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax Med-Surg: instruct how to put TED hose on, smooth out wrinkles, and not walk without assistance or nonslip socks to avoid falling. TRU HCA: anti-embolism stockings promote venous return; ensure no wrinkles.
B: Incorrect. Wrinkles should be smoothed out.
C: Incorrect. Nonslip footwear/assistance is taught to prevent falls.
D: Incorrect. Rolling/tight banding can impair circulation; not recommended teaching.

stem: A client pauses after saying, “I’m not sure I can talk about this yet.” Which nurse action best uses silence as a therapeutic communication technique?
options:
A) Remain quiet and present, allowing the client time to think and break the silence when ready
B) Immediately fill the pause with advice about what the client should feel
C) Change the subject to unit visiting hours to lighten the mood
D) Say, “Don’t worry—everything will be fine,” and leave the room
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax Fundamentals: using silence allows the patient time to think and process; nurses should respectfully let the patient break the silence. Open RN Fundamentals: providing silence gives clients time to process, self-reflect, and broach a new topic; the nurse may use nonverbal cues but does not rush to speak.
B: Incorrect. Filling silence with advice interrupts processing and can be nontherapeutic.
C: Incorrect. Changing the subject is a nontherapeutic barrier.
D: Incorrect. False reassurance and leaving abandon therapeutic presence.
topic: Therapeutic communication — using silence gives the client time to think and process

stem: Parents ask how to burp their newborn who fusses with gas during feeds. Which teaching is correct?
options:
A) During and after feeding, hold the infant in a supported burping position and gently pat or rub the back to help release swallowed air
B) Pound firmly between the shoulder blades for several minutes every time, even if the baby is comfortable
C) Never burp bottle-fed or breastfed infants because burping always causes injury
D) Lay the infant completely flat and shake the torso to move air out of the stomach
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: burping removes trapped air; use shoulder/lap positions and gently rub or pat the back; breastfed often between breasts and at end; bottle-fed as needed during/after. MedlinePlus: burp several times during and after feeding with upright support and gentle patting.
B: Incorrect. OpenStax: do not pound harder—this can cause injury and does not improve burping.
C: Incorrect. Both breastfed and bottle-fed infants may swallow air and benefit from burping.
D: Incorrect. Supported upright/lap burping positions are taught; shaking is unsafe.
topic: Infant burping — gently pat/rub back during and after feeds to release trapped air

stem: A community nurse in Canada teaches outdoor workers about sunscreen. Which instruction matches Canadian public-health guidance?
options:
A) Use a broad-spectrum, water-resistant sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher and reapply at least every 2 hours (sooner if sweating/swimming)
B) Any lip balm without SPF fully replaces sunscreen for the face and body
C) Apply sunscreen once each spring and never reapply during outdoor work
D) Indoor tanning beds are a healthy way to build a protective base tan before summer
rationales:
A: Correct. Health Canada: broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher; apply ≥15 minutes before sun; reapply at least every 2 hours and after sweating/swimming. Canadian Cancer Society: broad-spectrum SPF 30+; reapply every 2 hours or after sweating/swimming; use with shade/clothing/hats.
B: Incorrect. SPF lip balm protects lips but does not replace full-body sunscreen.
C: Incorrect. Reapplication at least every 2 hours during exposure is required.
D: Incorrect. Health Canada: avoid tanning equipment; no healthy tan; increases melanoma risk.
topic: Canada sun safety — broad-spectrum water-resistant sunscreen SPF 30+; reapply about every 2 hours
jurisdiction_note: Health Canada and Canadian Cancer Society SPF 30+ guidance (stricter than some US SPF 15 minima)

stem: Parents of a toddler with hand, foot, and mouth disease ask for antibiotics “to clear it faster.” Which nurse response is best?
options:
A) Antibiotics will not make this viral illness go away faster; focus on comfort, fluids, and fever/pain relief as directed, and hand hygiene to limit spread
B) Start leftover amoxicillin from a sibling’s ear infection today
C) Antibiotics are required for every child with HFMD to prevent lifelong carriage
D) Give aspirin every 4 hours until the rash disappears
rationales:
A: Correct. CPS: no treatment for the infection; antibiotics won’t help it go away faster; comfort, fluids, acetaminophen/ibuprofen for mouth-sore pain; handwashing. CDC: usually get better in 7–10 days with minimal/no medical treatment; manage pain/fever; never give aspirin to children.
B: Incorrect. Leftover antibiotics are inappropriate for this viral illness and unsafe.
C: Incorrect. HFMD is viral; antibiotics are not routinely indicated.
D: Incorrect. CDC: never give aspirin to children (Reye risk context for viral illness).
topic: Hand-foot-and-mouth disease — supportive care; antibiotics do not shorten the viral illness
source_1_publisher: Canadian Paediatric Society — Caring for Kids
source_2_title: About Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease

stem: A colleague repeatedly humiliates a nurse in front of clients. Which TeamSTEPPS tool is most appropriate to manage this interpersonal conflict constructively?
options:
A) Use the DESC script (Describe, Express, Suggest, Consequences) in a private, respectful conversation focused on win-win resolution
B) Ignore the behaviour indefinitely because conflict tools are only for medication orders
C) Yell the same insults back at the colleague in the hallway to “even the score”
D) Post the colleague’s name and complaints on social media for public shaming
rationales:
A: Correct. AHRQ TeamSTEPPS DESC tool: constructive approach for managing/resolving conflict, especially interpersonal/hostile or harassing behaviours risking harm; use private location and “I” statements. CUSP/TeamSTEPPS notes: DESC = Describe, Express, Suggest, Consequences.
B: Incorrect. DESC is intended for conflict management, including interpersonal conflict affecting safety/teamwork.
C: Incorrect. Retaliatory public confrontation is not DESC and harms patients/team.
D: Incorrect. Public shaming is unprofessional and not a TeamSTEPPS conflict tool.
topic: TeamSTEPPS DESC script — constructive approach for interpersonal/hostile conflict

stem: An Ontario nurse plans to discontinue nursing services for a client who still needs care. Which action best meets CNO accountabilities?
options:
A) Arrange timely alternative or replacement services, or give the client a reasonable opportunity to arrange them—do not abandon the client
B) Stop all care immediately without notice because the nurse is annoyed with the client
C) Walk away mid-shift without communicating with the client, team, or employer
D) Refuse to explore any options and leave the client without access to ongoing care
rationales:
A: Correct. CNO Discontinuing or Declining to Provide Care: nurses cannot abandon/neglect clients; ensure ongoing access to care; discontinue only after other options explored. Code of Conduct 3.13: arrange timely alternative/replacement services or provide reasonable opportunity to arrange them. Professional misconduct regulation also addresses discontinuation without alternatives.
B: Incorrect. Annoyance alone is not a basis to abandon needed services without alternatives.
C: Incorrect. Clear communication with client/team/employer is required.
D: Incorrect. Exploring options and ensuring access to care are required.
topic: CNO — do not abandon clients; arrange alternative/replacement services when discontinuing care

stem: A daycare asks how to limit spread of hand, foot, and mouth disease. Which instruction is best?
options:
A) Promote frequent handwashing with soap and water, clean/disinfect toys and surfaces, and keep symptomatic children home from daycare/school
B) Stop all handwashing because HFMD is not contagious
C) Encourage hugging and sharing drinks with children who have active mouth sores
D) Tell parents HFMD never spreads through saliva or stool
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC: wash hands often, clean/disinfect surfaces, avoid close contact with infected persons. CPS: handwashing best prevention; wash toys/surfaces; children should stay home from school/child care if they have symptoms; spreads via saliva/stool.
B: Incorrect. HFMD is very contagious; hand hygiene is essential.
C: Incorrect. Avoid close contact/kissing/hugging while infectious; do not share fluids with mouth sores.
D: Incorrect. CPS/CDC: spreads through saliva/droplets and stool/contact with contaminated objects.

stem: A provider orders IV potassium chloride for a hospitalized client with hypokalemia. Which nursing action is essential for safe administration?
options:
A) Never give potassium as an IV push or bolus; administer only as a diluted IV infusion at a controlled rate
B) Push undiluted potassium chloride concentrate rapidly through a peripheral IV for fastest correction
C) Add concentrated potassium to a running IV and bolus the line without an infusion pump
D) Give the entire daily potassium deficit as a single undiluted IV push at the start of the shift
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax Pharmacology: never push or bolus potassium IV—rapid administration can cause dysrhythmias and death; use premixed/diluted infusions. Merck: when IV potassium is required, give as infusion with concentration and rate limits (e.g., routine ≤10 mEq/hour; peripheral concentration ≤40 mEq/L).
B: Incorrect. Undiluted IV push of potassium concentrate can be fatal.
C: Incorrect. Rapid uncontrolled bolus bypasses safe infusion controls.
D: Incorrect. Deficits are replaced with controlled infusion, not a single undiluted push.
topic: IV potassium — never administer as IV push/bolus; use diluted infusion
source_1_section: Safety Alert — Potassium and IV Bolus or Push

stem: Complete the safety teaching for intravenous potassium chloride replacement.
options: {"template": "Nurses must never give potassium as an IV {B1}; instead, administer a {B2} infusion, commonly keeping routine peripheral rates within limits such as about {B3}.", "blanks": {"B1": [{"key": "B1a", "text": "push or bolus"}, {"key": "B1b", "text": "piggyback on a pump"}, {"key": "B1c", "text": "diluted infusion"}, {"key": "B1d", "text": "oral liquid only forever"}], "B2": [{"key": "B2a", "text": "diluted, rate-controlled"}, {"key": "B2b", "text": "undiluted concentrate"}, {"key": "B2c", "text": "free-flow gravity bolus"}, {"key": "B2d", "text": "intramuscular depot"}], "B3": [{"key": "B3a", "text": "≤10 mEq/hour (with concentration limits)"}, {"key": "B3b", "text": "100 mEq in 1 minute"}, {"key": "B3c", "text": "any rate the client prefers"}, {"key": "B3d", "text": "undiluted push q5min"}]}}
rationales:
B1a: Correct. Never give potassium as an IV push or bolus (OpenStax).
B1b: Incorrect. Piggyback on a pump is an infusion method, not the forbidden action named here.
B1c: Incorrect. Diluted infusion is the correct route modality, not the forbidden action.
B1d: Incorrect. Oral liquid may be used when appropriate but does not answer the IV safety blank.
B2a: Correct. Administer diluted, rate-controlled IV infusion (OpenStax/Merck).
B2b: Incorrect. Undiluted concentrate IV push/bolus is dangerous.
B2c: Incorrect. Free-flow gravity bolus lacks safe rate control.
B2d: Incorrect. Potassium replacement is not given as an IM depot for this indication.
B3a: Correct. Merck: routine infusion rates should not exceed about 10 mEq/hour with concentration limits.
B3b: Incorrect. 100 mEq in 1 minute is a lethal rapid bolus pattern.
B3c: Incorrect. Client preference does not override safe infusion limits.
B3d: Incorrect. Undiluted push dosing is contraindicated.

stem: The nurse prepares to give subcutaneous unfractionated heparin. Which technique is correct?
options:
A) Inject into the abdomen at least 2 inches (5 cm) from the umbilicus and do not massage the site afterward
B) Inject into the deltoid IM and vigorously massage to speed absorption
C) Always inject directly into the umbilicus and rub hard for 2 minutes
D) Give as an IV push of undiluted concentrate through a central line without verification
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax Clinical Skills: preferred heparin SQ site is abdomen ≥2 in from umbilicus; do not massage (hematoma risk). Open RN Skills: abdomen >2 inches from umbilicus; do not massage after heparin.
B: Incorrect. Heparin prophylaxis is subcutaneous, not IM deltoid with massage.
C: Incorrect. Avoid the umbilicus; massage increases hematoma risk.
D: Incorrect. This item addresses subcutaneous technique, not unverified IV concentrate push.
topic: Subcutaneous heparin — abdomen ≥2 inches from umbilicus; do not massage

stem: Parents ask whether they can put a little honey on their 6-month-old’s soother. Which teaching is correct?
options:
A) Do not give any honey (including on food, formula, water, or soothers) until the infant is over 1 year old because of infant botulism risk
B) Honey is required daily for all infants starting at 2 months to prevent constipation
C) Any heated honey is always sterile and safe for newborns
D) Only raw honey is unsafe; pasteurized honey is risk-free for infants
rationales:
A: Correct. Health Canada: do not give any honey to infants <1 year; never add to food/water/formula/soother. CDC: no honey before 12 months; do not add to food, water, formula, or pacifier.
B: Incorrect. Honey is not a required infant remedy and is contraindicated under age 1.
C: Incorrect. Spores are not easily destroyed by heat/cooking.
D: Incorrect. Health Canada notes spores may be in pasteurized and unpasteurized honey.
topic: Infant feeding safety — no honey under 12 months (infant botulism risk)

stem: A postpartum client reports nipple pain with feeding. Which teaching best promotes an effective deep latch?
options:
A) Wait for a wide-open mouth, bring the baby to the breast so the chin presses into the breast, and aim for a deep latch with flanged lips
B) Only place the tip of the nipple between tightly pursed lips and keep the baby’s chin away from the breast
C) Force the latch while the mouth is barely open and pull the breast to the baby across the crib
D) Avoid any areola in the mouth and stop feeding at the first swallow
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: wait for wide mouth; bring baby to breast; nipple deep; chin deep into breast; lips flanged. OWH: chin to breast, wide mouth, deep latch signs include comfort and flanged lips.
B: Incorrect. Shallow nipple-only latch causes pain and poor transfer.
C: Incorrect. Forcing a barely open mouth is ineffective and traumatic.
D: Incorrect. Effective latch includes more breast/areola tissue, not nipple tip only.
topic: Breastfeeding latch — wide mouth, deep latch with chin into breast and flanged lips
source_2_section: Signs of a good latch; helping latch

stem: A client says, “Everything is useless now.” Which nurse response best uses clarification?
options:
A) “I’m not sure I understand what you mean by useless—can you give an example of what feels useless?”
B) “Don’t say that—you should feel grateful you are here.”
C) “Let’s talk about the cafeteria menu instead.”
D) “Everyone feels useless sometimes, so it doesn’t matter.”
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax Fundamentals: clarifying helps when communication is confusing/ambiguous. Open RN: clarification asks the client to further define meaning (example: “I’m not sure I understand… can you give an example?”).
B: Incorrect. Judging/disapproval is nontherapeutic.
C: Incorrect. Changing the subject is a barrier.
D: Incorrect. Minimizing dismisses the client’s experience.
topic: Therapeutic communication — clarifying ambiguous client statements

rationales:

R2: Indicated. Open-ended leads support therapeutic exploration.
R3: Not indicated. Changing the subject is a barrier.
R4: Not indicated. Minimizing/false reassurance is nontherapeutic.

stem: A parent asks how much fluoride toothpaste to use for a 4-year-old. Which teaching is correct?
options:
A) Use a pea-sized amount of fluoride toothpaste, supervise brushing, and teach the child to spit rather than swallow
B) Fill the entire brush head with adult toothpaste and have the child swallow it for systemic benefit
C) Never use fluoride toothpaste at any age because fluorosis is inevitable with pea-sized amounts
D) Use a full ribbon of toothpaste and rinse vigorously with mouthwash after every brush
rationales:
A: Correct. CPS Caring for Kids: by age 3–4 use pea-sized fluoride toothpaste; spit; supervise. CDC: ages 3–6 use no more than pea-sized amount; teach spit, not swallow.
B: Incorrect. Excess toothpaste increases swallowing/fluorosis risk.
C: Incorrect. Age-appropriate fluoride toothpaste prevents decay when used correctly.
D: Incorrect. Full ribbon exceeds pediatric amount guidance.

stem: An Ontario nurse is asked by a colleague to backdate a medication administration entry that was never given. Which response reflects professional accountability?
options:
A) Refuse—falsifying a record relating to nursing practice is professional misconduct and documentation must remain accurate
B) Agree to falsify the entry if it helps the unit’s chart audit scores
C) Delete another nurse’s notes so the timeline looks cleaner
D) Document the medication as given before it is administered to save time
rationales:
A: Correct. O. Reg. 799/93 lists falsifying a record relating to the member’s practice as professional misconduct. CNO Documentation: nurses must not falsify a record, including signing/issuing documents known to be false or misleading.
B: Incorrect. Falsification remains misconduct regardless of workplace pressure.
C: Incorrect. Altering/deleting others’ documentation is prohibited.
D: Incorrect. CNO: do not document before care is provided.
topic: Ontario — falsifying a practice record is professional misconduct
jurisdiction_note: Ontario O. Reg. 799/93 professional misconduct + CNO Documentation standard

stem: A hospitalized client is colonized with vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus (VRE). Which infection-control action is most appropriate in acute care?
options:
A) Place the client on Contact Precautions and wear a gown and gloves for care involving contact with the client or environment
B) Use Airborne Precautions with a negative-pressure room and N95 for all VRE colonization
C) No PPE is needed because colonization never transmits in hospitals
D) Use Droplet Precautions with a surgical mask only and leave the door open to the hallway
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC Appendix A lists MDROs including VRE for Contact + Standard Precautions when judged clinically/epidemiologically significant; OpenStax lists VRE among MDROs and Contact Precautions require gown and gloves.
B: Incorrect. Airborne/AIIR is not the routine category for VRE colonization.
C: Incorrect. Contact transmission of MDROs is a recognized healthcare risk.
D: Incorrect. Droplet-only PPE does not address contact/environmental transmission of VRE.

stem: A nurse reports a latex allergy. Which workplace action best protects the nurse while maintaining infection-control barriers?
options:
A) Provide readily accessible suitable non-latex (or otherwise appropriate alternative) gloves so barrier protection continues without latex exposure
B) Require continued powdered latex gloves because ‘hypoallergenic’ always means latex-free
C) Stop all glove use for blood exposure tasks so the allergy resolves
D) Only wear latex gloves inside-out to neutralize proteins
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: use latex-free alternatives such as neoprene or vinyl for latex sensitivity. OSHA BBP: hypoallergenic gloves, liners, powderless gloves, or similar alternatives shall be readily accessible to employees allergic to the gloves normally provided.
B: Incorrect. Hypoallergenic labeling must not be assumed to mean latex-free.
C: Incorrect. Barrier protection is still required for blood/OPIM exposure.
D: Incorrect. Inside-out latex still exposes the wearer to latex proteins.
topic: Latex allergy — provide latex-free / alternative gloves for allergic staff or clients

stem: A client is admitted with suspected pharyngeal diphtheria. Which isolation plan is correct?
options:
A) Use Droplet Precautions (with Contact as indicated) and continue until the client is off effective antimicrobial therapy and follow-up cultures are negative per guidance
B) No isolation is needed because diphtheria is only foodborne
C) Use Airborne Precautions in an AIIR for the entire hospital stay regardless of cultures
D) Use Contact Precautions only for 2 hours after the first antibiotic dose, then discontinue all precautions
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC Appendix A: pharyngeal diphtheria — Droplet + Standard until off antimicrobial treatment and culture-negative (2 cultures 24 h apart). Merck: isolation with respiratory-droplet (and contact) precautions until sequential cultures after antibiotics are negative.
B: Incorrect. Respiratory diphtheria spreads by droplets/secretions.
C: Incorrect. Routine category is Droplet (+ Contact as indicated), not indefinite Airborne/AIIR solely for diphtheria.
D: Incorrect. Precautions continue until treatment completion and culture clearance criteria are met.

stem: After gastric resection, a client develops postprandial weakness, sweating, dizziness, and palpitations suggestive of dumping syndrome. Which dietary teaching is most appropriate?
options:
A) Eat smaller, more frequent meals and decrease carbohydrate (especially hyperosmolar/high-sugar) intake
B) Drink large volumes of sugary soda with every large meal to ‘dilute’ the stomach contents
C) Eat only two very large high-carbohydrate meals daily
D) Replace all meals with undiluted fruit juice boluses for rapid emptying
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: dumping after gastric surgery — dietary modifications with smaller, more frequent meals and decreased carbohydrate intake usually help. MedlinePlus post–gastric bypass: eat 6 small meals; avoid foods/drinks high in sugar/carbohydrates; do not drink while eating.
B: Incorrect. Sugary liquids with large meals worsen dumping/hyperosmolar symptoms.
C: Incorrect. Large high-carbohydrate meals provoke dumping.
D: Incorrect. Rapid carbohydrate boluses worsen symptoms.

stem: A client with Parkinson disease has impaired balance and a shuffling gait. Which nursing action best reduces fall risk?
options:
A) Teach fall-prevention strategies and support home safety adaptations (for example grab bars) while maximizing safe activity
B) Encourage running on wet floors without assistive devices to ‘challenge balance’
C) Remove all lighting so the client learns to walk in the dark
D) Keep pathways cluttered with cords to build agility
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: therapists may teach adaptive strategies and home adaptations (e.g., grab bars) to reduce fall risk while maximizing activity. OpenStax: environments should promote safety and help clients avoid falls and other hazards.
B: Incorrect. Unsafe challenge increases fall/injury risk.
C: Incorrect. Poor lighting increases fall risk.
D: Incorrect. Clutter and cords are fall hazards.

stem: A client arrives with suspected acute coronary syndrome. Unless contraindicated, which antiplatelet action is appropriate on arrival?
options:
A) Give non–enteric-coated aspirin 160–325 mg for the client to chew (then swallow) to speed absorption
B) Give only enteric-coated aspirin 81 mg to swallow whole without chewing, and delay any antiplatelet therapy for 24 hours
C) Never give aspirin in ACS because it always worsens thrombosis
D) Administer aspirin as an intramuscular injection into the deltoid for fastest effect
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: all patients given aspirin 160–325 mg (not enteric-coated) if not contraindicated; chewing the first dose quickens absorption. OpenStax: administer 325 mg aspirin for platelet aggregation in MI care.
B: Incorrect. Initial ACS dosing is chewed non–enteric-coated 160–325 mg, not delayed enteric 81 mg only.
C: Incorrect. Early aspirin reduces mortality risk in ACS/MI.
D: Incorrect. Oral chewed aspirin is the standard initial route described here, not IM.
topic: Suspected ACS/MI — chewed non–enteric-coated aspirin 160–325 mg unless contraindicated

stem: Which statement best reflects the Five Rights of Nursing Delegation?
options:
A) Delegation decisions should address the right task, right circumstance, right person, right communication/directions, and right supervision/evaluation
B) Once a task is delegated, the RN has no accountability for patient outcomes
C) Any unstable critical-care task may be freely delegated without assessing competence
D) The Five Rights replace the need for facility policies and nurse practice act compliance
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax and NCSBN/ANA National Guidelines list the Five Rights: right task, circumstance, person, communication/directions, and supervision/evaluation.
B: Incorrect. The RN retains accountability for appropriate delegation and outcomes.
C: Incorrect. Right circumstance requires stable/appropriate conditions; competence must be verified.
D: Incorrect. Delegation still must comply with law, standards, and employer policy.

stem: An Ontario nurse is asked to sign a letter that intentionally misstates a client’s clinical status. Which statement is correct?
options:
A) Signing or issuing, in a professional capacity, a document the nurse knows or ought to know contains a false or misleading statement is professional misconduct
B) False statements are acceptable if the employer requests them for convenience
C) Only physicians can commit documentation-related professional misconduct in Ontario
D) Nurses may knowingly issue misleading documents if no one is expected to read them
rationales:
A: Correct. O. Reg. 799/93 lists signing/issuing a known false or misleading professional document as misconduct. CNO Documentation likewise prohibits falsifying records and signing/issuing documents with false or misleading statements.
B: Incorrect. Employer convenience does not authorize false professional documents.
C: Incorrect. The Nursing Act regulation applies to nurses.
D: Incorrect. Knowingly issuing false/misleading documents is misconduct regardless of expected readership.

stem: A client starting disulfiram for alcohol use disorder asks what to avoid. Which teaching is most accurate?
options:
A) Avoid alcoholic beverages and alcohol-containing products (e.g., some cough syrups/elixirs); unpleasant reactions can still occur for days after the last dose
B) Alcohol is safe with disulfiram if limited to one beer with meals
C) Only distilled spirits interact; wine and beer never cause a reaction
D) Disulfiram may be started while the client is currently intoxicated to ‘reset’ tolerance
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: drinking within 12 hours of disulfiram causes flushing/tachycardia/sweating and possibly hypotension; medications containing alcohol (tinctures, elixirs, some OTC cough/cold preparations) must also be avoided; effects may persist days after the last dose. OpenStax: abstain ≥12 hours before starting; reactions can occur up to 2 weeks after discontinuation; avoid nontraditional alcohol sources (mouthwash, cough syrup, hand sanitizer).
B: Incorrect. Even small amounts of alcohol can trigger a reaction.
C: Incorrect. Any alcohol source can trigger the reaction.
D: Incorrect. Disulfiram must not be given during intoxication; wait ≥12 hours after drinking.
topic: Disulfiram — avoid alcohol and alcohol-containing products; reaction risk persists after last dose

stem: A client prescribed oral metronidazole asks about drinking alcohol. Which instruction is correct?
options:
A) Avoid alcohol while taking metronidazole and for at least 3 days after the final dose to reduce risk of a disulfiram-like reaction (flushing, headache, nausea/vomiting)
B) Alcohol is encouraged because it improves metronidazole absorption
C) Only red wine interacts; clear liquors are always safe
D) Alcohol may be resumed the same evening as the last dose
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: a disulfiram-like reaction may occur if alcohol is ingested within 3 days of use. MedlinePlus: do not drink alcoholic beverages or take products with alcohol/propylene glycol while taking metronidazole and for at least 3 days after the final dose.
B: Incorrect. Alcohol can cause an unpleasant reaction, not improved absorption.
C: Incorrect. Any alcohol may trigger the reaction.
D: Incorrect. Continue avoidance for at least 3 days after the last dose.
topic: Metronidazole — avoid alcohol during therapy and for 3 days after last dose (disulfiram-like reaction)

stem: For a client taking metronidazole, indicate whether each teaching point is Indicated or Not indicated.

R2: Indicated. Continue avoidance ≥3 days after last dose.

R4: Not indicated. Alcohol increases risk of adverse reaction.
R5: Not indicated. Risk window continues for at least 3 days after the final dose.

stem: Which teaching is essential for a client starting oral alendronate for osteoporosis?
options:
A) Take with a full glass of plain water on an empty stomach in the morning, and remain sitting or standing upright for at least 30 minutes before lying down or taking other food/medications
B) Take with milk at bedtime and lie flat immediately to improve absorption
C) Crush the tablet into orange juice and take with breakfast
D) Take only with coffee to enhance bone uptake
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: take with 6–8 oz water and sit/stand ≥30 minutes to prevent esophageal irritation. MedlinePlus: morning empty stomach; do not lie down for ≥30 minutes; swallow tablet with plain water only (not tea/coffee/juice/milk).
B: Incorrect. Bedtime/lying flat and milk increase esophageal risk and impair absorption.
C: Incorrect. Do not crush into juice; take whole with plain water before food.
D: Incorrect. Coffee is not an appropriate liquid vehicle.
topic: Alendronate — take with plain water on empty stomach; remain upright ≥30 minutes

stem: After a below-knee amputation, a client reports burning pain in the missing foot. Which nursing response is most appropriate?
options:
A) Acknowledge that phantom limb pain is a real neuropathic sensation after amputation and assess/manage the pain
B) Tell the client the pain is imaginary because the foot is gone
C) Ignore the report because phantom sensations never require treatment
D) Immediately remove the residual-limb dressing and discard all analgesics as unnecessary
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: phantom pain is caused by misinterpreted signals, but the pain is real. Merck lists phantom limb pain as a neuropathic/deafferentation pain syndrome felt in the region of an amputated body part.
B: Incorrect. Dismissing the pain as imaginary is inaccurate and nontherapeutic.
C: Incorrect. Phantom pain often requires assessment and management.
D: Incorrect. Do not discard needed dressings/analgesics based on misunderstanding of phantom pain.

rationales:
R1: Indicated. OpenStax: pain is real; assess/describe.
R2: Indicated. OpenStax: rule out other medical causes such as infection.
R3: Indicated. Neuropathic phantom pain warrants management (OpenStax/Merck context).
R4: Not indicated. Dismissive and inaccurate.

stem: While assessing a closed chest-tube drainage system, the nurse notes continuous bubbling in the water-seal chamber. What is the priority interpretation and action?
options:
A) Continuous bubbling may indicate an air leak; check the drain/tubing for disconnection, dislodgement, or loose connections, assess the client, and notify the provider if the problem cannot be corrected
B) Continuous bubbling always means the system is perfectly sealed and needs no further assessment
C) Ignore bubbling and clamp the chest tube tightly for the remainder of the shift without assessment
D) Pour oil into the water-seal chamber to stop all bubbling permanently
rationales:
A: Correct. Open RN: continuous bubbling in the water-seal chamber may indicate an air leak; check connections/site and notify if uncorrected. RCH: continuous bubbling indicates a large air leak between drain and patient—check disconnection/dislodgement/loose connection, assess, and notify medical staff if not remedied.
B: Incorrect. Continuous bubbling is a cue for possible air leak, not assurance of a perfect seal.
C: Incorrect. Indiscriminate prolonged clamping without troubleshooting is unsafe.
D: Incorrect. Not an appropriate intervention.
topic: Chest tube water-seal chamber — continuous bubbling suggests air leak; check connections and notify
source_1_title: Chapter 6 Manage Chest Tube Drainage Systems
source_1_publisher: Open RN / Nursing Advanced Skills (NCBI Bookshelf)
source_1_section: Water seal chamber; continuous bubbling may indicate air leak

stem: Which action correctly provides prophylaxis against gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum for a healthy term newborn?
options:
A) Instill erythromycin 0.5% ophthalmic ointment into both eyes as soon as possible after birth (ideally soon after delivery; ensure within 24 hours if delayed)
B) Wait until the 2-week well-baby visit to apply any eye ointment
C) Apply antibiotic ointment to only one eye to ‘test tolerance’
D) Flush both eyes with undiluted household bleach instead of ointment
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC: erythromycin 0.5% ointment in each eye in a single application at birth, as soon as possible after delivery (vaginal or cesarean), with a system to ensure prophylaxis <24 hours if delayed. Merck: topical antimicrobial ointment to both eyes; erythromycin 0.5% recommended in the United States.
B: Incorrect. Prophylaxis is given soon after birth, not delayed weeks.
C: Incorrect. Both eyes require application.
D: Incorrect. Dangerous and not indicated.
topic: Newborn ocular prophylaxis — erythromycin 0.5% ointment both eyes soon after birth
source_1_title: Gonococcal Infections Among Neonates — STI Treatment Guidelines
source_1_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_2_title: Initial Evaluation and Preventive Care in the Healthy Term Newborn

stem: An Ontario nurse realizes that a recently used substance may be impairing judgment before a scheduled shift. Which statement is correct?
options:
A) Practising nursing while impaired by any substance is professional misconduct; the nurse must not practise while impaired and should seek help if health affects safe practice
B) Working impaired is acceptable if the nurse ‘feels fine enough’ to finish charting only
C) Only illegal substances count; prescribed medications never impair practice
D) Impairment is solely an employer HR issue and is never a professional-misconduct concern in Ontario
rationales:
A: Correct. O. Reg. 799/93 lists practising while the member’s ability is impaired by any substance as professional misconduct. CNO Code of Conduct 6.8: nurses do not practise when impaired by any substance; 6.7: seek help if health affects safe practice.
B: Incorrect. Impairment precludes safe practice regardless of limited tasks.
C: Incorrect. Any impairing substance is within the regulation’s scope.
D: Incorrect. It is defined professional misconduct under Ontario regulation and CNO standards.
topic: Ontario — practising nursing while impaired by any substance is professional misconduct
jurisdiction_note: O. Reg. 799/93 s.1 item 6 + CNO Code of Conduct 6.8

stem: A client with alcohol use disorder is prescribed oral naltrexone with counseling. Which teaching is most accurate?
options:
A) Naltrexone is an opioid antagonist that can reduce alcohol craving and block some of the pleasurable effects of drinking; it is used along with counseling/support, not as a standalone cure
B) Naltrexone works like disulfiram and always causes severe flushing and vomiting after any alcohol
C) Naltrexone replaces alcohol craving with opioid dependence and should be stopped after one dose
D) Naltrexone prevents alcohol withdrawal seizures and is the only treatment needed without counseling
rationales:
A: Correct. MedlinePlus: naltrexone decreases craving for alcohol and is used with counseling/social support. OpenStax PMH: naltrexone is an opioid antagonist that blocks the pleasurable parts of drinking; adherence and counseling matter.
B: Incorrect. Disulfiram (not naltrexone) causes the aversive alcohol reaction.
C: Incorrect. Naltrexone is not an opioid agonist and is not addictive replacement therapy.
D: Incorrect. It does not treat withdrawal as monotherapy; counseling/support remain part of care.
topic: Naltrexone for AUD — opioid antagonist reduces alcohol craving/reward; used with counseling
source_1_publisher: MedlinePlus / U.S. National Library of Medicine

stem: A client starts a second-generation (atypical) antipsychotic. Which monitoring plan best addresses a common class risk?
options:
A) Assess weight/BMI and, per orders, fasting glucose and lipids at intervals; teach diet/activity because metabolic syndrome risk (weight gain, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia) is increased
B) Ignore weight and labs because atypical agents never affect metabolism
C) Only monitor for agranulocytosis weekly and skip metabolic measures for all atypical agents
D) Restrict all fluid intake permanently to prevent metabolic syndrome
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: metabolic side effects include insulin resistance, hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia, weight gain; nursing interventions include assess weight/BMI, fasting glucose and lipids, educate on diet/exercise. Merck: metabolic syndrome risk is greater with second-generation antipsychotics.
B: Incorrect. Metabolic effects are a recognized SGA risk.
C: Incorrect. ANC monitoring is specific to clozapine; metabolic monitoring applies more broadly to SGAs.
D: Incorrect. Fluid restriction is not the metabolic prevention strategy.
topic: Second-generation antipsychotics — monitor weight/BMI, fasting glucose, and lipids for metabolic syndrome
source_1_section: Second-Generation Antipsychotics; Table 15.4 Metabolic side effects

stem: Parents of a healthy term newborn ask how to balance safe sleep with preventing a flat spot on the baby’s head. Which teaching is best?
options:
A) Place the baby on the back to sleep, and provide supervised tummy time when the baby is awake (CPS suggests about 10–15 minutes at least 3 times/day)
B) Put the baby to sleep prone every night to flatten the tummy instead of the head
C) Never allow the baby on the tummy while awake because tummy time is unsafe at any age
D) Leave the baby alone on a soft pillow for unsupervised tummy sleep naps
rationales:
A: Correct. CPS Caring for Kids: back sleep for SIDS risk reduction; supervised tummy time when awake 10–15 minutes at least 3 times/day helps prevent flat head and supports development. CDC HIOPS: ensure infants have supervised tummy time every day when awake.
B: Incorrect. Prone sleep increases SIDS risk.
C: Incorrect. Supervised awake tummy time is recommended.
D: Incorrect. Tummy time must be supervised; soft bedding/sleep on tummy is unsafe.
topic: Supervised tummy time while awake — supports development and helps prevent positional flat head; sleep on back
source_1_title: Preventing flat heads in babies who sleep on their backs
source_1_publisher: Canadian Paediatric Society — Caring for Kids
source_1_section: What else can I do to prevent my baby from getting a flat head?

stem: An infant of a diabetic mother is at risk for neonatal hypoglycemia. Which nursing action best supports prevention in the first hours of life?
options:
A) Encourage early breastfeeding initiation (within about 30–60 minutes), promote skin-to-skin to reduce cold stress, and follow facility protocol for glucose monitoring of at-risk newborns
B) Delay the first feed for 12 hours so the infant sleeps uninterrupted
C) Avoid all glucose checks because asymptomatic term newborns never become hypoglycemic
D) Place the infant under a cold draft to increase metabolic rate and raise glucose
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: encourage breastfeeding within 30–60 minutes, skin-to-skin to prevent cold stress, frequent feeds, and monitoring of at-risk newborns (IDM, SGA/LGA, etc.). Merck: at-risk neonates who are not sick should start early, frequent feedings; high-risk infants often treated preventively.
B: Incorrect. Delayed feeding increases hypoglycemia risk.
C: Incorrect. At-risk infants require protocolized screening even before symptoms.
D: Incorrect. Cold stress depletes glucose stores.
topic: Neonatal hypoglycemia prevention — early feeding and skin-to-skin for at-risk newborns; monitor glucose
source_1_title: 24.2 Care of Common Problems in the Newborn
source_1_section: Care of the Newborn with Hypoglycemia

stem: An infant is fitted with a Pavlik harness for developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH). Which caregiver teaching is correct?
options:
A) The harness holds the hips abducted and externally rotated to keep the femoral head in the acetabulum; keep it on as directed by the care team—padded/double diapering alone is not effective treatment
B) Remove the harness permanently after one hour and rely only on triple diapering
C) The harness should force the hips into full adduction against the midline
D) Parents should freely cut and redesign all straps without clinician guidance
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: Pavlik harness holds affected hips abducted and externally rotated; padded diapers and double/triple diapering are not effective. AboutKidsHealth: soft straps keep legs bent up and apart; worn as directed (often nearly continuous early).
B: Incorrect. Double/triple diapering is ineffective; harness wear follows care-team plan.
C: Incorrect. Goal is abduction/external rotation, not forced adduction.
D: Incorrect. Application/adjustment is by/with health professionals; straps are marked.
topic: DDH — Pavlik harness holds hips abducted/externally rotated; double diapering is ineffective

stem: A nurse intercepts a wrong-dose medication before administration (near miss). What is the priority leadership/safety action after ensuring the client remains safe?
options:
A) Report the near miss/error according to agency policy (incident/event report) so the organization can analyze system factors and improve safety—not to assign personal blame
B) Hide the event because no harm occurred and reporting is never useful
C) Document only in a personal diary and never notify the supervisor or safety system
D) Publicly shame the pharmacist on social media instead of using the event reporting system
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax Fund 11.3: after ensuring safety and notifying the team, document via incident report; aim is not blame but identifying system issues and continuous improvement. AHRQ PSNet: incident reporting captures events/near misses from frontline staff to detect safety problems for further investigation.
B: Incorrect. Near misses should be reported for learning.
C: Incorrect. Use the formal reporting pathway and notify appropriate leaders.
D: Incorrect. Unprofessional and not a safety system.
topic: Medication error/near miss — report via incident report for system learning, not blame
source_2_publisher: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) — PSNet

stem: An Ontario nurse has reasonable grounds to suspect that a 10-year-old client may be in need of protection because of neglect. What is the nurse’s legal duty?
options:
A) Promptly report the suspicion and the information on which it is based directly to a children’s aid society; the nurse must not rely on someone else to report on their behalf
B) Wait until absolute proof of abuse is obtained in court before telling anyone
C) Only tell a coworker and assume the coworker will call if they feel like it
D) Post the child’s identifying details on social media instead of contacting a society
rationales:
A: Correct. Ontario CYFSA guidance: anyone with reasonable grounds to suspect a child is/may be in need of protection must promptly report to a children’s aid society; must report directly and not rely on someone else (s.125). CNO: if abuse involves a child/youth, CYFSA requires health professionals to report suspected abuse.
B: Incorrect. Reasonable grounds to suspect are enough; certainty is not required.
C: Incorrect. Cannot rely on someone else to report.
D: Incorrect. Report to a society; protect confidentiality except as required for the report.
topic: Ontario CYFSA — duty to report child under 16 in need of protection directly to children’s aid society
jurisdiction_note: Ontario Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017 (CYFSA) s.125 duty to report; CNO accountability guidance.

stem: A community nurse teaches a household with confirmed cryptosporidiosis about hand hygiene. Which statement is most accurate?
options:
A) Wash hands with soap and water at key times; alcohol-based hand sanitizers are not effective against Cryptosporidium
B) Alcohol-based hand sanitizer alone is preferred after diaper changes because it kills Crypto oocysts
C) Hand hygiene is unnecessary once watery diarrhea begins
D) Only antibacterial soap with bleach must be used; plain soap and water never help
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC Preventing Crypto and Merck Prevention: alcohol-based sanitizers are not effective against this parasite; soap-and-water handwashing at key times is recommended.
B: Incorrect. Alcohol-based sanitizers are not effective against Crypto (CDC/Merck).
C: Incorrect. Hand hygiene remains essential to limit fecal-oral spread.
D: Incorrect. Thorough soap-and-water handwashing is the recommended hygiene practice; bleach is not required for routine handwashing.

stem: During an outbreak investigation teaching session, which statement about Legionnaires’ disease transmission is most accurate?
options:
A) People usually get it by breathing mist from water systems contaminated with Legionella; in general it is not spread person to person
B) It spreads mainly by casual skin contact, so gloves alone stop community outbreaks
C) It is almost always transmitted by coughing directly onto others in the same room
D) It only comes from spoiled food, never from building water systems
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC: breathe mist containing Legionella; in general not person to person. Merck: acquired by inhaling aerosols of contaminated water; not transmitted person to person (rare probable exception).
B: Incorrect. Transmission is via aerosols/aspiration of contaminated water, not casual skin contact.
C: Incorrect. Person-to-person spread is not the usual route.
D: Incorrect. Building plumbing/water aerosols (showers, hot tubs, cooling towers) are classic sources.
topic: Legionnaires’ disease — inhale contaminated water mist; generally not person-to-person

stem: A client with a femoral fracture develops sudden shortness of breath and new confusion about 36 hours after injury. Which complication should the nurse suspect first?
options:
A) Fat embolism syndrome related to long-bone fracture
B) Simple anxiety with no need to assess oxygenation
C) Delayed wound hematoma that never affects breathing
D) Benign muscle spasm that explains acute hypoxemia
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: fat embolism after long-bone fractures causes rapid-onset hypoxemia often with neurologic changes (and petechial rash). OpenStax: fat embolism risk after long-bone fractures; monitor for neurologic changes or shortness of breath, commonly 24–72 hours after fracture.
B: Incorrect. New dyspnea and confusion require urgent respiratory/neuro assessment for embolism.
C: Incorrect. Hematoma does not explain acute dyspnea and confusion in this pattern.
D: Incorrect. Muscle spasm does not cause acute hypoxemic respiratory syndromes.
topic: Fat embolism after long-bone fracture — dyspnea/hypoxemia and neurologic changes

options: {"columns": ["Indicated", "Not indicated"], "rows": [{"key": "R1", "text": "Notify the provider promptly and activate rapid response if indicated"}, {"key": "R2", "text": "Apply oxygen as needed and support airway/breathing while awaiting orders"}, {"key": "R3", "text": "Continue to monitor neurologic status and respiratory pattern closely"}, {"key": "R4", "text": "Reassure that dyspnea after long-bone fracture never needs escalation"}, {"key": "R5", "text": "Delay assessment because fat embolism only occurs after 2 weeks"}]}

R2: Indicated. OpenStax: apply oxygen as necessary; Merck describes severe hypoxemia needing support.
R3: Indicated. OpenStax/Merck: neurologic and respiratory changes are hallmark cues to monitor.
R4: Not indicated. Dyspnea/neuro changes require urgent escalation.
R5: Not indicated. OpenStax notes common onset 24–72 hours after fracture, not a 2-week delay only.

stem: A client with cirrhosis develops confusion and asterixis. Besides treating precipitating factors, which medication is commonly used for hepatic (portosystemic) encephalopathy?
options:
A) Oral lactulose (often with a nonabsorbable antibiotic such as rifaximin as indicated)
B) High-dose intravenous insulin as first-line encephalopathy therapy
C) Routine thrombolysis for every episode of asterixis
D) Disulfiram to reverse ammonia-related confusion
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: treatment includes correcting the acute cause, oral lactulose, and nonabsorbable antibiotics such as rifaximin. OpenStax hepatic encephalopathy table lists lactulose (and antibiotics) among treatments.
B: Incorrect. Insulin is not first-line therapy for hepatic encephalopathy.
C: Incorrect. Thrombolysis is not the treatment for asterixis from encephalopathy.
D: Incorrect. Disulfiram is for alcohol aversion, not ammonia/encephalopathy treatment.
topic: Hepatic encephalopathy — lactulose as standard treatment with cause correction

stem: An adolescent presents with sudden severe unilateral scrotal pain, nausea, and a high-riding tender testis. What is the priority nursing/medical action?
options:
A) Treat as a surgical emergency—facilitate immediate evaluation for manual detorsion/urgent surgery to restore blood flow
B) Schedule elective outpatient follow-up in 2 weeks because torsion is never urgent
C) Apply ice and discharge home without provider notification
D) Start oral antibiotics alone and cancel any surgical consult
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: emergency; immediate manual detorsion followed by surgical intervention. MedlinePlus: surgery as soon as possible; salvage best if within about 6 hours.
B: Incorrect. Delay risks permanent testicular damage.
C: Incorrect. Requires emergency evaluation, not home ice alone.
D: Incorrect. Antibiotics alone do not treat ischemia from torsion; surgery is needed.

stem: A charge nurse is assigning tasks on a busy unit. Which action best reflects safe leadership practice?
options:
A) Assign/delegate only to staff with verified education and competency for the task, considering patient acuity and skill mix—not census alone
B) Give the most complex unstable clients to the least experienced float nurse without orientation or competency check
C) Ignore acuity and assign solely by alphabetical room numbers
D) Delegate nursing judgment and initial assessment to untrained assistive personnel
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax Right Person: RN ensures required education/competencies. AHRQ: adequate staffing depends on acuity, skill mix, expertise—not numbers alone.
B: Incorrect. Unverified competency for complex unstable clients is unsafe.
C: Incorrect. Acuity and skill mix must inform assignments.
D: Incorrect. Nursing process/judgment cannot be delegated (OpenStax principles).

stem: An Ontario charge nurse knowingly assigns a nursing function to a team member who has not been trained or demonstrated competence for that function. Which statement is most accurate?
options:
A) Directing a member/student/team member to perform nursing functions they are not adequately trained or competent to perform is professional misconduct under O. Reg. 799/93
B) Ontario regulations encourage assigning any task to anyone regardless of competence
C) Only the client can be disciplined for staff competency gaps
D) Training and competence never matter if the shift is short-staffed
rationales:
A: Correct. O. Reg. 799/93 s.1 item 3 defines this directing as professional misconduct. OpenStax Right Person reinforces verifying education/competency before assigning/delegating.
B: Incorrect. The regulation prohibits directing inadequately trained/incompetent performance.
C: Incorrect. Accountability for directing unsafe assignment rests with the directing nurse under the misconduct regulation.
D: Incorrect. Staffing pressure does not authorize incompetent assignment.

stem: An older adult with GERD asks how to reduce nighttime heartburn. Which teaching point is most appropriate?
options:
A) Raise the head of the bed and avoid lying down for several hours after eating
B) Lie flat immediately after large evening meals to promote digestion
C) Place pillows under the knees only; head-of-bed elevation never helps reflux
D) Skip all lifestyle measures because only surgery treats GERD
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck Treatment of GERD: elevate head of bed; limit food within 4 hours of bedtime. MedlinePlus: raise head of bed; avoid lying down 2–3 hours after eating.
B: Incorrect. Lying down soon after eating worsens reflux (MedlinePlus/Merck).
C: Incorrect. Head-of-bed elevation is a standard nonpharmacologic measure.
D: Incorrect. Most people manage GERD with lifestyle changes and medicines; surgery is uncommon first-line.
topic: GERD — elevate head of bed; avoid lying down soon after eating

stem: An older adult with chronic venous insufficiency has dependent leg edema. Which self-care instruction is most appropriate?
options:
A) Elevate the legs periodically and use prescribed compression stockings
B) Keep the legs dangling dependent all day to improve arterial inflow
C) Avoid compression because stockings always worsen venous edema
D) Never change position; prolonged standing is preferred therapy
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: elevate legs above the right atrium ≥3 times/day for ≥30 minutes; compression is recommended. OpenStax: compression stockings and elevating legs assist venous return.
B: Incorrect. Dependent dangling worsens venous pooling/edema.
C: Incorrect. Compression is a mainstay of CVI treatment.
D: Incorrect. Prolonged standing worsens symptoms; position changes are encouraged.
topic: Chronic venous insufficiency — elevate legs and use compression

stem: A client starting long-term phenytoin asks about mouth care. Which teaching is most accurate?
options:
A) Phenytoin can cause gum overgrowth; good oral hygiene and dental follow-up help reduce gum damage
B) Phenytoin never affects the gums, so toothbrushing can be skipped
C) Mouth care is unnecessary because phenytoin sterilizes the oral cavity
D) Clients should stop all dental visits while taking phenytoin
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: long-term hydantoins (phenytoin) can cause gingival hyperplasia. MedlinePlus: care for teeth/gums/mouth is very important to decrease gum damage risk.
B: Incorrect. Gingival hyperplasia is a recognized long-term effect.
C: Incorrect. Phenytoin does not sterilize the mouth; oral care remains essential.
D: Incorrect. Dental awareness/follow-up supports gum health during therapy.

stem: A client with a fentanyl transdermal patch asks about home safety. Which instruction is most important?
options:
A) Do not cut or alter the patch, and avoid heating pads or other direct external heat over the application site
B) Cut the patch in half if pain is mild so the dose is smaller
C) Apply a heating pad over the patch to speed pain relief
D) Hot tubs and electric blankets over the patch are encouraged
rationales:
A: Correct. Health Canada Sandoz PM: do not use if altered/cut/damaged; avoid direct external heat (heating pads, electric blankets, saunas, etc.). NCBI Open RN: never apply heat over fentanyl patches—increases release and can cause overdose.
B: Incorrect. Cutting/altering the patch is contraindicated and unsafe.
C: Incorrect. External heat increases absorption and overdose risk.
D: Incorrect. Hot whirlpool/sauna/electric blankets are listed heat sources to avoid.

stem: A client taking allopurinol for gout develops a new widespread itchy rash. What is the priority teaching action?
options:
A) Stop allopurinol immediately and seek urgent medical care because rash may precede severe hypersensitivity reactions
B) Double the next dose to treat the rash as a gout flare
C) Continue allopurinol and ignore any skin changes

B: Incorrect. Dose increase is dangerous with possible hypersensitivity; stop the drug.

stem: The nurse prepares to instill prescribed otic drops for an adult client. How should the nurse straighten the ear canal?
options:
A) Gently pull the auricle (pinna) upward and backward
B) Pull the auricle firmly downward and forward only
C) Never touch the pinna; insert the dropper deep into the middle ear
D) Pull both earlobes toward the nose simultaneously
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: for an adult, pull the auricle up and back. MedlinePlus: pull the ear backward and upward (adult).
B: Incorrect. Down-and-back is the pediatric/young-child technique, not the adult default.
C: Incorrect. Dropper should not be forced deep; tip should stay clean and not traumatize the canal.
D: Incorrect. Not a recommended canal-straightening method.

stem: A client with borderline personality disorder asks which psychotherapy approach is considered the gold standard for this diagnosis. Which response is most accurate?
options:
A) Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT), which teaches skills such as mindfulness and distress tolerance
B) Benzodiazepines alone are first-line and replace the need for any psychotherapy
C) Only electroconvulsive therapy is effective for borderline personality disorder
D) No psychotherapy helps; medication cures the core personality pattern
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: DBT was created for BPD and is considered the gold standard; skills include mindfulness, distress tolerance, interpersonal effectiveness, and emotion regulation. Merck: psychotherapy is the mainstay; CBT approaches include dialectical behavioral therapy.
B: Incorrect. Merck: benzodiazepines are not recommended; psychotherapy is the mainstay.
C: Incorrect. ECT is not the gold-standard first-line treatment for BPD core features.
D: Incorrect. Psychotherapy is primary treatment; medications are adjunctive and not consistently effective for core BPD symptoms.
topic: Borderline personality disorder — DBT as gold-standard psychotherapy

stem: Five minutes after starting packed red blood cells, a client reports chills, dyspnea, and back pain. What is the nurse’s priority action?
options:
A) Stop the transfusion immediately and keep the IV line open with normal saline
B) Increase the infusion rate to finish the unit faster before notifying anyone
C) Ignore symptoms for 30 minutes because reactions never occur early
D) Restart the same unit after a brief pause without further investigation
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: if reaction symptoms occur, stop transfusion immediately and keep IV open with normal saline; send product/samples for investigation. OpenStax Skills: immediately stop the transfusion and notify the provider.
B: Incorrect. Speeding the infusion worsens exposure during a possible hemolytic/allergic reaction.
C: Incorrect. Most reactions occur in the first 15–20 minutes; early symptoms require action.
D: Incorrect. Merck: the implicated unit should not be restarted.
topic: Suspected transfusion reaction — stop transfusion immediately; keep IV open with normal saline

stem: A community health nurse teaches a Canadian household that keeps a non-restricted firearm. Which storage teaching is most appropriate?
options:

B) Leave firearms loaded and unlocked on a closet shelf because out of sight equals safe storage
C) Store loaded firearms under a child’s bed for quick access during play

A: Correct. RCMP: unload and lock firearms; store ammunition separately or lock it up. CDC: store unloaded and locked with ammunition secured separately; out of sight/reach is not enough.
B: Incorrect. CDC: out of sight/reach is not safe storage.
C: Incorrect. Loaded unlocked access by children is a preventable injury risk.
D: Incorrect. Locking devices and secure storage are recommended/required.

stem: A teen athlete collides during a game and shows confusion and headache suggesting concussion. What is the most appropriate immediate guidance?
options:
A) Remove the athlete from play now; do not return the same day; seek healthcare clearance before return to sport
B) Finish the game if the athlete says they feel fine after a water break
C) Return to full contact immediately to 'shake it off'
D) Allow same-day return whenever symptoms last less than 2 minutes
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC HEADS UP: remove right away; keep out the day of injury until cleared by a healthcare provider. CPS Caring for Kids: no return until cleared by a doctor; stepwise return-to-play.
B: Incorrect. Athletes should not judge severity themselves; same-day return is unsafe.
C: Incorrect. Early return increases risk of repeat concussion.
D: Incorrect. Brief symptom duration does not authorize same-day return.

stem: A community nurse teaches workers about preventing noise-induced hearing loss. Which instruction is most appropriate?
options:
A) Wear hearing protection (earplugs or earmuffs) during loud noise exposure around 85 dBA or higher, and reduce time near the noise when possible
B) Hearing protection is never needed because NIHL always reverses completely overnight
C) Stand closer to loud machinery so exposure time is shorter and safer
D) Only protect hearing after permanent deafness is already diagnosed
rationales:
A: Correct. NIDCD: long/repeated exposure ≥85 dBA can cause NIHL; wear earplugs/protective devices; move away if needed. CDC/NIOSH: REL 85 dBA/8 hours; always wear hearing protection in noisy areas; reduce time in noisy areas.
B: Incorrect. NIHL can be permanent; prevention is key.
C: Incorrect. Closer exposure increases intensity/risk.
D: Incorrect. Prevention should occur before irreversible loss.

stem: An immunocompetent older adult has localized herpes zoster (shingles) on the trunk; lesions can be completely covered with a dressing. Which infection-control approach is most appropriate?
options:
A) Standard Precautions (Routine Practices) with lesions covered until dry and crusted
B) Airborne and Contact Precautions in a negative-pressure room for the entire admission regardless of immune status
C) Droplet Precautions only for 24 hours after the first vesicle appears
D) No precautions are needed even if lesions are uncovered and draining
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC Appendix A: localized zoster in immunocompetent hosts with containable/coverable lesions → Standard Precautions until lesions dry and crusted. PHO: localized shingles require Routine Practices (vs airborne+contact for disseminated).
B: Incorrect. Airborne + Contact is for disseminated disease or localized disease in immunocompromised hosts until dissemination is ruled out.
C: Incorrect. Zoster is not managed with Droplet-only precautions for 24 hours.
D: Incorrect. Covering lesions and Standard/Routine Practices are required until crusted; uncovered draining lesions increase transmission risk.

stem: For an immunocompetent adult with localized, coverable herpes zoster lesions, indicate whether each action is Indicated or Not indicated.
options: {"columns": ["Indicated", "Not indicated"], "rows": [{"key": "R1", "text": "Cover lesions completely and use Standard/Routine Practices until lesions are dry and crusted"}, {"key": "R2", "text": "Place immediately in airborne isolation for disseminated disease without assessing lesion extent or immune status"}, {"key": "R3", "text": "Prefer immune caregivers when available; avoid susceptible HCWs providing direct care if alternatives exist"}, {"key": "R4", "text": "Leave vesicles uncovered in shared spaces to 'air dry' faster"}, {"key": "R5", "text": "Escalate to Airborne + Contact if disease is disseminated or the host is immunocompromised until dissemination is ruled out"}]}
rationales:
R1: Indicated. CDC: Standard until dry/crusted when localized and coverable; PHO: Routine Practices for localized shingles.
R2: Not indicated. Airborne isolation is not automatic for localized immunocompetent coverable disease.
R3: Indicated. CDC notes susceptible HCWs should not provide direct care when immune caregivers are available.
R4: Not indicated. Lesions should be covered to reduce transmission.
R5: Indicated. CDC: disseminated (any patient) or localized immunocompromised until dissemination ruled out → Airborne + Contact.
topic: NGN matrix — localized vs disseminated herpes zoster precautions

stem: Complete the infection-control teaching for localized herpes zoster in an immunocompetent adult.
options: {"template": "For localized, coverable shingles in an immunocompetent client, use {B1} and keep lesions {B2} until they are {B3}.", "blanks": {"B1": [{"key": "B1a", "text": "Standard Precautions / Routine Practices"}, {"key": "B1b", "text": "Airborne isolation for every localized case"}, {"key": "B1c", "text": "Droplet Precautions alone for 24 hours"}, {"key": "B1d", "text": "No precautions of any kind"}], "B2": [{"key": "B2a", "text": "completely covered"}, {"key": "B2b", "text": "fully uncovered at all times"}, {"key": "B2c", "text": "soaked continuously with alcohol"}, {"key": "B2d", "text": "shared uncovered with roommates"}], "B3": [{"key": "B3a", "text": "dry and crusted"}, {"key": "B3b", "text": "still blistering and wet"}, {"key": "B3c", "text": "painted with talcum powder only"}, {"key": "B3d", "text": "left open overnight intentionally"}]}}
rationales:
B1a: Correct. CDC Standard Precautions / PHO Routine Practices for localized shingles.
B1b: Incorrect. Airborne is for disseminated or immunocompromised localized until ruled out.
B1c: Incorrect. Not a Droplet-only 24-hour rule.
B1d: Incorrect. Precautions and covering are required.
B2a: Correct. CDC specifies lesions that can be contained/covered.
B2b: Incorrect. Covering reduces transmission.
B2c: Incorrect. Not an isolation teaching point.
B2d: Incorrect. Increases exposure risk.
B3a: Correct. Duration is until lesions dry and crusted (CDC/PHO).
B3b: Incorrect. Wet vesicles remain infectious.
B3c: Incorrect. Unrelated and inappropriate.
B3d: Incorrect. Contradicts covering until crusted.

stem: Which practice best reduces infection risk when using a multidose medication vial?
options:
A) Dedicate the multidose vial to a single patient when possible and use a new sterile needle and syringe for every entry
B) Leave a needle in the vial septum between doses so the vial stays 'open' for faster access
C) Reuse the same syringe for several patients if only the needle is changed
D) Carry one multidose vial from room to room and enter it with previously used syringes
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC: dedicate multidose vials to a single patient whenever possible; new sterile syringe/needle each patient. OpenStax: dedicate to single patient when possible; new needles/syringes every injection; do not leave needles in vials.
B: Incorrect. CDC/OpenStax: do not leave a needle in the septum (contamination pathway).
C: Incorrect. CDC: never reuse a syringe for more than one patient even if the needle is changed.
D: Incorrect. If a multidose vial enters a patient treatment area it must be single-patient only; never enter with used syringes.
topic: Multidose vials — dedicate to a single patient when possible; new sterile needle/syringe each entry

source_1_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

stem: Indicate whether each medication-preparation action is Indicated or Not indicated for safe multidose vial use.
options: {"columns": ["Indicated", "Not indicated"], "rows": [{"key": "R1", "text": "Assign the multidose vial to one patient whenever possible"}, {"key": "R2", "text": "Use a new sterile needle and syringe for every access, even for the same patient"}, {"key": "R3", "text": "Leave a needle parked in the vial septum between withdrawals"}, {"key": "R4", "text": "If the vial enters a patient room/bay, treat it as single-patient use only"}, {"key": "R5", "text": "Enter a multidose vial with a syringe that already injected another patient after changing only the needle"}]}
rationales:
R1: Indicated. CDC and OpenStax: dedicate multidose vials to a single patient when possible.
R2: Indicated. OpenStax: new needles/syringes for every injection; CDC: new sterile syringe and needle.
R3: Not indicated. Both sources prohibit leaving a needle in the septum.
R4: Indicated. CDC/OpenStax: vial entering immediate patient treatment area → single-patient only.
R5: Not indicated. Never enter a vial with a syringe used on another patient; never reuse syringes across patients.
topic: NGN matrix — multidose vial and safe injection practices indicated vs not

stem: A nurse sustains a needlestick with a hollow-bore needle used on a client with known HIV infection. After washing the site with soap and water, which next action is the priority?
options:
A) Report the exposure immediately and seek urgent evaluation so HIV PEP can start as soon as possible (within 72 hours)
B) Wait 1 week to see if a rash develops before reporting
C) Squeeze the puncture site forcefully to 'bleed out' the virus and skip occupational health
D) Delay care until the source client's full genotype results return next month
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC: wash skin after contact; report and get medical care right away; PEP must start within 72 hours; sooner is better. Merck: start PEP as soon after exposure as possible; ideally within 24–36 hours and no later than 72 hours.
B: Incorrect. Delay beyond the urgent window reduces PEP effectiveness.
C: Incorrect. Do not rely on squeezing; report and follow exposure protocol.
D: Incorrect. Do not delay PEP while awaiting non-urgent source details (CDC/Merck emphasize prompt start).
topic: Occupational blood exposure — wash, report, start HIV PEP as soon as possible (within 72 hours)
client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
source_1_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_1_section: Prevent HIV exposures at work; Managing HIV exposures at work

stem: After a percutaneous exposure to blood from a client with HIV, indicate whether each action is Indicated or Not indicated.
options: {"columns": ["Indicated", "Not indicated"], "rows": [{"key": "R1", "text": "Wash the exposed skin with soap and water immediately"}, {"key": "R2", "text": "Report the exposure and obtain urgent medical evaluation for PEP"}, {"key": "R3", "text": "Start PEP as soon as possible, within 72 hours of exposure"}, {"key": "R4", "text": "Wait several days 'to see what happens' before seeking care"}, {"key": "R5", "text": "Assume household soap is unnecessary because gloves were worn earlier in the shift"}]}
rationales:
R1: Indicated. CDC: wash hands/skin immediately after blood/body-fluid contact.
R2: Indicated. CDC: report and see a clinician/ER right away; Merck: follow occupational exposure PEP policies.
R3: Indicated. CDC ≤72 h; Merck ideally 24–36 h and no later than 72 h.
R4: Not indicated. Delay reduces benefit of PEP.
R5: Not indicated. Immediate washing after exposure is still required.

stem: Which teaching point best reduces Listeria risk in pregnancy?
options:
A) Avoid unheated deli meats/cold cuts and cheeses made with unpasteurized milk; choose safer heated or pasteurized options
B) Eat only raw sprouts and refrigerated pâté because they are safest in pregnancy
C) Listeria cannot affect pregnancy, so no dietary changes are needed
D) Unpasteurized soft cheeses are preferred over pasteurized hard cheeses
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC safer choices: reheat deli meats; avoid unpasteurized milk cheeses. PHAC: higher-risk foods include non-dried deli meats, soft/semi-soft cheeses, unpasteurized milk; pregnant people are high risk.
B: Incorrect. CDC lists raw sprouts and refrigerated pâté among foods to avoid/choose safer alternatives.
C: Incorrect. Pregnancy is a high-risk group; infection can harm the fetus/newborn (PHAC).
D: Incorrect. Unpasteurized soft cheeses are higher risk; pasteurized hard cheeses are safer choices.
topic: Pregnancy Listeria prevention — avoid unheated deli meats and unpasteurized soft cheeses

stem: A pregnant client asks whether Tdap is needed this pregnancy after receiving Tdap 2 years ago. Which response is most accurate?
options:
A) Yes — Tdap is recommended during every pregnancy (ideally in the third trimester) to protect the newborn from pertussis
B) No — one lifetime Tdap dose means no further doses are ever given in pregnancy
C) Tdap is contraindicated in all pregnancies and must wait until the child is age 5
D) Only live-virus Tdap is used, and it must be given in the first trimester exclusively
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC: Tdap during each pregnancy irrespective of prior history; preferably early 27–36 weeks. NACI: Tdap every pregnancy irrespective of history; ideally 27–32 weeks.
B: Incorrect. Prior Tdap does not remove the every-pregnancy recommendation.
C: Incorrect. Tdap in pregnancy is recommended and considered safe in cited guidance.
D: Incorrect. Tdap is not a live-virus vaccine; timing is third-trimester focused, not first-trimester exclusive.
topic: Tdap in every pregnancy to protect the newborn from pertussis
jurisdiction_note: CDC prefers early 27–36 weeks; NACI ideally 27–32 weeks; both recommend Tdap in every pregnancy.

source_2_title: Update on immunization in pregnancy with Tdap vaccine
source_2_publisher: Public Health Agency of Canada / Canada.ca

stem: Indicate whether each teaching statement about maternal Tdap is Indicated or Not indicated.
options: {"columns": ["Indicated", "Not indicated"], "rows": [{"key": "R1", "text": "Recommend Tdap during every pregnancy, even if Tdap was given previously"}, {"key": "R2", "text": "Explain that vaccination in pregnancy helps protect the newborn from pertussis in early infancy"}, {"key": "R3", "text": "State that Tdap is ideally timed in the third trimester (about 27–36 weeks; NACI often cites 27–32)"}, {"key": "R4", "text": "Tell the client a dose 5 years ago means no Tdap is ever needed again in future pregnancies"}, {"key": "R5", "text": "Advise delaying all Tdap until the infant finishes kindergarten regardless of pregnancy"}]}
rationales:
R1: Indicated. CDC and NACI: every pregnancy irrespective of prior Tdap.
R2: Indicated. Purpose is newborn protection via maternal antibodies (CDC/NACI).
R3: Indicated. CDC early 27–36; NACI ideally 27–32 — both third-trimester windows.
R4: Not indicated. Prior dose does not replace every-pregnancy dosing.
R5: Not indicated. Delaying until childhood misses infant protection.

stem: Which action best describes medication reconciliation at a care transition?
options:
A) Create/verify a complete current medication list (including OTCs) and compare it with new orders to find and resolve discrepancies
B) Skip home medications and chart only whatever is easiest to remember from shift report
C) Reconcile only brand-name drugs and ignore vitamins, supplements, and OTC products
D) Perform reconciliation solely at annual wellness visits, never at admission or discharge
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: identify/verify accurate list (name, dose, frequency, route, why) including OTCs/vitamins/supplements; compare to provider list at any transition. AHRQ MATCH: single shared medication list as one source of truth for ordering/reconciliation across disciplines.
B: Incorrect. Incomplete lists drive transition errors.
C: Incorrect. OTCs/vitamins/supplements must be included (OpenStax).
D: Incorrect. Reconciliation is required at admission, transfer, discharge, and related transitions.
topic: Medication reconciliation at care transitions — compare complete home list to orders

source_1_section: Guiding Principles; One Source of Truth

stem: At hospital admission, indicate whether each medication-reconciliation action is Indicated or Not indicated.
options: {"columns": ["Indicated", "Not indicated"], "rows": [{"key": "R1", "text": "Obtain a complete list of prescription drugs, OTCs, vitamins, and supplements with dose/frequency/route"}, {"key": "R2", "text": "Compare the home list with admission orders to identify omissions, duplications, or dosing errors"}, {"key": "R3", "text": "Use one shared, updatable medication list as the reference point for the team"}, {"key": "R4", "text": "Ignore discrepancies because 'the pharmacy will notice eventually'"}, {"key": "R5", "text": "Omit reconciliation at transfer/discharge because admission paperwork already exists"}]}
rationales:
R1: Indicated. OpenStax requires complete list including OTCs/vitamins/supplements.
R2: Indicated. OpenStax: compare lists and scrutinize duplications/incorrect dosages/omissions; AHRQ centers reconciliation on that comparison.
R3: Indicated. AHRQ MATCH: one source of truth shared by all disciplines.
R4: Not indicated. Discrepancies must be identified and resolved, not deferred passively.
R5: Not indicated. Reconciliation is needed at each transition (admission, transfer, discharge).
topic: NGN matrix — medication reconciliation actions indicated vs not
